This lab moved from what the camera sees to where, and how many:

Part 1: the pre-installed YOLOX-Nano detector, first on uploaded images (Object Detection Brick) and then on a live camera feed (Video Object Detection Brick), with the annotated video streamed to the browser.
Path A: a custom box-and-wheel detector, trained in Edge Impulse as both FOMO and YOLO, checked on static images, with the model info, detections, and latency printed in the log.
Path B: the same model on the live camera, with detections turned into counts per class and sent over Bridge RPC to the MCU, which displays them on the LED matrix.

Key takeaways:

Detection = classification + localization. It is evaluated with IoU and mAP, not accuracy alone, and the confidence threshold is the main knob that trades false positives for false negatives.
FOMO and YOLO answer different questions. FOMO gives where, fast. YOLO adds how big, and on the test images it also counted far more reliably, at about 1.6 (Nano) to 2.5 (Small) times FOMO’s end-to-end latency. Choose by the information and accuracy the application needs.
Measure on the board, not in the estimate. Edge Impulse’s latency estimates missed in both directions (11 ms vs. 160 ms measured for FOMO, 1,841 ms vs. 331 ms for YOLO-Pro Small).
The Bricks hide the inference pipeline, including NMS and drawing, so the engineering moves to what the application does with the detections.
Live detection needs an explicit “nothing seen” state. The Video Object Detection Brick is silent on empty frames; a timeout turns that silence into “zero”.
Keep hardware calls in one place. Callbacks record state; a single loop talks to the MCU, and only when something changed.

Detection is also where the vision labs meet the generative ones: a fast detector can find where to look, and the model from the Vision-Language Models lab can then describe what is there, on a crop instead of the whole frame, at a fraction of the cost. Building that pipeline is a natural next project.

title: Object Detection
text:
The Image Classification lab trained a classifier and deployed it to the Arduino UNO Q, first on static images and then on a live camera feed, with the result driving the LED matrix over Bridge. This lab takes the next step in computer vision: object detection.
A classifier answers one question about the whole image: what is this? A detector answers two questions for every object it finds: what is it, and where is it? That second answer is what makes counting, tracking, sorting, and spatial reasoning possible.
This lab has two parts:

Part 1 runs the UNO Q’s pre-installed object detection examples. The first is a static image detector: a photo uploaded through a web browser comes back with bounding boxes drawn on it. The second runs the same model on a live camera feed.
Part 2 builds a custom object detector with Edge Impulse Studio, trained to find boxes and wheels on a workbench, and deploys it to the UNO Q with App Lab Bricks, first for static images and then for live webcam inference.

As before, the lab uses the UNO Q’s dual-brain architecture: Python on the MPU for AI inference and an Arduino sketch on the MCU for physical feedback. This time the MCU does not just show a label. It shows a count of each object type on the LED matrix, updated as objects enter and leave the camera’s view.



Understand how object detection differs from image classification, and how detectors are evaluated (IoU, mAP).
Run the pre-installed Object Detection and Video Object Detection Bricks.
Label a bounding-box dataset and train FOMO and YOLO models in Edge Impulse Studio.
Deploy a custom detector through App Lab Bricks, on static images and on a live camera feed.
Turn detections into counts and send them to the MCU over Bridge RPC.
Handle the “nothing detected” case in a live detection app.

title: Object Detection
text:
Object detection builds on image classification but extends it in an important way:

Image classification assigns a single label to the entire image and answers: “What is the main object or scene in this image?”
Object detection identifies and locates multiple objects in an image and answers: “Which objects are in this image, and where is each one?” Its output is a list of predictions, each with a class label, a confidence score, and a location.

 
A detector therefore combines two tasks:

Localization: finding where each object is, usually as a rectangular bounding box.
Classification: deciding what each localized object is, exactly as a classifier would, but per region.

This makes detection harder than classification. An image can contain several objects of different classes, at different sizes, partially hidden behind each other, against a cluttered background, and an edge application usually needs all of that in real time.


Early detectors worked in two stages: first propose regions that might contain an object, then classify each region (R-CNN and its descendants). They are accurate but too slow for an edge device.
Every model in this lab is a single-stage detector, which predicts locations and classes in one forward pass through the network:

YOLO (You Only Look Once) divides the image into a grid and predicts boxes and classes for every cell at once. It is the family behind the UNO Q’s pre-installed model (YOLOX).
SSD MobileNet pairs a MobileNet backbone with a Single Shot Detector head.
FOMO (Faster Objects, More Objects), developed by Edge Impulse, drops the bounding box entirely and predicts only each object’s centroid. Section 0.7.1 looks at it in more detail.




Accuracy alone does not describe a detector, because a prediction can have the right class in the wrong place. Three measures matter:

Intersection over Union (IoU) measures how well a predicted box overlaps the ground-truth box drawn by a human: the area of their intersection divided by the area of their union. An IoU of 1.0 is a perfect match. A detection usually counts as correct when IoU ≥ 0.5.

 

Mean Average Precision (mAP) combines classification and localization into one number. For each class, precision is averaged across recall levels, and the result is averaged across classes. “mAP@0.5” means a detection counts as correct when its IoU is at least 0.5. Edge Impulse reports mAP for YOLO and SSD models.

 

Frames per second (FPS), or its inverse, latency per frame. At the edge, a model that is 3% more accurate but three times slower is often the wrong choice.




A detector often reports the same object several times, with slightly different boxes and confidences. Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) cleans this up: keep the most confident box, discard every other box of the same class that overlaps it beyond an IoU threshold, and repeat. On the UNO Q, NMS is not something to implement: the Edge Impulse model file (.eim) already includes it, so the Bricks receive the final, de-duplicated list.



The Raspberry Pi Object Detection lab, and the object detection chapters of EdgeML Made Easy, train this same box-and-wheel detector and run it on a Raspberry Pi. The UNO Q approach differs as follows:



Table 3: Object detection on the Raspberry Pi and the UNO Q.










Aspect

USB webcam (or CSI via the Media Carrier)

On the Pi, the whole inference pipeline is written by hand, which is the best way to understand it. On the UNO Q, the Bricks hide that pipeline, so the work moves to what the application does with the detections.

title: Object Detection
text:
The UNO Q ships with a general-purpose detector: a YOLOX-Nano model trained on the COCO dataset, which recognizes 80 everyday classes such as person, cup, cell phone, bottle, chair, cat, and dog. Two examples use it.



Table 4: The pre-installed object detection examples.










Example
Bricks
Input




Detect objects on images
object_detection and web_ui
Static image uploaded in the browser


Detect Objects on Camera
video_object_detection and web_ui
Live USB webcam






First, confirm the exact App IDs on the board, since they can change between App Lab releases:
arduino-app-cli app list --examples | grep -i detect
 
The two used here are examples:inspirational/object-detection (Detect objects on images) and examples:inspirational/video-generic-object-detection (Detect Objects on Camera). The list also shows short, single-purpose examples for each Brick, under examples:bricks/arduino/object_detection/... and examples:bricks/arduino/video_object_detection/.... One of them, 02_count_objects, counts detections per label, which is the starting point for Section 0.10.


The static image example works exactly like the image classification example, with one difference: the board sends back an image with the boxes drawn on it, not just a list of labels.
Browser (your PC)                          UNO Q (MPU / Python)
+-------------------+                     +-------------------------+
|                   |   Upload image      |                         |
|  Web UI (port     | ------------------> |  ObjectDetection Brick  |
|  7000)            |   (base64 via       |  (YOLOX-Nano, COCO)     |
|                   |    WebSocket)       |                         |
|  Shows annotated  | <------------------ |  draw_bounding_boxes()  |
|  image + count    |   PNG with boxes    |  -> base64 PNG          |
+-------------------+                     +-------------------------+




This step does not need a webcam.

arduino-app-cli app start examples:inspirational/object-detection
 



On the host computer, open http://<UNO_Q_IP_ADDRESS>:7000. Upload a photo with several everyday objects in it (a desk with a cup, a phone, and a bottle works well), set the confidence threshold slider, and click Run detection.
 
Try the same image at different thresholds. At a high threshold (0.7), only the objects the model is sure about appear. At a low one (0.2), more objects appear, along with false positives. That slider is the single most important tuning knob in any detection application, and Part 2 returns to it.

As with the classification example, the results go to the browser over WebSocket, not to the terminal log.




cat /var/lib/arduino-app-cli/examples/inspirational/common/\
object-detection/python/main.py

Where the examples live. The App ID examples:inspirational/object-detection maps to the folder /var/lib/arduino-app-cli/examples/inspirational/common/object-detection. The common/ level holds examples that run on every board, and board-specific ones sit next to it, such as platform_unoq/. If a path in this lab does not exist on the board, find it with sudo find /var/lib/arduino-app-cli/examples -type d -name "object-detection".

The core of it, in a simplified excerpt:
from arduino.app_utils import *
from arduino.app_bricks.web_ui import WebUI
from arduino.app_bricks.object_detection import ObjectDetection

object_detection = ObjectDetection()

def on_detect_objects(client_id, data):
    image_bytes = base64.b64decode(data.get('image'))
    pil_image = Image.open(io.BytesIO(image_bytes))
    confidence = data.get('confidence', 0.5)

    results = object_detection.detect(pil_image,
                                      confidence=confidence)
    img_with_boxes = object_detection.draw_bounding_boxes(
        pil_image, results)
    # ... encode img_with_boxes as a base64 PNG into `response` ...
    ui.send_message('detection_result', response)

ui = WebUI()
ui.on_message('detect_objects', on_detect_objects)
App.run()
Compared to the classification example:

ObjectDetection() replaces ImageClassification(), and detect() replaces classify().
draw_bounding_boxes() is new. The Brick draws the boxes and labels, so the application never handles pixel coordinates unless it needs to.
The structure is otherwise identical: event-driven, no user_loop, no Bridge, no MCU.

The result of detect() is a dictionary with a single key, detection, holding one entry per object found:
{
  "detection": [
    {"class_name": "cup", "confidence": "87.50",
     "bounding_box_xyxy": [41.0, 112.0, 98.0, 180.0]},
    {"class_name": "cell phone", "confidence": "64.12",
     "bounding_box_xyxy": [150.0, 60.0, 210.0, 170.0]}
  ]
}
The values above are illustrative, but the format is exact. Two details matter:

bounding_box_xyxy is [x1, y1, x2, y2]: the top-left and bottom-right corners, in pixels.
confidence in the result is a string, formatted as a percentage from 0 to 100 ("87.50"). The confidence parameter passed to detect() is a float from 0.0 to 1.0. Mixing the two scales is an easy mistake, so convert with float(obj["confidence"]) / 100 before comparing.

Stop the example when done:
arduino-app-cli app stop examples:inspirational/object-detection
 



Connect the webcam through the powered hub and start the second example:
arduino-app-cli app start \
  examples:inspirational/video-generic-object-detection
Open http://<UNO_Q_IP_ADDRESS>:7000 again. This time the page shows the live camera feed with bounding boxes drawn in real time, each labeled with its class and confidence. On the right are a Confidence slider, a Feedback panel, and a running list of Recent detections with their confidence and timestamp. Point the camera at a cup, a phone, or a person.
 
The Feedback panel is the example’s “special reaction”: when one of a handful of COCO classes appears (cat, cell phone, clock, cup, dog, or potted plant), it shows a short message for that object. Here, a cup on the desk triggered “Need a break?”. Note also that the confidence slider is set to 0.51, and the cup is detected at only 0.55–0.57: raise the threshold slightly and the cup disappears, while the keyboard (0.87–0.89) stays. That is the threshold trade-off from Step 2, now happening live.
The architecture has one extra piece:
USB webcam -> VideoObjectDetection Brick -> model runner (YOLOX-Nano)
                                             |                \
                                 detections (WebSocket)   annotated video
                                             |           (port 4912, /embed)
                                on_detect_all(callback)          |
                                             |                   |
                               ui.send_message("detection")      |
                                             \                  /
                                              Browser (port 7000)
The video with boxes is produced by the model runner itself and served on port 4912; the web page simply embeds http://<UNO_Q_IP>:4912/embed in an iframe. The Python code never touches a frame. It only receives the detections, through callbacks. The source:
cat /var/lib/arduino-app-cli/examples/inspirational/common/\
video-generic-object-detection/python/main.py
from arduino.app_utils import App
from arduino.app_bricks.web_ui import WebUI
from arduino.app_bricks.video_objectdetection import (
    VideoObjectDetection,
)
from datetime import datetime, UTC

ui = WebUI()
detection_stream = VideoObjectDetection(confidence=0.5,
                                        debounce_sec=0.0)

ui.on_message(
    "override_th",
    lambda sid, threshold: detection_stream.override_threshold(threshold),
)

def send_detections_to_ui(detections: dict):
  for key, values in detections.items():
    for value in values:
      entry = {
        "content": key,
        "confidence": value.get("confidence"),
        "timestamp": datetime.now(UTC).isoformat()
      }
      ui.send_message("detection", message=entry)

detection_stream.on_detect_all(send_detections_to_ui)

App.run()
Note the shape of detections. It is grouped by label, with a list of every instance of that label in the frame:
{
  "cup":    [{"confidence": 0.91, "bounding_box_xyxy": (41, 112, 98, 180)}],
  "person": [{"confidence": 0.88, "bounding_box_xyxy": (...)},
             {"confidence": 0.62, "bounding_box_xyxy": (...)}]
}
That grouping makes counting trivial: len(detections["person"]) is the number of people in the frame. Note also that here confidence is a float from 0 to 1, unlike the static Brick’s percentage string.
The slider calls override_threshold(), which changes the threshold inside the running model without restarting the app.
Stop the example:
arduino-app-cli app stop \
  examples:inspirational/video-generic-object-detection



As with image classification, both examples are also available in App Lab on the host computer: connect to the UNO Q over Wi-Fi, open Inspirations, and choose Detect objects on images or Detect Objects on Camera. The camera example must run in Network Mode, because the webcam occupies the hub. While an app runs, its card shows Running, and the bottom bar shows its name with a Stop button.
 
Two more Inspirations use the same detector and are worth a look:

Detect Objects on Smartphone Camera runs the same live detection on a phone’s camera instead of a USB webcam. Without a webcam or a powered hub, this is a way to try live detection right away.
Object Hunting turns detection into a game: the app gives a list of objects to find and show to the camera.




The pre-installed detector is impressive, but it has the same limitations the classification example had:

It knows only COCO’s 80 classes and has never seen the objects of a specific project.
Results stay in the browser. Nothing physical happens.
YOLOX-Nano is sized for general use, not for the speed a given application might need.

Part 2 trains a model on custom objects, deploys it with the same two Bricks, and connects it to the MCU.

title: Object Detection
text:
Part 2 reuses the project from the Raspberry Pi object detection lab and the EdgeML Made Easy chapter, so the two boards can be compared directly.


The scenario is an industrial facility that must sort and count wheels and special boxes passing in front of a camera.
 
Each image may contain any number of boxes and wheels, or none at all:

box
wheel
(background, meaning no objects, is handled implicitly)

The system should continuously capture frames, detect every object, count them by class, and show the counts on the UNO Q’s LED matrix:
USB webcam -> VideoObjectDetection Brick -> custom EI model
                                                  |
                                {"Box": [...], "Wheel": [...]}
                                                  |
                                     count per class (Python)
                                                  |
                            Bridge.call("show_counts", boxes, wheels)
                                                  |
                                        MCU (Arduino sketch)
                                        -> LED matrix: boxes | wheels
As in the Image Classification lab, the custom model is deployed in two steps:

Path A (Section 0.8) uses the Object Detection Brick, reusing the static image example with the custom model. It is quick to set up and ideal for checking the model.
Path B (Section 0.9) uses the Video Object Detection Brick for live camera inference, and Section 0.10 adds counting and MCU actuation. This is the path for real projects.

title: Object Detection
text:
An object detection dataset needs more than images in labeled folders: every object in every image needs a bounding box and a label. That makes labeling the most time-consuming part of the project.


The labeled, preprocessed dataset from the Raspberry Pi project is public on Roboflow Universe: box-versus-wheel-auto-dataset. It has 153 images at 320×320, already split into train, validation, and test sets, with augmentation applied.
Download it in YOLOv8 format (a zip file). Inside, each split has an images folder and a labels folder. Every image_id.jpg has a matching image_id.txt with one line per object, class_id x_center y_center width height, normalized to the image size. data.yaml maps the class IDs to names: 0 is box and 1 is wheel (alphabetical order).
 



A model trained on the actual objects, under the actual lighting, performs better on the actual bench. To capture on the UNO Q, reuse the capture_images.py script from the Image Classification lab, with two changes: set label = "box-wheel" (the real labels are added later, per object), and capture at 320×320 or crop to square afterward.

Capture about 60 images. Vary the angles, backgrounds, distances, and lighting, and vary how many objects appear in each frame, from zero to several of each kind. Include some frames with no objects at all.

Copy the images to the host computer (scp -r arduino@<UNO_Q_IP>:~/dataset ./dataset) and label them. Labeling works directly in Edge Impulse Studio (Data acquisition > Labeling queue), or in Roboflow, as in the Raspberry Pi project, which offers auto-labeling and exports to several formats:

Create a project (for example, “box-versus-wheel”) and upload the raw images.
Draw a box around every object, or use Auto Label / Label Assist and correct its suggestions.

 

Mark background-only images with the Null tool, so they are kept with no annotations.

 

Split into train, validation, and test, resize to 320×320 (stretch), and add augmentation (for example, ±15° rotation, crop, brightness, and exposure).

 

Export in YOLOv8 format.


Why not label in Edge Impulse directly? For a small dataset, it is the shortest path. A dataset labeled on a free Edge Impulse account cannot be exported for training elsewhere, though, while a Roboflow export can also train a YOLO model with Ultralytics, as in the Raspberry Pi lab.





In Edge Impulse Studio, create a new project (for example, “UNO-Q - Custom Object Detection”).
On the Dashboard, under Project info, set the Labeling method to Bounding boxes (object detection).
Go to Data acquisition > Upload data. Choose Select a folder, pick the train folder (with its images and labels subfolders), set the label format to YOLO TXT, choose the Training category, and upload.
Repeat for the test and valid folders, into the Test category.

 

Check the label names. After uploading, open a few samples. If the objects are labeled 0 and 1 instead of box and wheel, the class names did not come across. Rename them now (in Data acquisition, filter by label and use Edit labels), because these strings are exactly what the Python callbacks match against later.

 

Shortcut: the project used in this lab is public: UNO Q - Custom Object Detection. Click Clone to copy it, dataset and impulses included, and compare the results.

title: Object Detection
text:
This lab trains two models on the same dataset and compares them on the board: FOMO, the fastest option, and YOLO, the most precise. Edge Impulse’s Experiments feature lets one project hold both impulses side by side.


FOMO (Faster Objects, More Objects) uses a MobileNetV2 backbone to extract a feature map, then classifies each cell of a coarse grid instead of regressing box coordinates. The image is divided by a factor of 8, so a 160×160 input becomes a 20×20 grid, and each cell answers “is the center of a box, or of a wheel, here?”
 
Neighboring cells that fire for the same class are merged into one object, located at their centroid.
 
The trade-off is clear:

What FOMO gains: speed and memory. The FOMO model itself is much smaller and faster than SSD or YOLO, and it handles many small, well-separated objects well. (In an application, the end-to-end gap is smaller than the models alone suggest, as Section 0.8 measures.)
What FOMO loses: object size. FOMO reports where an object is, not how big it is. The “box” it returns is a cell-sized square around the centroid, not a fitted rectangle. The Brick’s draw_bounding_boxes() knows this: for a FOMO model, it draws circles instead of rectangles.

For counting boxes and wheels, size does not matter, so FOMO is a good fit. Anything that needs an object’s extent (distance estimation, cropping an object for a second model, overlap checks) needs YOLO.




Go to Create impulse. When asked for a target device, choose Arduino UNO Q (this only affects the latency estimates, not the training).
Set the input to 160×160, resize mode Squash.
Add an Image processing block and an Object Detection (Images) learning block.
Click Save Impulse.
In the Image tab, set Color depth to RGB, then click Save parameters and Generate features.
In the Object detection tab, choose FOMO (Faster Objects, More Objects) MobileNetV2 0.35.
Train with 60 epochs, learning rate 0.001, and no data augmentation if the dataset is the Roboflow one, which is already augmented.

Edge Impulse reports an F1 score for FOMO rather than mAP, because there are no boxes to compute IoU against, only centroids.
 

For FOMO, this lab uses the float32 version. The model is small in memory and fast, and in training the quantized (int8) version’s F1 score dropped below 0.70.





Go to Experiments and create a new impulse.
Set the input to 320×320 (the resolution of the Roboflow dataset).
Add Image and Object Detection (Images) blocks and generate RGB features as before.
In the Object detection tab, choose a YOLO architecture. At the time of writing, Edge Impulse offers its own YOLO-Pro family. Start with the Small variant (6.9M parameters).
Train, starting with 30 epochs (YOLO benefits from more, given the time).

Edge Impulse reports mAP@0.5 (and mAP@[0.5:0.95]) for this model.

For YOLO-Pro Small, this lab deploys the quantized (int8) version. Check its mAP in the Model version selector before deploying: if it is close to the float32 value, int8 is the better choice, because it is smaller and usually faster on the UNO Q’s CPU.

 



Go to Model testing, select the version to deploy (float32 for FOMO, int8 for YOLO), and click Classify all for each impulse. Look at the test images where the models disagree: FOMO typically misses objects that touch each other (their centroids fall in the same cell), while YOLO is more likely than expected to miss very small objects at 320×320.
Record the results for comparison with the on-board measurements in Section 0.11.



Table 5: Test-set results and Edge Impulse latency estimates.











Model
Input
Metric (test set)
Estimated latency (EI)




FOMO MobileNetV2 0.35
160×160
F1 = 0.82
11 ms


YOLO-Pro Small (6.9M)
320×320
mAP@0.5 = 0.99
1,841 ms







F1 and mAP are not directly comparable. FOMO’s F1 counts a detection as correct when its centroid lands on the right object; YOLO’s mAP@0.5 also requires the predicted box to overlap the labeled box by at least 50%. So 0.82 against 0.99 does not mean YOLO is “20% better”. Compare the models on what the application needs, here whether the counts are right, and on latency.


A smaller YOLO is also an option. The smallest variant, YOLO-Pro Pico (682K parameters), would have a much lower latency, probably at the cost of some mAP. When boxes are needed rather than centroids but YOLO-Pro Small turns out too slow, train a smaller variant as a third experiment and compare. YOLO-Pro Nano (2.4M parameters, int8) kept mAP@0.5 at 0.99 on the validation set, counted all six test images correctly, and ran more than twice as fast as Small on the live stream (see Section 0.8.8 and Section 0.11). As the next section shows, measure on the board before deciding: the Edge Impulse estimate above turned out far too pessimistic.

title: Object Detection
text:
This path puts the custom model into the static image example from Part 1. It is limited to uploads, but it is the fastest way to see the model running on the board and to inspect what it returns.


cp -r /var/lib/arduino-app-cli/examples/inspirational/common/\
object-detection/ ~/ArduinoApps/my-detector-bricks
The copy appears in App Lab’s Apps list, but still as Detect objects on images: App Lab shows the name: field from app.yaml, not the folder name, and cp copied the example’s app.yaml unchanged. Give it its own name:
sed -i 's/^name: .*/name: My Detector (Custom Images)/' \
  ~/ArduinoApps/my-detector-bricks/app.yaml
Alternatively, in Arduino App Lab, copy Detect objects on images to My Apps under a new name, which sets the name automatically.
 



This is the same flow as in the Image Classification lab:

In the copied app, open Bricks > Object Detection > AI models and click Train new AI model.
Log in to the Arduino / Edge Impulse account and open the object detection project.
Make sure the impulse to deploy (start with FOMO) is the active one.
In Deployment, select Arduino UNO Q as the target. Under model optimizations, choose the same version tested earlier (float32, unoptimized), and click Build.
When the build finishes, click Go to Arduino to send the model to App Lab.

 



In the app’s AI Models area, download the model to the UNO Q and select it. app.yaml is updated to point to it:
name: My Detector (Custom Images)
icon: 🏞️
description: Custom object detection in the browser
bricks:
- arduino:web_ui: {}
- arduino:object_detection:
    model: ei-model-<PROJECT_ID>-1
App Lab stores the model in its own folder, /home/arduino/.arduino-bricks/models/custom-ei/ei-model-<PROJECT_ID>-<VERSION>/.



The App Lab flow above works, but it takes several hops between Edge Impulse, App Lab, and the board. There is a shorter path: download the model file and point the Brick at it.
It works because of how the Brick runs the model. The Object Detection Brick starts the Edge Impulse runner in a container with --model-file ${EI_OBJ_DETECTION_MODEL}, and that container can see the folder /home/arduino/.arduino-bricks/ei-models. Any variable set in a Brick’s variables: block in app.yaml is passed to the container and takes priority over the default model.

In Edge Impulse Deployment, select Arduino UNO Q (or Linux (AARCH64)), choose float32, and click Build. The browser downloads a file such as uno-q-custom-object-detection-linux-aarch64-v12-fomo-mobilenetv2.eim.
Copy it to the board (from the host computer):

scp ~/Downloads/uno-q-custom-object-detection-linux-aarch64-v12-\
fomo-mobilenetv2.eim arduino@<UNO_Q_IP>:~/

On the UNO Q, move it into the models folder under a short name, and make it executable (an .eim file is a program, and the runner needs to execute it):

mkdir -p ~/.arduino-bricks/ei-models
mv ~/uno-q-custom-object-detection-linux-aarch64-v12-fomo-mobilenetv2.eim \
  ~/.arduino-bricks/ei-models/box-wheel-fomo.eim
chmod +x ~/.arduino-bricks/ei-models/box-wheel-fomo.eim

Edit app.yaml: remove the model: line and set the variable instead. Removing model: is not optional. When it is present, the CLI applies that model’s configuration, which mounts only the App Lab model’s own folder into the container, so the runner cannot see ei-models/ and fails with ENOENT: no such file or directory. Selecting a model in App Lab writes the line back, so check app.yaml again after going back to App Lab.
Any terminal editor works. With nano app.yaml, place the cursor on a line and press Ctrl+K to delete it, then type the new lines and save with Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X. The result:

name: My Detector (Custom Images)
icon: 🏞️
description: Custom object detection in the browser
bricks:
- arduino:web_ui: {}
- arduino:object_detection:
    variables:
      EI_OBJ_DETECTION_MODEL: >-
        /home/arduino/.arduino-bricks/ei-models/box-wheel-fomo.eim

Start the app:

cd ~/ArduinoApps/my-detector-bricks
arduino-app-cli app start .
 
Upload an image in the browser: if the labels are Box and Wheel, the Brick is running the custom model. COCO classes such as cup or person mean the variable did not take effect; check the path and the chmod. If the app fails to start with container ... ei-obj-detection-runner-1 is unhealthy, read the runner’s own log, which shows the actual error:
docker logs --tail 20 my-detector-bricks-ei-obj-detection-runner-1
This option has a second advantage: switching models becomes a one-line change. Copy the YOLO .eim next to the FOMO one, and the two can be compared by editing app.yaml and restarting the app.



Before running, replace python/main.py with a version that also prints what the model expects and what it finds. The model info is worth reading once: it gives the exact label strings the callbacks must use, the input size, and the model type (object_detection for YOLO, constrained_object_detection for FOMO).
from arduino.app_utils import App
from arduino.app_bricks.web_ui import WebUI
from arduino.app_bricks.object_detection import ObjectDetection
from PIL import Image
import io
import base64
import time

object_detection = ObjectDetection()


def print_model_info(detector):
    info = detector.get_model_info()
    if info is None:
        print("Failed to retrieve model info.")
        return
    print("Model info:")
    for attr in dir(info):
        if not attr.startswith("_") and not callable(getattr(info, attr)):
            print(f"  {attr}: {getattr(info, attr)}")


def encode_png(pil_image):
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    pil_image.save(buf, format="PNG")
    return base64.b64encode(buf.getvalue()).decode("utf-8")


def on_detect_objects(client_id, data):
    try:
        image_data = data.get("image")
        confidence = data.get("confidence", 0.5)
        if not image_data:
            ui.send_message("detection_error",
                            {"error": "No image data"})
            return

        pil_image = Image.open(io.BytesIO(base64.b64decode(image_data)))

        start = time.perf_counter()
        results = object_detection.detect(pil_image,
                                          confidence=confidence)
        latency_ms = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000

        if results is None:
            ui.send_message("detection_error",
                            {"error": "No results returned"})
            return

        detections = results.get("detection", [])
        counts = {}
        for obj in detections:
            name = obj["class_name"]
            counts[name] = counts.get(name, 0) + 1
            box = [round(v) for v in obj["bounding_box_xyxy"]]
            print(f"  {name:6s} {float(obj['confidence']):5.1f}%  "
                  f"box={box}")
        print(f"Counts: {counts}  |  Latency: {latency_ms:.1f} ms\n",
              flush=True)

        annotated = object_detection.draw_bounding_boxes(pil_image,
                                                         results)
        if annotated is None:
            annotated = pil_image
        ui.send_message("detection_result", {
            "success": True,
            "result_image": encode_png(annotated),
            "detection_count": len(detections),
            "processing_time": f"{latency_ms:.2f} ms",
        })

    except Exception as e:
        ui.send_message("detection_error", {"error": str(e)})


print_model_info(object_detection)
ui = WebUI()
ui.on_message("detect_objects", on_detect_objects)

App.run()



cd ~/ArduinoApps/my-detector-bricks
arduino-app-cli app start .
In a second terminal, follow the logs:
cd ~/ArduinoApps/my-detector-bricks
arduino-app-cli app logs . --follow
Open http://<UNO_Q_IP>:7000 and upload test images of boxes and wheels (the test folder of the dataset is a good source). For the FOMO model, the browser shows circles at each object’s centroid. The log shows each detection, the counts, and the latency.
 
Here the FOMO model got everything right: three boxes and one wheel, each marked by a circle at its centroid. Note the labels, Box and Wheel, with capital letters: these are the exact strings the code must match in Section 0.10.
More test images, though, quickly show FOMO’s limits. Two failures are typical:

Missed objects. In the image below, the model found three of the four wheels and one of the three boxes. The misses are objects cut by the image edge, partly hidden behind others, or seen from an unusual angle.

 

One object, several centroids. When an object is large in the frame, it covers many cells of FOMO’s grid, and separate groups of cells can each report a centroid. The single box below was counted three times.

 
Both explain why the F1 score in Table 5 was 0.82, and both matter for counting: a miss lowers the count, a split raises it. Keep the objects at roughly the distance and size they had in the training images, and if they must appear large in the frame, prefer YOLO, which fits one box to each object.
The log for six test images, starting with the one above:
 
Three things are worth reading in it:

The model info confirms what was trained: a 160×160 input, two labels, ['Box', 'Wheel'], and model_type: constrained_object_detection, which is how Edge Impulse identifies a FOMO model (a YOLO model reports object_detection).
The boxes are small, fixed-size squares (16 or 32 pixels wide), centered on each object, because FOMO reports centroids, not object sizes. Their coordinates also go up to 288, beyond the model’s 160×160 input: the Brick returns them in the uploaded image’s pixel space, so they can be used directly on the original image.
The first inference is the slowest. The first and third images are the same file, with identical detections, yet they took 232.6 ms and 159.4 ms. The first call after the app starts pays a one-time warm-up cost. Ignoring it, the other five took between 146 and 186 ms, about 160 ms on average, against an estimate of about 11 ms in Edge Impulse.


Latency here includes more than the model. The time measured around detect() also covers encoding the image, sending it to the model runner container over HTTP, resizing it to 160×160, and returning the result. The model itself is a small fraction of the 160 ms. When measuring, always discard the first call and average several. That end-to-end number is the one the application actually sees, and it is why Edge Impulse’s estimate alone is not enough to choose a model.




Deploy the YOLO-Pro Small impulse the same way, this time choosing Quantized (int8) under model optimizations. With the direct .eim option, this is a one-line change in app.yaml (point EI_OBJ_DETECTION_MODEL to box-wheel-yolo.eim) and an app restart. Copy and rename the file as for FOMO:
mv ~/uno-q-custom-object-detection-linux-aarch64-v15-yolo-pro-small.eim \
  ~/.arduino-bricks/ei-models/box-wheel-yolo.eim
chmod +x ~/.arduino-bricks/ei-models/box-wheel-yolo.eim
Upload the same test images.
The browser now shows fitted rectangles, and the two scenes where FOMO failed come out right. The single large box is counted once:
 
And the crowded scene, where FOMO found three wheels and one box, is now complete, with four wheels and three boxes:
 
YOLO counted all six test images correctly, against two for FOMO. The log shows why it costs more:
 

The model info reports a 320×320 input and model_type: object_detection, the YOLO family. The labels are the same, so the Python code does not change.
The boxes now have real sizes, fitted to each object.
The latency is about 331 ms on average after the warm-up call (536 ms), about twice FOMO’s 160 ms.

That last number deserves a second look. Edge Impulse estimated 1,841 ms for this model, more than five times what the board actually measured. For FOMO, the estimate was 11 ms against 160 ms measured. The estimates were wrong in both directions: one ignores the fixed cost of moving the image to the runner, and the other did not anticipate how fast the runner executes this model on the UNO Q. Always measure on the board before choosing a model.



If YOLO-Pro Small counts well but more speed is needed, train a smaller variant and compare it on the board. Here, YOLO-Pro Nano (2.4M parameters) was trained, deployed as Quantized (int8), and installed next to the others:
mv ~/uno-q-custom-object-detection-linux-aarch64-v16-yolo-pro-nano.eim \
  ~/.arduino-bricks/ei-models/box-wheel-yolo-nano.eim
chmod +x ~/.arduino-bricks/ei-models/box-wheel-yolo-nano.eim
With EI_OBJ_DETECTION_MODEL pointed to box-wheel-yolo-nano.eim and the app restarted, it also counted all six test images correctly, including the crowded scene:
 
In the timing script of Section 0.11, it took about 221 ms per image, against 342 ms for Small in the same measurement. Table 6 compares all the models side by side.

title: Object Detection
text:
Path B moves to the live camera. Rather than building a web page from scratch, it starts from the Detect Objects on Camera example, which already streams the annotated video to the browser, and swaps in the custom model.


cp -r /var/lib/arduino-app-cli/examples/inspirational/common/\
video-generic-object-detection/ ~/ArduinoApps/box-wheel-counter
sed -i 's/^name: .*/name: Box Wheel Counter/' \
  ~/ArduinoApps/box-wheel-counter/app.yaml
As in Path A, the sed line renames the app in App Lab’s list. Alternatively, copy Detect Objects on Camera to My Apps in App Lab, naming it Box Wheel Counter.



From here on, the lab uses YOLO-Pro Nano, which counted every test image correctly in Path A and is the fastest of the YOLO models. (YOLO-Pro Small and FOMO work too, with the same code; only the model file changes.)
Open Bricks > Video Object Detection > AI Models and select the YOLO-Pro Nano model deployed in Path A (the same .eim works with both Bricks). app.yaml becomes:
name: Box Wheel Counter
icon: 📽️
description: Count boxes and wheels on a live camera feed
bricks:
- arduino:video_object_detection:
    model: ei-model-<PROJECT_ID>-1
- arduino:web_ui: {}
If the .eim file was loaded directly in Path A, do the same here. The video Brick uses a different variable name, EI_V_OBJ_DETECTION_MODEL, and, as in Path A, there is no model: line. The complete app.yaml is:
name: Box Wheel Counter
icon: 📽️
description: Count boxes and wheels on a live camera feed
bricks:
- arduino:video_object_detection:
    variables:
      EI_V_OBJ_DETECTION_MODEL: >-
        /home/arduino/.arduino-bricks/ei-models/box-wheel-yolo-nano.eim
- arduino:web_ui: {}
Edit it with nano app.yaml, as in Path A (Ctrl+K deletes the model: line).



The example’s main.py is generic: it forwards every detection to the browser, whatever the labels are. So the app already works with the custom model, without changing a line of Python.
cd ~/ArduinoApps/box-wheel-counter
arduino-app-cli app start .
Open http://<UNO_Q_IP>:7000, place boxes and wheels in front of the camera, and watch the detections appear on the video and in the list. Use the slider to find the threshold where real objects are detected reliably and empty background produces nothing.
 
This screenshot was taken with YOLO-Pro Small, before the switch to Nano. With the threshold at 0.76, the model finds the two boxes and the wheel, each with a tight bounding box at about 0.91 confidence. The Box and Wheel labels confirm that the video Brick is running the custom .eim file: EI_V_OBJ_DETECTION_MODEL took effect, even though it is not among the Brick’s declared variables.

The web page’s “special reactions” are keyed to COCO classes (cat, cup, and so on), so they never fire for box or wheel. That is expected.




Before modifying the code, here is what the Brick offers:
class VideoObjectDetection(camera: BaseCamera | None = None,
                           confidence: float = 0.3,
                           debounce_sec: float = 0.0,
                           camera_preview: bool = False)

camera: the camera to use. If None, the default USB camera is opened.
confidence: the minimum confidence (0.0 to 1.0) for a detection to reach the callbacks.
debounce_sec: the minimum time between two triggers for the same label. Useful for alarms (“a wheel appeared”), harmful for counting, which needs every frame. This lab keeps it at 0.
camera_preview: if True, a callback that declares a frame parameter also receives the current camera frame as JPEG bytes, without boxes drawn. Useful for saving snapshots of detections.

There are two ways to receive detections:

on_detect("wheel", callback): called whenever a specific label appears. The callback can take no arguments, or one dict with confidence and bounding_box_xyxy. If a frame has three wheels, it is called three times.
on_detect_all(callback): called once per frame with all detections, grouped by label. This is the one for counting.

One behavior is not obvious from the API, and it matters for this project: neither callback is called when a frame has no detections. When the last box leaves the camera’s view, the code receives nothing at all. It does not receive “zero boxes”; it simply stops hearing from the Brick. The next section deals with that.

title: Object Detection
Object Detection
text:
All the models were measured on the same UNO Q (4 GB) in two ways:

Path A (per image): a small app called ObjectDetection.detect() on six 320×320 images from the dataset, five rounds after one warm-up call, timing each call in Python. This is the end-to-end time the code waits, including the transfer to the model runner.
Path B (live stream): with the Video Object Detection Brick running, a script counted the result messages that the model runner sends for each camera frame over 30 seconds.

These numbers come from a separate timing run, so they differ a little from the first Path A test (about 160 ms for FOMO and 331 ms for YOLO-Pro Small, with a different set of images). Expect run-to-run differences of 10 to 15% in end-to-end timing. A few things stand out:

FOMO runs faster than the camera. The Brick asks the camera for 10 FPS (the log says throttling to requested 10 FPS), and FOMO keeps up with every frame: the runner reports about 23 ms of processing per frame. The rest of the 139 ms in Path A is the trip from Python to the runner and back, not the model.
YOLO-Pro Small gives about 3 counts per second, enough for objects sitting on a bench, and is faster than the pre-installed YOLOX-Nano, which has a larger input and 80 classes.
YOLO-Pro Nano more than doubles the live frame rate of Small (about 7.6 against 3.3 FPS) with the same validation mAP@0.5. In Path A the gain looks smaller (221 against 342 ms), because about 115 ms of every call is the fixed trip to the runner, the same for every model.
The first call is always slower. Ignore it when measuring.

To measure the live frame rate, start the video app and run this script inside its container. It opens a second connection to the runner and counts results for 30 seconds:
# fps.py: run with
#   docker exec -i <app>-main-1 python - < fps.py
import json, time
from websockets.sync.client import connect

with connect("ws://ei-video-obj-detection-runner:4912") as ws:
    stamps = []
    end = time.monotonic() + 30
    while time.monotonic() < end:
        msg = json.loads(ws.recv(timeout=10))
        if msg.get("type") == "classification":
            stamps.append(time.monotonic())

frames = len(stamps) - 1
print(f"{frames / (stamps[-1] - stamps[0]):.2f} FPS")
Unlike the on_detect_all callback, which stays silent on empty frames, the runner sends a result for every frame, so the count is correct whether or not objects are in view. (The live measurements above were taken with an empty scene.)

For this project, the measurements decide it: YOLO-Pro Nano counted every test image correctly and runs at about 7.6 frames per second live, which is why the live counter uses it. YOLO-Pro Small counted just as well, but at 3.3 FPS. FOMO is faster still but miscounted four of six images. FOMO remains the right choice when objects are small and well separated, or when the hardware is much weaker than the UNO Q, as on a microcontroller. The same dataset was trained for the Raspberry Pi in EdgeML Made Easy. There, an SSD MobileNetV2 (320×320) took roughly 0.5 to 1.3 s per image on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, and moving to FOMO cut the latency dramatically. On the UNO Q, at the same 320×320 input, YOLO-Pro Small takes about 0.34 s per image end to end (3.3 FPS live) and YOLO-Pro Nano about 0.22 s (about 7.6 FPS live), and FOMO’s own processing takes about 23 ms per frame. The UNO Q pipeline adds the hop to the model runner, so compare end-to-end times measured on each board, not Edge Impulse’s estimates, before drawing conclusions about the hardware.

title: Object Detection
text:
Train on a custom dataset. Capture and label about 60 images of objects on a real bench (Option B in Section 0.6). Train YOLO-Pro Nano on it and compare it with the model trained on the Roboflow dataset. Which one counts better on that bench, and why?
Threshold sweep. In the live app, try thresholds of 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7. For each, count false positives (blocks lit with no object) and false negatives (objects not counted) over one minute with a fixed arrangement of objects. Which threshold would you ship?
Stabilize the count. The count flickers when an object is at the edge of the frame. Modify main.py so the MCU shows the most frequent count over the last N frames (a mode filter) instead of the latest one. How large must N be before the flicker stops, and how much slower does the display react when an object is added or removed?
Left or right? Use bounding_box_xyxy to decide whether each wheel is on the left or the right half of the image, and show the result on the matrix instead of the class split. Where is “the middle”? In Path A, the static Brick returned coordinates in the uploaded image’s pixels, not the model’s 160×160. Check which space the video Brick uses before hard-coding a value: print a few boxes while moving an object from one edge of the frame to the other.
Log to CSV. Log each change in the counts (timestamp, boxes, wheels) to a CSV file on the UNO Q. After 5 minutes of adding and removing objects, plot the counts over time.
Snapshot on detection. Create the detector with camera_preview=True and declare def on_all_detections(detections, frame). Save a JPEG whenever the wheel count reaches 3. These snapshots are also a cheap way to collect new training data from the real deployment.
FOMO vs. YOLO on touching objects. Place two wheels so that they touch. Compare how both models count them.

title: Object Detection
text:
This lab moved from what the camera sees to where, and how many:

Part 1: the pre-installed YOLOX-Nano detector, first on uploaded images (Object Detection Brick) and then on a live camera feed (Video Object Detection Brick), with the annotated video streamed to the browser.
Path A: a custom box-and-wheel detector, trained in Edge Impulse as both FOMO and YOLO, checked on static images, with the model info, detections, and latency printed in the log.
Path B: the same model on the live camera, with detections turned into counts per class and sent over Bridge RPC to the MCU, which displays them on the LED matrix.

Key takeaways:

Detection = classification + localization. It is evaluated with IoU and mAP, not accuracy alone, and the confidence threshold is the main knob that trades false positives for false negatives.
FOMO and YOLO answer different questions. FOMO gives where, fast. YOLO adds how big, and on the test images it also counted far more reliably, at about 1.6 (Nano) to 2.5 (Small) times FOMO’s end-to-end latency. Choose by the information and accuracy the application needs.
Measure on the board, not in the estimate. Edge Impulse’s latency estimates missed in both directions (11 ms vs. 160 ms measured for FOMO, 1,841 ms vs. 331 ms for YOLO-Pro Small).
The Bricks hide the inference pipeline, including NMS and drawing, so the engineering moves to what the application does with the detections.
Live detection needs an explicit “nothing seen” state. The Video Object Detection Brick is silent on empty frames; a timeout turns that silence into “zero”.
Keep hardware calls in one place. Callbacks record state; a single loop talks to the MCU, and only when something changed.

Detection is also where the vision labs meet the generative ones: a fast detector can find where to look, and the model from the Vision-Language Models lab can then describe what is there, on a crop instead of the whole frame, at a fraction of the cost. Building that pipeline is a natural next project.

title: Overview
text:
These labs explore machine learning systems on the Arduino UNO Q, a hybrid board that pairs a Linux microprocessor with a real-time microcontroller. The Qualcomm QRB2210 MPU runs Debian Linux, Python, and inference engines such as llama.cpp, while the STM32U585 MCU drives LEDs, sensors, and actuators. The two talk through Bridge, an RPC layer that lets Python code call functions in an Arduino sketch. This split mirrors many real edge AI products, where a capable processor runs the model and a microcontroller handles timing-critical I/O.
The UNO Q has about the compute of a Raspberry Pi 3, so it runs small language and vision-language models as well as classic vision models. Those limits make the trade-offs of edge deployment easy to see: model size, quantization, memory, and latency all show up directly in what the board can and cannot do.
 


The UNO Q is available from the Arduino Store and its authorized distributors:

Arduino UNO Q 2 GB (ABX00162): ~$59
Arduino UNO Q 4 GB (ABX00173): ~$79

The 2 GB variant is enough for setup and the vision labs. The 4 GB variant is recommended for the generative AI labs.




Arduino UNO Q: The 2 GB or 4 GB variant.
USB-C data cable: A cable that carries data, not a charge-only one.
Host computer: Linux, macOS, or Windows, with an SSH client.
Network: Wi-Fi with internet access, shared by the board and the host.
USB webcam and USB-C hub: For the vision labs, since the UNO Q has no built-in camera.

title: Vision-Language Models (VLM)
text:
The Small Language Models lab ran a text model on the UNO Q: llama-cli and llama-server loaded a single GGUF file (Qwen_Qwen3.5-0.8B-Q8_0.gguf), Python called it, and every answer came from the board, with no cloud call.
Text is an awkward interface for many real problems, though. Consider a mosquito breeding-site inspection: what matters is visual, such as water sitting in an old tire, a plant saucer that never drains, or a bucket left open after the rain. A health agent walking through a neighborhood does not type numbers into a form; they look.
This lab gives the same board eyes. By the end, the UNO Q looks at a photo (or a frame from a webcam) and answers a question like “Is this a potential mosquito breeding site, and why?”, and the lab shows exactly what it costs to run that on four small CPU cores.
 
The costs get as much attention as the results. Vision on this hardware works, but it is slow, and the slowness reveals something real about how these models work.


This lab builds on the Small Language Models lab. It assumes that llama.cpp is already built from source, that the Qwen3.5-0.8B GGUF is downloaded, and that you are comfortable running llama-server by hand and calling it from Python.




A text-only Qwen runs from a single GGUF file. To make it describe an image, add one more file, the mmproj, and the same model can suddenly talk about a photo. That second file holds the vision machinery, and what is inside it explains both how the model “sees” and why some of the serving flags matter.


Qwen3.5 is not a text model with vision bolted on. Qwen describes it as a unified vision-language foundation: the model was trained on text and image tokens together from the start, an approach called early fusion. That matters because the older mental model (a frozen language model with a separately trained adapter attached to a frozen image encoder) is the LLaVA or Moondream recipe, and this model was not built that way. Its vision and language sides were trained together.

This is also why Qwen3.5 beats the earlier Qwen3-VL models on visual benchmarks rather than inheriting from them: it is a different family.

At inference, there is still a clear pipeline, and llama.cpp makes it visible by splitting the weights across two files. The -m file holds the language model. The mmproj file holds the vision encoder and the small connector that links it to the language side. The split is a packaging convenience, not a sign that the base is text-only: the model runs without the mmproj to skip the vision pathway and save memory, as in the SLM lab.
image -> vision encoder -> projector / connector -> language model -> text
         |------------ mmproj GGUF ------------|   |-- -m GGUF --|
            (inference path; weights split across two files)



 

Vision encoder. The image is resized and cut into a grid of small patches. The patches go into the vision encoder, a Vision Transformer (ViT), which returns one feature vector per patch, describing what is in that region and how it relates to its neighbors. These vectors live in the encoder’s own space and have nothing to do with the language model’s vocabulary or embedding dimensions.
Multimodal connector (early fusion). The connector resolves that mismatch. The language model reads token embeddings in its own d-dimensional space. Text gets there through a lookup table, but image patches have no such table. The connector reshapes the visual vectors to the model’s embedding dimension and places them in the region of that space the model already understands, so that a patch of fur in the image behaves the way the text embedding for “fur” would. In an early-fusion model, this alignment is learned jointly with the rest of the network rather than trained afterward as an add-on.
Spliced embeddings (input stream). Once mapped, the visual vectors are spliced into the token stream where an image placeholder sits, and the model processes one mixed sequence of text and image embeddings. From the model’s point of view, there is no special “image mode”: the picture has become something that reads like tokens.
Language model. Internally, Qwen3.5 is not a vanilla transformer. It is an efficient hybrid of linear-attention blocks, with full attention only on periodic layers. Sparse mixture-of-experts appears in the Qwen3.5 family highlights, but the 0.8B’s own specification lists a plain feed-forward network (intermediate dimension 3584) with no experts and no router. That detail does not change the picture here, but it is why the architecture is described as a hybrid rather than a standard decoder.

That is why “describe this image” produces a caption: the model continues the sequence conditioned on the visual embeddings it can read.

The vision pathway produces no text. It emits embeddings and nothing else. Every word in the answer comes from the language model; the projector’s only job is to make the image legible.




Each image becomes a real block of embeddings that occupies a specific stretch of the context window: not one token, but many. A single image alone takes hundreds to low thousands of tokens. Qwen3.5 uses dynamic resolution, so a larger or busier image produces more visual tokens. The --image-min-tokens and --image-max-tokens flags cap that number (they apply only to dynamic-resolution models, which is why they matter here), and Section 0.6.1 returns to them.
The immediate consequence is that the -c 1024 context used for text overflows before a prompt is even added. Use 4096.




If llama-server is still running from the SLM lab, stop it first (Ctrl+C in its terminal). It holds port 8081 and some RAM, and this lab needs both.

sudo ss -ltnp | grep 8081      # should print nothing

Vision needs two files: the model and its mmproj. One warning can save an afternoon: the two must come from the same model, because their embedding dimensions must match. Pair a projector with the wrong base model, and the load fails outright with an n_embd mismatch. The base model is already on the board: the same 0.8B GGUF used for text works here, with the vision pathway switched on or off depending on whether --mmproj is passed. There is no separate “text-only” and “VL” download to keep track of, just the model plus its matching projector.
The Unsloth Qwen3.5-0.8B page on Hugging Face, for example, lists all the available files and versions:
 
The SLM lab downloaded the model from Bartowski, so download the matching projector from the same repository. Saving it as mmproj-F16_0.8B.gguf keeps it apart from the 2B projector downloaded later:
cd ~/models
wget -c -O mmproj-F16_0.8B.gguf \
  "https://huggingface.co/bartowski/Qwen_Qwen3.5-0.8B-GGUF/\

The mmproj usually comes in BF16, F16, and F32 versions. On the UNO Q, prefer F16. The board’s Cortex-A53 cores have no native BF16 path, so BF16 weights are converted on the fly, which wastes memory bandwidth the board cannot spare.

Switching the 0.8B’s projector from BF16 to F16 cut the description time for a 640×640 image from 4 minutes to about 1 minute: same model, same image, just a friendlier weight format.





This is the command for the 0.8B model. Run it in the foreground the first time to read the startup log:
cd ~/llama.cpp

./build/bin/llama-server \
  -m       /home/arduino/models/Qwen_Qwen3.5-0.8B-Q8_0.gguf \
  --mmproj /home/arduino/models/mmproj-F16_0.8B.gguf \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8081 \
  -c 4096 -t 4 \
  -n 256 \
  --jinja \
  --image-max-tokens 256 \
  --reasoning off \
  --reasoning-budget 0 \
  --alias qwen3.5-0.8b
Four flags deserve a comment:

--host 0.0.0.0 makes the WebUI reachable from a desktop or phone, not only from the board itself. Without it, the server binds to localhost, and a laptop cannot see it.
--jinja turns on the model’s own chat template. Without it, generation can fail to stop, because the generic fallback template does not register Qwen’s end-of-turn token as a stop string, and the model keeps going until it fills the context. In the first test without --jinja, the endless generation looked exactly like a frozen board.
-n 256 caps the output length as a safety net. Section 0.10 revisits it, because it interacts with the thinking trace in a surprising way.
--alias qwen3.5-0.8b gives the server a stable name that does not depend on the GGUF filename or on which model is loaded. Client code can always ask for "model": "qwen3.5-0.8b", which keeps the model-swapping pattern in Section 0.8 simple.

On startup, look for a clip / mtmd block confirming that the projector loaded, a line reporting that image support is enabled, and HTTP server listening on 0.0.0.0:8081.
 
If a request later returns “image processing requires a vision model,” the mmproj did not load. Check that --mmproj was passed and that the file path is correct.
Then open http://<UNO_Q_IP>:8081/ on a desktop or phone and drop in an image.

Use images no larger than 640×640.

 

The whole request took about a minute and a half, which is good for such a small model. Power peaked at 2.3 W during this request, and the temperature rose by about 20 °C (to 56 °C).



On this generated scene, the 0.8B’s description of the whole scene was good. It named the platform, the children, the ladder, the path, the clouds, and the mountains. Then it called the hanging papayas “quinces or similar fruits.”
That is the signature of a small VLM: the gist is solid, and the specifics are unreliable. For a breeding-site screen, this matters. The model can reliably say “there is a container with standing water,” but it should not be trusted to identify the container as a specific 200-liter drum. Design the question around what the model is actually good at.




The embedded WebUI is the quickest smoke test, but repeatable work needs the API. The server speaks the OpenAI-compatible format, so the image goes as a base64 data URI inside an image_url content block.
Create a directory for test images and copy a few images there, for example:
/home/arduino/ArduinoApps/images/test-papaya.png

A trap to avoid: do not paste the base64 string directly into a curl -d '...' argument. A base64 image is large enough to exceed the shell’s argument-size limit, and curl fails with Argument list too long before the request is sent. Write the body to a file (or pipe it on stdin) so that it never goes through the command line.

With the server running, go to the image directory:
cd ~/ArduinoApps/images
Encode the image:
IMG=$(base64 -w 0 test-papaya.png)
Then ask the model to describe it:
cat > /tmp/req.json <<EOF
{
  "max_tokens": 256,
  "messages": [{
    "role": "user",
    "content": [
      {"type": "image_url",
       "image_url": {"url": "data:image/png;base64,$IMG"}},
      {"type": "text", "text": "Describe this image."}
    ]
  }]
}
EOF

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8081/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data @/tmp/req.json

Match the media type to the file (image/png for a .png, image/jpeg for a .jpg). A single-model llama-server ignores the model field, so it can be left out.

 
It works. For real work, though, Python is cleaner, and it avoids the argument-length trap entirely by putting the image in the request body rather than on the command line.
Create a Python script in the terminal (App Lab or VS Code also work):
cd ~/ArduinoApps
nano image_caption.py
Enter the script, then save it with Ctrl+X and y:
import base64
import mimetypes
import requests

SERVER = "http://127.0.0.1:8081/v1/chat/completions"


def encode_image(path):
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        return base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode("utf-8")


def describe_image(
    path,
    prompt="Describe this image. Keep it to a paragraph.",
    max_tokens=256,
):
    mime = mimetypes.guess_type(path)[0] or "image/jpeg"
    data_uri = f"data:{mime};base64,{encode_image(path)}"
    payload = {
        "messages": [{
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": data_uri}},
                {"type": "text", "text": prompt},
            ],
        }],
        "temperature": 0.7,
        "max_tokens": max_tokens,
    }
    r = requests.post(SERVER, json=payload, timeout=300)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(describe_image("images/test-papaya.png"))

Note the timeout=300. On this board, a vision request can take 1 to 2 minutes, and a default request timeout would give up long before the model does.

Now try an image from the dataset used later in this lab (Section 0.9). Change the path in the script to point at it:
 
Run the script:
python3 image_caption.py
 



The tests surfaced a few lessons:
Symptom one: it runs forever. The fix is --jinja plus the -n cap. If both are set and generation still runs away, the WebUI’s own “max tokens” setting is overriding the server’s -n; lower it in the sampler panel too.
Symptom two: it freezes at 2%. A tall two-panel collage uploaded at full resolution left the progress bar parked at 2% with an ETA of 113 seconds. Ten minutes later it was still at 2%. The natural suspicion was memory, with swap thrashing as the model spilled past 4 GB, but free -h showed swap at zero. The board was not out of memory; it was out of time. A large, busy image makes the dynamic-resolution encoder produce many patches, and the ViT must process every one of them on four CPU cores. The encoder was not stuck; it was facing tens of minutes of computation.
The lesson is clear: on this board, vision is compute-bound by image size, not memory-bound at reasonable sizes. Resolution is the single biggest lever available.
Reading free -h correctly. Checking memory in the middle of a 2B description showed this:
          total    used    free  shared  buff/cache  available
Mem:      3.6Gi   1.5Gi    83Mi    36Mi       2.2Gi      2.1Gi
Swap:     1.8Gi    20Mi   1.8Gi
The free column says 83 MiB, which looks alarming but is not. llama-server memory-maps the GGUF, so the model weights appear under buff/cache (the 2.2 GiB), not under used. The number that matters is available: 2.1 GiB, with swap almost untouched at 20 MiB. The 2B fits comfortably; it is just slow.


Once it is clear that the work is compute-bound, the fixes follow. The most direct one targets the encoder’s token budget. Because Qwen3.5 uses dynamic resolution, llama-server can cap how many tokens an image may become:
--image-max-tokens 256
Encoding time scales with that count, so capping it directly reduces the work, and the model often describes a scene well with far fewer image tokens than the default. Start at 256 and tune.
After that:

Downscale the input to about 448 to 512 pixels, which complements the token cap.
Keep the output short, since every generated token costs real time on this CPU.
Rebuild llama.cpp with OpenBLAS (-DGGML_BLAS=ON -DGGML_BLAS_VENDOR=OpenBLAS) for a one-time gain, since encoding and prefill are dominated by matrix multiplication. Measure before and after, because the gain on Arm varies.

One more setting, unrelated to speed but worth including: for image workloads, drop --cache-prompt. In a known issue, each image adds 1,000+ KV tokens to the prompt cache, the cache grows without bound across repeated requests, and the process is eventually killed for running out of memory. The in-slot cache still works within a session, so a single-slot setup loses nothing meaningful by turning it off. On a 4 GB board, that is cheap insurance.

The timing, RAM, and energy rows were measured in October 2026 with --image-max-tokens 256; the next subsection explains how.
The bigger projector is not optional: the 2B needs its own 668 MB projector, because the small one does not match. The file is three times larger because the vision encoder inside it is bigger, which is also why encoding is slower: every patch passes through a heavier tower.
So the 2B is a real trade-off, not a free upgrade. It writes clearer answers and stays within the RAM budget, but four minutes before the first word, and six for a full description, rule out anything interactive. The two models are best treated as two tiers. The 0.8B is the fast screen when an answer is needed in about a minute. The 2B is the quality pass when correctness matters more than latency and the device can take its time. --image-max-tokens is the dial between them, and tuning it on the 2B is the most useful experiment to run.


To put real numbers on that trade-off, the whole board was measured while it worked. A FNIRSI FNB58 USB meter sat between the charger and the UNO Q’s USB-C port, logging voltage and current 100 times per second to a computer. On the board, a script started llama-server with the same flags as in Section 0.4, waited for the CPU to cool below 45 °C, recorded 15 seconds of idle, and then sent each request, noting when it was sent, when the first token arrived, and when the answer ended. Aligning the two clocks gives the power in every phase. Each model described two 640×640 images (the bucket and the tire from this lab) twice, after an uncounted warm-up request. The board used Wi-Fi only, with no display and nothing on its USB port except the meter; a Modulino Thermo and an idle expansion carrier were attached and are part of the idle power.
The same session also ran text-only prompts on both models (the SLM lab reports those numbers), so the whole test run fits in one picture:
 
Two things stand out before looking at any single request. Across the whole run, with both models and including brief spikes, the board never draws more than about 3.5 W, and it idles at only 0.5 W. Single requests peak lower: about 2.3 W for the 0.8B in the WebUI test above, and a mean of 2.4 to 2.7 W while answering (Table 1). And the CPU peaked at 68.7 °C with no heatsink or fan, while the clock stayed at 2.0 GHz on every core for the whole run: no thermal throttling, even during six-minute requests.
Zooming in on one description per model shows where the time and energy go:
 
Each request has three phases, visible in the power line:

The image encoder (spiky line, about 1.5 to 1.9 W). The vision tower in the projector turns the picture into 256 image tokens. The power jumps up and down because the encoder does not keep all four cores busy. llama-server does not report this phase separately, so its length is estimated as the time to first token minus the time the language model needs to read the same number of tokens as text. That puts it at about 41 s on the 0.8B and about 193 s on the 2B, the heavier tower described above.
The language model reads the prompt (flat line, about 1.9 W). The 274 tokens (256 from the image, the rest from the text and the chat template) pass through the model in batches: about 25 s on the 0.8B and 61 s on the 2B.
The answer (flat line, about 2.4 to 2.7 W). One token at a time: 47 s for 256 tokens on the 0.8B and 103 s on the 2B.

The four runs of each case agreed within 1%. The numbers show three things:

Reading the image is half the bill. On the 0.8B, reaching the first word costs about as much as writing 256 tokens; on the 2B, it costs more. Shorter answers save less than expected, while fewer image tokens (--image-max-tokens) or a smaller input image save more.
The 2B costs about 2.8 times the energy per image, while drawing slightly less power. It is not hungrier, just slower: four cores working for six minutes instead of two.
In battery terms, a 10 Wh power bank holds 36,000 J, enough for about 150 descriptions with the 0.8B, or about 50 with the 2B, if the board did nothing else. Between requests, the 0.5 W idle power adds up too: about 30 J per minute of waiting.


The total in the table includes the board’s idle power. Subtracting idle (0.5 W) gives the extra energy the inference itself costs: about 180 J per image on the 0.8B and about 490 J on the 2B.





The previous section established the trade-off. In practice, the right approach is not to pick one model and keep it, but to swap. A camera pointed at a yard all day sees mostly frames that are obviously nothing: dry ground, a wall, a parked car. A handful are ambiguous and deserve a second, slower opinion. The natural pattern is a fast screen on the 0.8B and a slower deep read on the 2B, only for the frames that need it. The board cannot comfortably run both at once (see the RAM numbers in Table 1), so “swap” here means one server at a time on the same port, not two processes in parallel.


Use the same models directory as before. The 2B model may already be there from the SLM lab:
cd /home/arduino/models

# 2B language model: UD-Q4_K_XL, the quality/size sweet spot
wget -c https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.5-2B-GGUF/\
resolve/main/Qwen3.5-2B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf

# Its matching projector. Do NOT reuse the 0.8B's mmproj
# (n_embd mismatch).
wget -c https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.5-2B-GGUF/\
resolve/main/mmproj-F16.gguf -O mmproj-F16_2B.gguf



Wrap each model’s launch command in its own script, so that switching takes one command instead of retyping the flags:
nano ~/run-qwen-0.8b-vision.sh
