The inference with the SSD MobileNet model worked well, but the latency was high. The inference varied from 0.5 to 1.3 seconds on a Raspi-Zero, which means around or less than 1 FPS (1 frame per second). One alternative to speed up the process is to use FOMO (Faster Objects, More Objects).
This machine learning algorithm lets us count multiple objects and find their location in an image in real-time using up to \(30\times\) less processing power and memory than MobileNet SSD or YOLO. The main reason this is possible is that while other models calculate the object’s size by drawing a square around it (bounding box), FOMO ignores the size of the image, providing only the information about where the object is located in the image through its centroid coordinates.


In a typical object detection pipeline, the first stage is extracting features from the input image. FOMO uses MobileNetV2 to perform this task. MobileNetV2 processes the input image to produce a feature map that captures essential characteristics, such as textures, shapes, and object edges, in a computationally efficient way.
 
Once these features are extracted, FOMO’s simpler architecture, focused on center-point detection, interprets the feature map to determine where objects are located in the image. The output is a grid of cells, where each cell represents whether or not an object center is detected. The model outputs one or more confidence scores for each cell, indicating the likelihood of an object being present.
The following image shows how it works.
FOMO divides the image into blocks of pixels using a factor of 8. For the input of \(96\times 96\), the grid would be \(12\times 12\) \((96/8=12)\). For a \(160\times 160\), the grid will be \(20\times 20\), and so on. Next, FOMO will run a classifier through each pixel block to calculate the probability that there is a box or a wheel in each of them and, subsequently, determine the regions that have the highest probability of containing the object (If a pixel block has no objects, it will be classified as background). From the overlap of the final region, the FOMO provides the coordinates (related to the image dimensions) of the centroid of this region.
 
Trade-off Between Speed and Precision:

Grid Resolution: FOMO uses a grid of fixed resolution, meaning each cell can detect if an object is present in that part of the image. It does not provide high localization accuracy, but it is fast and computationally light, which matters for edge devices.
Multi-Object Detection: Since each cell is independent, FOMO can detect multiple objects simultaneously in an image by identifying multiple centers.

This section explores YOLOv8, YOLO11, and YOLO26. Ultralytics YOLO is a family of real-time object detection and image segmentation models. The models build on recent advances in deep learning and computer vision and offer strong speed and accuracy. Their streamlined design suits various applications and adapts easily to different hardware platforms, from edge devices to cloud APIs.


The YOLO (You Only Look Once) model is a highly efficient and widely used object detection algorithm known for its real-time processing capabilities. Unlike traditional object detection systems that repurpose classifiers or localizers to perform detection, YOLO frames the detection problem as a single regression task. This approach enables YOLO to predict multiple bounding boxes and their class probabilities from full images in one evaluation, which greatly increases its speed.



Single Network Architecture:

YOLO uses a single neural network to process the entire image. This network divides the image into a grid and, for each grid cell, directly predicts bounding boxes and associated class probabilities. This end-to-end training improves speed and simplifies the model architecture.

Real-Time Processing:

YOLO can perform object detection in real time. Depending on the version and hardware, YOLO can process images at high frames per second (FPS). This suits applications requiring quick and accurate object detection, such as video surveillance, autonomous driving, and live sports analysis.

Evolution of Versions:

Over the years, YOLO has improved substantially, from YOLOv1 to YOLO26, the current generation (2026). Each iteration has introduced enhancements in accuracy, speed, and efficiency. YOLOv8, for instance, incorporates advancements in network architecture, improved training methodologies, and better support for various hardware.
YOLO11 offers substantial improvements in accuracy, speed, and parameter efficiency compared to prior versions such as YOLOv8 and YOLOv10.

 
Accuracy and Efficiency:

While early versions of YOLO traded off some accuracy for speed, recent versions balance both better. The newer models are faster and more accurate, detecting small objects (such as bees) and performing well on complex datasets.

Wide Range of Applications:

YOLO’s versatility has led to its adoption in numerous fields. It is used in traffic monitoring systems to detect and count vehicles, security applications to identify potential threats and agricultural technology to monitor crops and livestock. Its application extends to any domain requiring efficient and accurate object detection.

Community and Development:

YOLO continues to evolve and is supported by a strong community of developers and researchers. Open-source implementations and extensive documentation have made it accessible for customization and integration into various projects. Popular deep learning frameworks like Darknet, TensorFlow, and PyTorch support YOLO, further broadening its applicability.
Ultralytics YOLO can not only Detect (our case here) but also Segment and Pose models pre-trained on the COCO dataset and Classify models pre-trained on the ImageNet dataset. Track mode is available for all Detect, Segment, and Pose models. Recent versions can also predict Oriented Bounding Boxes (OBB), which rotate to match the orientation of an object and give a tighter fit than axis-aligned boxes.




Ultralytics YOLO supported tasks






Each YOLO generation comes in several sizes. For YOLOv8, for example:

YOLOv8n (Nano): Smallest model, fastest inference, lowest accuracy
YOLOv8s (Small): Balanced performance for edge devices
YOLOv8m (Medium): Higher accuracy, moderate computational requirements
YOLOv8l (Large): High accuracy, requires more computational resources
YOLOv8x (Extra Large): Highest accuracy, most computationally intensive


For Raspberry Pi applications, the nano variants (YOLOv8n, YOLO11n, or YOLO26n) are the practical choice because of their size and speed.




In 2026, Ultralytics released YOLO26, the current generation of the family. The package, the CLI, and the Python API are the same as for YOLOv8 and YOLO11, so trying it only requires a different model name:
yolo predict model='yolo26n' \
     source='https://ultralytics.com/images/bus.jpg'
from ultralytics import YOLO

model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt")
The YOLO26 nano variant is smaller than YOLO11n (2.4 M parameters and 5.5 GFLOPs, compared to 2.6 M parameters and 6.5 GFLOPs), and Ultralytics reports up to 43% faster CPU ONNX inference for YOLO26n than for YOLO11n on an Intel Xeon. That figure comes from a desktop-class CPU, so it indicates a direction rather than a number to expect on a Cortex-A53. Measure on your own board, as this lab does throughout.
Two differences matter for the code in this section:

YOLO26 is NMS-free by default. Its one-to-one detection head produces predictions directly, without Non-Maximum Suppression. The iou and agnostic_nms arguments used later therefore have no effect on a YOLO26 model unless the classic head is requested with end2end=False. The conf threshold still behaves as expected.
Export formats. This lab converts models to NCNN for faster inference on the Raspberry Pi. NCNN export works for YOLO26, but it cannot carry the end-to-end head and gives little speedup on this board. For YOLO26, ONNX is the better target (see Section 0.6.4.1).





First, confirm the system Python version:
python --version
On the current Raspberry Pi OS (based on Debian Trixie), it should be 3.13.x. Recent Ultralytics releases publish wheels for Python 3.13, so the system Python can be used directly, without installing another Python version through Pyenv.

On the legacy Raspberry Pi OS (Bookworm), the Python version is 3.11, and everything below still applies.



On the Raspi, deactivate the current environment and create a new working area:
deactivate
cd ~/Documents
mkdir YOLO
cd YOLO
mkdir models
mkdir images



The environment is created with access to the system packages, so that Debian’s own builds of NumPy, Pillow, and picamera2 are reused instead of being recompiled inside the venv:
python3 -m venv ~/yolo --system-site-packages
source ~/yolo/bin/activate

# Verify that the environment's Python is in use
which python
python --version



Debian Trixie mounts /tmp as a tmpfs, which lives in RAM. On a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, that leaves only about 208 MB:
findmnt /tmp
df -h /tmp
pip streams each wheel into a temporary file before installing it, and the PyTorch wheel alone is well over 400 MB. Without a change, the installation fails partway through with a misleading error:
OSError: [Errno 28] No space left on device
The disk is not full; /tmp is. Point pip at a temporary directory on the SD card instead:
mkdir -p ~/tmp
export TMPDIR=$HOME/tmp

This setting lasts for the current shell session. To make it permanent, append export TMPDIR=$HOME/tmp to the end of ~/yolo/bin/activate, so it is applied whenever the environment is active.




Inside the activated environment:

Update the packages list and upgrade pip:

sudo apt update
pip install -U pip

Install the CPU build of PyTorch first:

pip install torch torchvision \
    --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
This step matters. The default PyTorch wheels for aarch64 declare CUDA dependencies (cuBLAS, cuDNN, NCCL, Triton) for ARM datacenter parts. pip cannot know that a Cortex-A53 will never use them, so it downloads several gigabytes of libraries that cannot run on this board. Installing the CPU build first satisfies the requirement, and the CUDA chain is skipped. Confirm that the wheel name carries a +cpu suffix before continuing.

Install the ultralytics package:

pip install ultralytics

The ultralytics[export] variant also pulls in TensorFlow, OpenVINO, and CoreMLTools. None of them are used in this lab, and they take a long time to install on a Zero 2 W. The NCNN export used later downloads its own pnnx tool on demand, so the plain package is enough.


Reboot the device:

sudo reboot




After the Raspi boots, go to the working directory and activate the yolo env:
cd ~/Documents/YOLO
source ~/yolo/bin/activate
 and run inference on an image that will be downloaded from the Ultralytics website, using the YOLOv8n model (the smallest in the family) at the Terminal (CLI):
yolo predict model='yolov8n' \
     source='https://ultralytics.com/images/bus.jpg'

The YOLO model family is pre-trained with the COCO dataset. The first time a model is invoked, it is automatically downloaded to the current directory.

The inference result will appear in the terminal. In the image (bus.jpg), 4 persons, 1 bus, and 1 stop sign were detected:
 
Also, we got a message that Results saved to runs/detect/predict. Inspecting that directory, we can see a new image saved (bus.jpg). Download it from the Raspi to your desktop for inspection:
 
So, Ultralytics YOLO is correctly installed on the Raspi. On the Raspi-Zero, however, the inference latency is high, several seconds, even with the smallest model of the family (YOLOv8n).


The procedure is the same for the newer versions; only the model name changes (model='yolo11n' or model='yolo26n'). YOLO11n is faster than YOLOv8n but appears slightly less precise, as it does not detect the “stop sign”:
 
YOLO26n is faster than both and shows the same precision as YOLO11n:
 




Deploying computer vision models on edge devices with limited computational power, such as the Raspi-Zero, can cause latency issues. One alternative is to use a format optimized for performance, which lets even devices with limited processing power handle computer vision tasks.
Of all the model export formats supported by Ultralytics, NCNN is a high-performance neural network inference framework optimized for mobile platforms. NCNN was designed from the start for deployment on mobile phones and has no third-party dependencies. It is cross-platform, and its authors report it running faster than other open-source frameworks (such as TFLite) on mobile CPUs.
NCNN delivers the best inference performance when working with Raspberry Pi devices. NCNN is highly optimized for mobile embedded platforms (such as ARM architecture).
Move the downloaded YOLO models to the ./models folder and bus.jpg to ./images. Then convert the models and rerun the inference:

Export the YOLO PyTorch models to NCNN format, creating yolov8n_ncnn_model, yolo11n_ncnn_model, and yolo26n_ncnn_model:

yolo export model=./models/yolov8n.pt format=ncnn
yolo export model=./models/yolo11n.pt format=ncnn
yolo export model=./models/yolo26n.pt format=ncnn

Run inference with the exported models:

yolo predict task=detect model='./models/yolov8n_ncnn_model' \
     source='./images/bus.jpg'
yolo predict task=detect model='./models/yolo11n_ncnn_model' \
     source='./images/bus.jpg'
yolo predict task=detect model='./models/yolo26n_ncnn_model' \
     source='./images/bus.jpg'

The first inference, when the model is loaded, usually has a high latency, but from the second one on, the inference time decreases.

Neither YOLOv8n nor YOLO11n detects the “stop sign” after conversion, and YOLO11n is the faster of the two. The optimized models are faster but also less accurate.
 
Every YOLO26 export prints the following warning:
WARNING ⚠️ NCNN export does not support end2end models,
disabling end2end branch.
The converted YOLO26 model therefore uses the classic one-to-many head, which requires NMS, and not the end-to-end head of the PyTorch test above. This costs YOLO26 twice: the heavier head, and a conversion that barely helps. The next section measures it.
 


NCNN is the right target for YOLOv8 and YOLO11, but not for YOLO26. ONNX Runtime keeps the end-to-end head and is considerably faster on this board:
yolo export model=./models/yolo26n.pt format=onnx
yolo predict task=detect model=./models/yolo26n.onnx \
     source=./images/bus.jpg imgsz=640
 
Steady-state results measured on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W (second run of each, bus.jpg):










Model
Format
Head
Inference (ms)
Postprocess (ms)




YOLO11n
PyTorch
one-to-many
4672
276


YOLO11n
NCNN
one-to-many
2748
533


YOLO26n
PyTorch
end-to-end
2750
36


YOLO26n
PyTorch (end2end=False)
one-to-many
4515
192


YOLO26n
NCNN
one-to-many
5436
826


YOLO26n
ONNX
end-to-end
2274
265




The PyTorch rows run at \(640\times 480\) and the exported rows at \(640\times 640\). Ultralytics letterboxes to a rectangle for PyTorch inference but exports at a fixed square, so the exported models process about 33% more pixels. Multiply the PyTorch numbers by 1.33 before comparing them directly with the exported ones; imgsz=640 does not change this.

Two lessons come out of this table:

The end-to-end head is what makes YOLO26 fast. Switching it off with end2end=False costs 1.6× on the same runtime and the same image (2750 → 4515 ms), and the postprocess column shows why: 36 ms without NMS against 192 ms with it.
A conversion that helps one model can fail to help another. Comparing like with like (one-to-many head, \(640\times 640\)), NCNN cuts YOLO11n’s latency by more than half, but improves YOLO26n by roughly 10%. Since NCNN also forces the slower head, converting YOLO26 to NCNN leaves it worse off than the plain PyTorch model.

The vendor benchmark says YOLO26n is faster than YOLO11n, and on this board it is, in PyTorch and in ONNX. Following the NCNN recipe that works well for YOLOv8 and YOLO11, however, makes YOLO26 the slowest of the three. No single model or format is best: the model and the export path have to be chosen together and measured on the target hardware.




To start, call the Python interpreter to explore how the YOLO model works, line by line:
python
Now call the YOLO library from Ultralytics and load the model:
from ultralytics import YOLO

model = YOLO("./models/yolov8n_ncnn_model")
Next, run inference over an image (use bus.jpg again):
img = "./images/bus.jpg"
result = model.predict(img, save=True, imgsz=640, conf=0.5, iou=0.3)
 
We can verify that the result is almost identical to the one we get running the inference at the terminal level (CLI), except that the stop sign was not detected with the reduced NCNN model. Note that the latency was reduced.
Now analyze the content of result.
For example, we can see result[0].boxes.data, showing us the main inference result, which is a tensor shape (4, 6). Each line is one of the objects detected, being the 4 first columns, the bounding boxes coordinates, the 5th, the confidence, and the 6th, the class (in this case, 0: person and 5: bus):
 
We can access several inference results separately, as the inference time, and have it printed in a better format:
inference_time = int(result[0].speed["inference"])
print(f"Inference Time: {inference_time} ms")
Or we can have the total number of objects detected:
print(f"Number of objects: {len (result[0].boxes.cls)}")
 
With Python, we can create a detailed output that meets our needs (See Model Prediction with Ultralytics YOLO for more details). Run a Python script instead of entering the code line by line in the interpreter, as shown below. Use nano as the text editor. First, create an empty Python script named, for example, yolov8_tests.py:
nano yolov8_tests.py
Enter the code lines:
from ultralytics import YOLO

# Load the YOLOv8 model
model = YOLO("./models/yolov8n_ncnn_model")

# Run inference
img = "./images/bus.jpg"
result = model.predict(img, save=False, imgsz=640, conf=0.5, iou=0.3)

# print the results
inference_time = int(result[0].speed["inference"])
print(f"Inference Time: {inference_time} ms")
print(f"Number of objects: {len (result[0].boxes.cls)}")
 
Then enter the commands [CTRL+O] + [ENTER] +[CTRL+X] to save the Python script.
Run the script:
python yolov8_tests.py
The result is the same as running the inference at the terminal level (CLI) and with the built-in Python interpreter.

Calling the YOLO library and loading the model for inference for the first time takes a long time, but the inferences after that will be much faster. For example, the first single inference can take several seconds, but after that, the inference time should be reduced to less than 1 second.



model.predict() accepts several arguments that override the defaults at inference time. The most useful ones on the Raspi are:








Argument
Default
Description




conf
0.25
Minimum confidence threshold; detections below it are discarded.


iou
0.7
IoU threshold for Non-Maximum Suppression; lower values remove more overlapping boxes.


imgsz
640
Image size for inference (an integer or a (height, width) tuple).


max_det
300
Maximum number of detections per image.


classes
None
Filters predictions to a list of class IDs.


save
False
Saves the annotated image (the CLI default is True).



The complete list, including the visualization arguments, is in the Ultralytics predict documentation.




Return to the “Box versus Wheel” dataset, labeled on Roboflow. On the Download Dataset, instead of Download a zip to computer option done for training on Edge Impulse Studio, choose Show download code. This option will open a pop-up window with a code snippet that should be pasted into the training notebook.
 
For training, adapt one of the public examples available from Ultralytics and run it on Google Colab. The author’s notebook below can be adapted to your project:

YOLOv8 Box versus Wheel Dataset Training [Open In Colab]




Run it with GPU (the NVidia T4 is free)
Install Ultralytics using PIP.
 
Now, you can import the YOLO and upload your dataset to the CoLab, pasting the Download code that we get from Roboflow. Note that our dataset will be mounted under /content/datasets/:

 

It is essential to verify and change the file data.yaml with the correct path for the images (copy the path on each images folder).

names:

- box
- wheel
nc: 2
roboflow:
  license: CC BY 4.0
  project: box-versus-wheel-auto-dataset
  url: https://universe.roboflow.com/marcelo-rovai-riila/ \
     box-versus-wheel-auto-dataset/dataset/5
  version: 5
  workspace: marcelo-rovai-riila
test: /content/datasets/Box-versus-Wheel-auto-dataset-5/ \
      test/images
train: /content/datasets/Box-versus-Wheel-auto-dataset-5/ \
       train/images
val: /content/datasets/Box-versus-Wheel-auto-dataset-5/ \
     valid/images

Define the main hyperparameters that you want to change from default, for example:
MODEL = 'yolov8n.pt'
IMG_SIZE = 640
EPOCHS = 25 # For a final project, you should consider
            # at least 100 epochs
Run the training (using CLI):
!yolo task=detect mode=train model={MODEL} \
  data={dataset.location}/data.yaml \
  epochs={EPOCHS}
  imgsz={IMG_SIZE} plots=True


The model took a few minutes to be trained and has a very good result (mAP50 of 0.995). At the end of the training, all results are saved in the folder listed, for example: /runs/detect/train/. There, you can find, for example, the confusion matrix.
 

Note that the trained model (best.pt) is saved in the folder /runs/detect/train/weights/. Now validate the trained model with the valid/images.

!yolo task=detect mode=val model={HOME}/runs/detect/train/\
       weights/best.pt data={dataset.location}/data.yaml
The results were similar to training.

Now perform inference on the images left aside for testing

!yolo task=detect mode=predict model={HOME}/runs/detect/train/\
     weights/best.pt conf=0.25 source={dataset.location}/test/\
     images save=True
The inference results are saved in the folder runs/detect/predict. Some of them are shown below:
 

Export the train, validation, and test results to Google Drive. To do so, mount the drive.
from google.colab import drive
drive.mount('/content/gdrive')
and copy the content of /runs folder to a folder that you should create in your Drive, for example:
!scp -r /content/runs '/content/gdrive/MyDrive/\
     10_UNIFEI/Box_vs_Wheel_Project'





Download the trained model /runs/detect/train/weights/best.pt to your computer. Using FileZilla FTP, transfer the best.pt to the Raspi models folder (before the transfer, you may change the model name, for example, box_wheel_320_yolo.pt).
Using FileZilla FTP, transfer a few images from the test dataset to ./YOLO/images.
Return to the YOLO folder and use the Python interpreter:
cd ~/Documents/YOLO
python
As before, import the YOLO library and define the model to use:
from ultralytics import YOLO

model = YOLO("./models/box_wheel_320_yolo.pt")
Now define an image and call the inference (the image result is saved this time for external verification):
img = "./images/1_box_1_wheel.jpg"
result = model.predict(img, save=True, imgsz=320, conf=0.5, iou=0.3)
Repeat for several images. The inference result is saved on the variable result, and the processed image on runs/detect/predict8
 
Using FileZilla FTP, we can send the inference result to our Desktop for verification:
 
The inference result is good. The model was trained based on the smaller base model of the YOLOv8 family (YOLOv8n). The issue is the latency, around 1 second (or 1 FPS on the Raspi-Zero). Converting the model to NCNN reduces this latency, as shown below.

The same model trained with YOLO11n has a latency of around 800 ms on the Raspi-Zero, similar to the YOLOv8n model converted to NCNN.

On a Raspberry Pi 5, the YOLO11n model trained on this dataset runs in around 400 ms:
 
The same model, when exported to NCNN, takes around 80 ms:
 



Converting the custom model to NCNN gives the same speedup seen earlier with the COCO models. Two practical points apply before running it.
Run the export from a terminal, not from a notebook cell. pnnx, the tool that performs the conversion, pins all four cores for a minute or more and allocates its own memory pools outside PyTorch’s allocator. On the Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, running it from inside a Jupyter notebook, on top of a Jupyter server and a kernel already holding several loaded models, repeatedly caused the board to reset. From a plain SSH session, the same export completes in about 90 seconds.
Export at the size the model was trained for. The custom model was trained at \(320\times 320\), so:
cd ~/Documents/YOLO
yolo export model=./models/box_wheel_320_yolo.pt format=ncnn imgsz=320
Then run inference at the same size:
yolo predict task=detect \
     model=./models/box_wheel_320_yolo_ncnn_model \
     source=./images/box_3_wheel_4.jpg imgsz=320
image 1/1 .../box_3_wheel_4.jpg: 320x320 3 boxs, 4 wheels, 519.3ms
Speed: 237.6ms preprocess, 519.3ms inference, 506.7ms postprocess
The inference takes about 519 ms, or roughly 2 FPS on the Zero 2 W, against approximately 2500 ms for the same model in its original PyTorch format.


Getting this wrong produces no error message, so it deserves emphasis.
A .pt model accepts any imgsz and letterboxes the input accordingly, so it is easy to treat the argument as something that can change freely at inference time. An exported model does not work this way. NCNN, ONNX, and TFLite all bake the input shape into the graph at conversion time. Passing a different imgsz at inference is either silently ignored or produces meaningless output.
Exporting the 320-trained model without specifying imgsz defaults the graph to 640. Running it then gives:
image 1/1 .../box_1.jpg: 320x320 113 boxs, 164 wheels, 2880.5ms
The model reports one hundred and thirteen boxes and one hundred and sixty-four wheels in an image containing a single box, most at confidence 1.00, and the image is covered in overlapping rectangles. Nothing crashed and nothing warned: the tensor simply did not match the graph the weights were compiled for.
The rule is straightforward: the imgsz used for training, for export, and for inference must all be the same value. After any export, check the first line of the prediction output and confirm that the shape is the expected one before trusting any result.

The export banner suggests an imgsz matching whatever the conversion used, not what the model was trained at. If the model is exported without the argument, that suggestion will recommend 640 for a 320 model.




Two consecutive runs of the same command on the same model give:



Run
Preprocess
Inference
Postprocess




First (cold)
289.7 ms
2545.1 ms
1540.9 ms


Second (warm)
237.6 ms
519.3 ms
506.7 ms



The difference is nearly a factor of five, with no change to the model or the command. The first call pays for loading the library code and faulting pages in from the SD card; the second finds them already resident. On a memory-constrained board, this penalty is larger than the inference itself, so always discard the first measurement and report the steady-state figure. A service that runs inference continuously pays this cost only once at startup.





All the models explored in this lab can detect objects in real-time using a camera. The captured image should be the input for the trained and converted model. For the Raspi-4 or 5 with a desktop, OpenCV can capture the frames and display the inference result.
However, creating a live stream with a webcam to detect objects in real-time is also possible. For example, start with the script developed for the Image Classification app and adapt it for a Real-Time Object Detection Web Application Using TensorFlow Lite and Flask.
This app version works for any TFLite/LiteRT model. Verify that the model is in its correct folder, for example:
model_path = "./models/ssd-mobilenet-v1-tflite-default-v1.tflite"
Download the Python script object_detection_app.py from GitHub.
Check the model and labels:
 
And on the terminal, run:
python object_detection_app.py
After starting, the terminal shows a message such as (the IP is from the author’s Raspberry Pi):

* Running on http://192.168.4.210:5000
Press CTRL+C to quit

And access the web interface:

On the Raspberry Pi itself (if you have a GUI): Open a web browser and go to http://localhost:5000
From another device on the same network: Open a web browser and go to http://<raspberry_pi_ip>:5000 (Replace <raspberry_pi_ip> with your Raspberry Pi’s IP address). For example: http://192.168.4.210: 5000/

Here are some screenshots of the app running on an external desktop
 
The key modules used in the object detection application are described below:

LiteRT:

Purpose: Efficient inference of machine learning models on edge devices.
Why: LiteRT offers reduced model size and optimized performance compared to full TensorFlow, which matters for resource-constrained devices like the Raspberry Pi. It supports hardware acceleration and quantization, further improving efficiency.
Key functions: Interpreter for loading and running the model, get_input_details(), and get_output_details() for interfacing with the model.

Flask:

Purpose: Lightweight web framework for creating the backend server.
Why: Flask’s simplicity and flexibility suit rapid development and deployment of web applications. It is less resource-intensive than larger frameworks, which suits edge devices.
Key components: route decorators for defining API endpoints, Response objects for streaming video, render_template_string for serving dynamic HTML.

Picamera2:

Purpose: Interface with the Raspberry Pi camera module.
Why: Picamera2 is the latest library for controlling Raspberry Pi cameras, offering improved performance and features over the original Picamera library.
Key functions: create_preview_configuration() for setting up the camera, capture_file() for capturing frames.

PIL (Python Imaging Library):

Purpose: Image processing and manipulation.
Why: PIL provides a wide range of image processing capabilities. It is used here to resize images, draw bounding boxes, and convert between image formats.
Key classes: Image for loading and manipulating images, ImageDraw for drawing shapes and text on images.

NumPy:

Purpose: Efficient array operations and numerical computing.
Why: NumPy’s array operations are much faster than pure Python lists, which is needed to process image data efficiently and model inputs/outputs.
Key functions: array() for creating arrays, expand_dims() for adding dimensions to arrays.

Threading:

Purpose: Concurrent execution of tasks.
Why: Threading allows simultaneous frame capture, object detection, and web server operation, needed to maintain real-time performance.
Key components: Thread class creates separate execution threads, and Lock is used for thread synchronization.

io.BytesIO:

Purpose: In-memory binary streams.
Why: Allows efficient handling of image data in memory without needing temporary files, improving speed and reducing I/O operations.

time:

Purpose: Time-related functions.
Why: Used for adding delays (time.sleep()) to control frame rate and for performance measurements.

jQuery (client-side):

Purpose: Simplified DOM manipulation and AJAX requests.
Why: It lets the web interface update dynamically and communicate with the server without page reloads.
Key functions: .get() and .post() for AJAX requests, DOM manipulation methods for updating the UI.


Regarding the main app system architecture:

Main Thread: Runs the Flask server, handling HTTP requests and serving the web interface.
Camera Thread: Continuously captures frames from the camera.
Detection Thread: Processes frames through the TFLite model for object detection.
Frame Buffer: Shared memory space (protected by locks) storing the latest frame and detection results.

And the app data flow, we can describe in short:

Camera captures frame → Frame Buffer
Detection thread reads from Frame Buffer → Processes through TFLite model → Updates detection results in Frame Buffer
Flask routes access Frame Buffer to serve the latest frame and detection results
Web client receives updates via AJAX and updates UI

This architecture allows efficient, real-time object detection with a responsive web interface on a resource-constrained edge device like a Raspberry Pi. Threading and efficient libraries like TFLite and PIL let the system process video frames in real time, while Flask and jQuery provide the interface.
You can test the app with another pre-processed model, such as the EfficientDet, changing the app line:
model_path = "./models/lite-model_efficientdet_lite0_\
   detection_metadata_1.tflite"

If we want to use the app for the SSD-MobileNetV2 model, trained on Edge Impulse Studio with the “Box versus Wheel” dataset, the code should also be adapted depending on the input details, as we have explored on its notebook.




This lab implemented object detection on edge devices like the Raspberry Pi and showed that computer vision tasks can run on resource-constrained hardware. It covered several aspects:

Model Comparison: The lab examined different object detection models, including SSD-MobileNet, EfficientDet, FOMO, and YOLO, comparing their performance and trade-offs on edge devices.
Training and Deployment: Using a custom dataset of boxes and wheels (labeled on Roboflow), the lab walked through the process of training models using Edge Impulse Studio and Ultralytics and deploying them on Raspberry Pi.
Optimization Techniques: To improve inference speed on edge devices, the lab explored optimization methods, such as model quantization (TFLite int8) and format conversion (e.g., to NCNN and ONNX), showing that the best export path depends on the model and must be measured on the target hardware.
Real-time Applications: The lab built a real-time object detection web application, showing how these models can be integrated into interactive systems.
Performance Considerations: Throughout the lab, the balance between model accuracy and inference speed was discussed, an important consideration for edge AI applications.

Object detection on edge devices supports many domains, from precision agriculture, industrial automation, and quality control to smart home applications and environmental monitoring. By processing data locally, these systems can offer reduced latency, improved privacy, and operation in environments with limited connectivity.
Looking ahead, potential areas for further exploration include:

Implementing multi-model pipelines for more complex tasks
Exploring hardware acceleration options for Raspberry Pi
Integrating object detection with other sensors for more comprehensive edge AI systems
Developing edge-to-cloud solutions that use both local processing and cloud resources

Object detection on edge devices can produce responsive systems that bring AI directly into the physical world.
