title: Setup
text:
DALL·E prompt - An electronics laboratory environment inspired by the 1950s, with a cartoon style. The lab should have vintage equipment, large oscilloscopes, old-fashioned tube radios, and large, boxy computers. The Raspberry Pi 5 board is prominently displayed, accurately shown in its real size, similar to a credit card, on a workbench. The Pi board is surrounded by classic lab tools like a soldering iron, resistors, and wires. The overall scene should be vibrant, with exaggerated colors and playful details characteristic of a cartoon. No logos or text should be included.


This chapter guides you through setting up the Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W (Raspi-Zero) and Raspberry Pi 5 (Raspi-5) models. It covers hardware setup, operating system installation, initial configuration, and tests.

The general instructions for the Raspi-5 also apply to the older Raspberry Pi versions, such as the Raspi-3 and Raspi-4.



The Raspberry Pi is a versatile single-board computer used by engineers across many disciplines. Developed by the Raspberry Pi Foundation, these compact devices combine low cost, substantial computing capacity, and extensive GPIO (General Purpose Input/Output) capabilities, which suits them to prototyping, embedded systems development, and advanced engineering projects.



Computational Power: Despite their small size, Raspberry Pis offer significant processing capabilities, with the latest models featuring multi-core ARM processors and up to 16 GB of RAM.
GPIO Interface: The 40-pin GPIO header allows direct interaction with sensors, actuators, and other electronic components, which supports hardware-software integration projects.
Extensive Connectivity: Built-in Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Ethernet, and multiple USB ports enable diverse communication and networking projects.
Low-Level Hardware Access: Raspberry Pis provide access to interfaces like I2C, SPI, and UART, allowing detailed control and communication with external devices.
Real-Time Capabilities: With proper configuration, Raspberry Pis can be used for soft real-time applications, making them suitable for control systems and signal processing tasks.
Power Efficiency: Low power consumption enables battery-powered and energy-efficient designs, especially in models like the Pi Zero.





Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W (Raspi-Zero):

Ideal for: Compact embedded systems
Key specs: 1 GHz quad-core CPU (ARM Cortex-A53), 512 MB RAM, minimal power consumption (around 600 mW at idle). The power-off “zombie current” is also very low, around 45 mA (225 mW), well below that of the full-size Raspberry Pi models.

Raspberry Pi 5 (Raspi-5):

Ideal for: More demanding applications such as edge computing, computer vision, and edgeAI applications, including LLMs.
Key specs: 2.4 GHz quad-core CPU (ARM Cortex A-76), up to 16 GB RAM, PCIe interface for expansions, higher power consumption (typically around 3–3.5 W at idle)






Embedded Systems Design: Develop and prototype embedded systems for real-world applications.
IoT and Networked Devices: Create interconnected devices and explore protocols like MQTT, CoAP, and HTTP/HTTPS.
Control Systems: Implement feedback control loops, PID controllers, and interface with actuators.
Computer Vision and AI: Use libraries like OpenCV and TensorFlow Lite for image processing and machine learning at the edge.
Data Acquisition and Analysis: Collect sensor data, perform real-time analysis, and create data logging systems.
Robotics: Build robot controllers, implement motion planning algorithms, and interface with motor drivers.
Signal Processing: Perform real-time signal analysis, filtering, and DSP applications.
Network Security: Set up VPNs, firewalls, and explore network penetration testing.

This tutorial guides you through setting up the most common Raspberry Pi models so that you can start your machine learning project quickly. It covers hardware setup, operating system installation, and initial configuration, with a focus on preparing your Pi for machine learning applications.






 

Processor: 1 GHz quad-core 64-bit Arm Cortex-A53 CPU
RAM: 512 MB SDRAM
Wireless: 2.4 GHz 802.11 b/g/n wireless LAN, Bluetooth 4.2, BLE
Ports: Mini HDMI, micro USB OTG, CSI-2 camera connector
Power: 5 V/2.5 A via micro USB port (12.5 W Micro USB power supply)




 

Processor:

Pi 5: Quad-core 64-bit Arm Cortex-A76 CPU @ 2.4 GHz
Pi 4: Quad-core Cortex-A72 (ARM v8) 64-bit SoC @ 1.5 GHz

RAM: 2 GB, 4 GB, 8 GB, or 16 GB options (8 GB or more recommended for AI tasks)
Wireless: Dual-band 802.11ac wireless (2.4 GHz and 5 GHz), Bluetooth 5.0
Ports: 2\(\times\) micro HDMI ports, 2\(\times\) USB 3.0 ports, 2\(\times\) USB 2.0 ports, CSI camera port, DSI display port
Power: 5 V/5 A via USB-C connector (27 W USB-C power supply); a 5 V/3 A supply limits USB peripherals to 600 mA


In the labs, we will use different names to address the Raspberry: Raspi, Raspi-5, Raspi-Zero, etc. Usually, Raspi is used when the instructions or comments apply to every model.







An operating system (OS) is the software that manages computer hardware and software resources, providing standard services for computer programs. It is the core software that runs on a computer, acting as an intermediary between hardware and application software. The OS manages the computer’s memory, processes, device drivers, files, and security protocols.

Key functions:

Process management: Allocating CPU time to different programs
Memory management: Allocating and freeing up memory as needed
File system management: Organizing and keeping track of files and directories
Device management: Communicating with connected hardware devices
User interface: Providing a way for users to interact with the computer

Components:

Kernel: The core of the OS that manages hardware resources
Shell: The user interface for interacting with the OS
File system: Organizes and manages data storage
Device drivers: Software that allows the OS to communicate with hardware


The Raspberry Pi runs a specialized version of Linux designed for embedded systems. This operating system, typically a variant of Debian called Raspberry Pi OS (formerly Raspbian), is optimized for the Pi’s ARM-based architecture and limited resources.

The latest version of Raspberry Pi OS (December 2025) is based on Debian Trixie.

Key features:

Lightweight: Tailored to run efficiently on the Pi’s hardware.
Versatile: Supports a wide range of applications and programming languages.
Open-Source: Allows for customization and community-driven improvements.
GPIO support: Enables interaction with sensors and other hardware through the Pi’s pins.
Regular updates: Continuously improved for performance and security.

Embedded Linux on the Raspberry Pi provides a full-featured operating system in a compact package, which suits projects ranging from simple IoT devices to more complex edge machine-learning applications. Its compatibility with standard Linux tools and libraries makes it a capable platform for development and experimentation.



To use the Raspberry Pi, we need an operating system. By default, the Raspberry Pi checks for an operating system on any SD card inserted in the slot, so we should install an operating system using Raspberry Pi Imager.

In November 2025, Raspberry Pi Imager 2.0 was released. It brings a new wizard interface, the option to preconfigure Raspberry Pi Connect, and improved accessibility for screen readers and other assistive technologies.

Raspberry Pi Imager is a tool for downloading and writing images on macOS, Windows, and Linux. It includes many popular operating system images for Raspberry Pi. We will also use the Imager to preconfigure credentials and remote access settings.
Follow the steps to install the OS in your Raspi.

Download and install the Raspberry Pi Imager on your computer.
Insert a microSD card into your computer (a 32GB SD card is recommended) .
Open Raspberry Pi Imager and select your Raspberry Pi model.

 

Choose the appropriate operating system:

For Raspi-Zero: For example, you can select, under Raspberry Pi OS (Other), Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit).


 

Due to its reduced SDRAM (512 MB), the recommended OS for the Raspi-Zero is the 32-bit version. However, to run some machine learning models, such as YOLO from Ultralytics, we should use the 64-bit version. Although Raspi-Zero can run a desktop, we will choose the LITE version (no Desktop) to reduce the RAM needed for regular operation.


For Raspi-5: We can select the full 64-bit version, which includes a desktop: Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit)

 

Select your microSD card as the storage device.
Click Next, then go to the Customization tab. The Imager guides you through setting the hostname, the Raspi username and password, configuring WiFi, and enabling SSH (this step is required).
Write the image to the microSD card.


In the examples here, we will use different hostnames depending on the device used: raspi, raspi-5, raspi-Zero, etc. Replace it with the one you are using.





Insert the microSD card into your Raspberry Pi.
Connect power to boot up the Raspberry Pi. For the Raspi-5, use a 5 V/3 A (or 5 A) external power supply. For the Raspi-Zero, use a 5 V/2.5 A external power supply (for light use, the computer’s USB port can also power the Raspi-Zero).

 

Wait for the initial boot process to complete (it may take a few minutes).


You can find the most common Linux commands to be used with the Raspi here or here.







The easiest way to interact with the Raspi-Zero is via SSH (“Headless”). You can use a Terminal (MAC/Linux), PuTTY (Windows), or any other SSH client.

The Raspberry Pi and the computer should be on the same WiFi network. The Raspberry Pi 5 supports dual-band 802.11ac Wi-Fi (2.4 GHz and 5 GHz), whereas the Raspberry Pi Zero 2W supports only 2.4 GHz.


Find your Raspberry Pi’s IP address (for example, check your router).
On your computer, open a terminal and connect via SSH:
ssh username@[raspberry_pi_ip_address]
Alternatively, if you do not have the IP address, you can try the following: bash ssh username@hostname.local for example, ssh mjrovai@rpi-5.local , ssh mjrovai@raspi.local , etc.



img


When you see the prompt:
mjrovai@rpi-5:~ $
It means that you are interacting remotely with your Raspi. It is a good practice to update/upgrade the system regularly. For that, you should run:
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt upgrade
sudo reboot  # Reboot to ensure all updates take effect
You should confirm the Raspi IP address. On the terminal, you can use:
hostname -I

 
Also check the current Python version:
python3 --version
With the latest Raspberry Pi OS (based on Debian Trixie), it should be 3.13:
 
As of January 2026, some packages, such as ExecuTorch, officially support only Python 3.10 to 3.12. Because Debian Trixie ships with Python 3.13 by default, those packages need a compatible Python version installed alongside the system one. One solution is Pyenv, which manages several Python versions for different projects without affecting the system Python. The labs that need it say so; for now, keep the system Python.

On the legacy Raspberry Pi OS (Debian Bookworm), the Python version is 3.11, and Pyenv is not needed.




When you want to turn off your Raspberry Pi, do not simply pull the power cord. The Raspi may still be writing data to the SD card, and cutting power at that moment can cause data loss or a corrupted SD card.
To shut down safely, use the command line:
sudo shutdown -h now

To avoid possible data loss and SD card corruption, before removing the power, you should wait a few seconds after shutdown for the Raspberry Pi’s LED to stop blinking and go dark. Once the LED goes out, it is safe to power down.




Transferring files between the Raspi and our main computer can be done using a pen drive, directly on the terminal (with scp), or an FTP program over the network.




Create a text file on your computer, for example, test.txt.
 

You can use any text editor. In the same terminal, an option is the nano.

To copy the file named test.txt from your personal computer to a user’s home folder on your Raspberry Pi, run the following command from the directory containing test.txt, replacing the <username> placeholder with the username you use to log in to your Raspberry Pi and the <pi_ip_address> placeholder with your Raspberry Pi’s IP address:
$ scp test.txt <username>@<pi_ip_address>:~/

Note that ~/ means that we will move the file to the ROOT of our Raspi. You can choose any folder in your Raspi. But you should create the folder before you run scp, since scp does not create folders automatically.

For example, transfer the file test.txt to the ROOT of the Raspi-Zero, which has an IP of 192.168.4.210:
scp test.txt mjrovai@192.168.4.210:~/
 
The terminals use different profiles to tell them apart. The above action happens on your computer. Now go to the Raspi (using SSH) and check that the file is there:
 



To copy a file named test.txt from a user’s home directory on a Raspberry Pi to the current directory on another computer, run the following command on your Host Computer:
$ scp <username>@<pi_ip_address>:myfile.txt .
For example:
On the Raspi, create a copy of the file with another name:
cp test.txt test_2.txt
And on the Host Computer (in my case, a Mac)
scp mjrovai@192.168.4.210:test_2.txt .
 




Transferring files using FTP, such as FileZilla FTP Client, is also possible. Follow the instructions, install the program for your Desktop OS, and use the Raspi IP address as the Host. For example:
sftp://192.168.4.210
 and enter your Raspi username and password. Pressing Quickconnect will open two windows, one for your host computer desktop (right) and another for the Raspi (left).
 





Using htop, a cross-platform interactive process viewer, you can monitor the resources in use on your Raspi, such as the list of processes, the running CPUs, and the memory used in real time. To launch htop, enter this command in the terminal:
htop
 
Regarding memory, among the devices in the Raspberry Pi family, the Raspi-Zero has the smallest amount of RAM (512 MB), compared to a selection of 2 GB to 16 GB on the Raspis 4 or 5. For any Raspi, it is possible to increase the memory available to the system with “Swap.” Swap memory, also known as swap space, is a technique that lets an operating system temporarily store data from RAM (Random Access Memory) on the SD card when the physical RAM is full. This allows the operating system (OS) to keep running when RAM is full, which can prevent crashes and slowdowns.
Swap memory benefits devices with limited RAM, such as the Raspi-Zero. Increasing swap can help run more demanding applications or processes, but frequent disk access slows the system, so the two must be balanced.
Check the swap memory with htop or with the command:
sudo swapon --show
 

On Debian Trixie, 2 GB of swap memory is configured by default on the Raspi-5 and 512 MB on the Raspi-Zero. Swap is managed by rpi-swap, which reads drop-in configuration files from /etc/rpi/swap.conf.d/. The same mechanism works on both boards. The legacy dphys-swapfile tool used in earlier versions of Raspberry Pi OS no longer applies.




Create the drop-in folder (if it does not exist):
sudo mkdir -p /etc/rpi/swap.conf.d
Create a configuration file, for example, fixedzram.conf:
sudo nano /etc/rpi/swap.conf.d/fixedzram.conf
Set the zram swap (in this case, 4 GiB):
[Main]
Mechanism=zram+file

[Zram]
RamMultiplier=2
MaxSizeMiB=4096

RamMultiplier=2: up to 2\(\times\) the physical RAM (limited by MaxSizeMiB).
MaxSizeMiB=4096: caps it at 4 GB, even if the multiplier permits more.

Reboot:
sudo reboot
Check the result:
swapon --show
free -h

The output should show /dev/zram0 with the new size, 4.0Gi.



By default, the Raspi-Zero’s swap is provided by zram, sized to roughly the physical RAM. This is insufficient for demanding machine learning applications such as YOLO, and on this particular board zram is not merely insufficient but counterproductive.

For machine learning work on the Zero 2 W, use a swap file and disable zram. This is the opposite of the usual advice. zram is a compressed swap device that lives inside RAM: it never removes a page from physical memory, it only stores it more densely. On a board with memory to spare, that is a good trade. The Zero 2 W has about 415 MB usable, and a full zram device consumes roughly a third of it to hold compressed cold pages, memory the running program can no longer use. A swap file on the SD card can genuinely evict a cold page and free real RAM.
Measured on a Zero 2 W running YOLO inference from a notebook (see the Object Detection lab), with zram compared to the same work using an SD swap file only:



Test
zram
SD swap file




YOLO11n, 320
7562 ms
1946 ms


YOLO11n, 640
13541 ms
5426 ms


Segmentation
36552 ms
8409 ms



With zram active, the Linux OOM killer repeatedly terminated the Python process before it could complete. The general lesson for edge AI is that an optimization that helps a laptop can be harmful on a board where RAM is the scarce resource. Always measure on the target hardware.

Two configurations follow: a fixed swap file (on SD/SSD), which is the recommended one for this board, and a fixed zram size, included for completeness.



Create the override directory (if it does not exist):
sudo mkdir -p /etc/rpi/swap.conf.d
Create an override file:
sudo nano /etc/rpi/swap.conf.d/fixedswapsize.conf
Add the following (2 GB = 2048 MiB):
[Main]
Mechanism=swapfile

[File]
FixedSizeMiB=2048

Mechanism=swapfile tells rpi-swap to use a classic swap file.
FixedSizeMiB is the exact size, in MiB.

Apply:
sudo systemctl restart rpi-swap
swapon --show

The output should show /var/swap with the configured size.



If the board runs only light tasks and SD card wear is a concern, a fixed zram size can be used instead. Do not use this configuration for the machine learning labs (see the warning above).

Create the drop-in file:
sudo nano /etc/rpi/swap.conf.d/fixedzram.conf
Set the zram swap:
[Main]
Mechanism=zram

[Zram]
FixedSizeMiB=2048
Apply and check:
sudo systemctl restart rpi-swap
swapon --show

The output should show /dev/zram0 with the new size.




By default, Trixie on the Zero 2 W uses rpi-swap with zram sized roughly to RAM$$1, capped by MaxSizeMiB (usually 2048), and no swap file unless one is added.
Multiple drop-in files in /etc/rpi/swap.conf.d/ are merged, so keep one clear override file per board and use case.

Always verify the result. Setting Mechanism=swapfile should leave the swap file as the only device, but some images also ship a separate systemd zram generator that survives the rpi-swap configuration:
swapon --show
free -h
If /dev/zram0 still appears alongside the swap file, disable it explicitly and reboot:
sudo systemctl mask systemd-zram-setup@zram0.service
sudo reboot
swapon --show
A correct result for machine learning work on the Zero 2 W shows a single entry, the swap file, and no zram device.

A note on the hardware watchdog. systemd arms the BCM2835 hardware watchdog with a 60-second timeout. Under heavy swapping to the SD card, systemd itself can be starved long enough to miss that deadline, and the board resets with no log entry. If the board reboots spontaneously during long, memory-heavy operations such as model conversion, lengthen the timeout in /etc/systemd/system.conf:
sudo sed -i \
  's/^#*RuntimeWatchdogSec=.*/RuntimeWatchdogSec=10min/' \
  /etc/systemd/system.conf
sudo systemctl daemon-reexec
Enabling a persistent journal first makes such events diagnosable, since by default the log does not survive a reboot:
sudo mkdir -p /var/log/journal
sudo systemd-tmpfiles --create --prefix /var/log/journal
sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald


To keep htop running, open another terminal window to continue working with your Raspi.






The Raspi suits computer vision applications, which need a camera. You can install a camera module connected to the Raspi CSI (Camera Serial Interface) port, or a standard USB webcam on the micro-USB port using a USB OTG adapter (Raspi-Zero) or directly on a USB port (Raspi-5).

USB webcams generally have lower quality than camera modules that connect to the CSI port. They also cannot be controlled using the raspistill and raspivid commands in the terminal or the picamera recording package in Python. Nevertheless, a USB camera can be a reasonable choice: it is much easier to set up multiple cameras on a single Raspberry Pi, long cables are possible, or you may simply have such a camera on hand.



There are now several Raspberry Pi camera modules. The original 5-megapixel model was released in 2013, followed by an 8-megapixel Camera Module 2 that was later released in 2016. The latest camera model is the 12-megapixel Camera Module 3, released in 2023.
The original 5 MP camera (Arducam OV5647) is no longer available from Raspberry Pi but can be found from several alternative suppliers. Below is an example of such a camera on a Raspi-Zero.
 
Here is another example of a v2 Camera Module, which has a Sony IMX219 8-megapixel sensor:
 
First, list the installed cameras:
rpicam-hello --list-cameras
If the command is not recognized, install it:
sudo apt install libcamera-apps
List the installed cameras again. If the camera is detected, the output looks like this:
 
Any camera module will work on the Raspberry Pis, but the config.txt file may need to be updated:
sudo nano /boot/firmware/config.txt
At the bottom of the file, for example, to use the 5 MP Arducam OV5647 camera, add the line:
dtoverlay=ov5647,cam0
Or for the v2 module, which has the 8MP Sony IMX219 camera:
dtoverlay=imx219,cam0
Save the file (CTRL+O [ENTER] CTRL+X) and reboot the Raspi:
sudo reboot
After the boot, you can see if the camera is listed:
rpicam-hello --list-cameras
 
 

libcamera is an open-source software library that supports camera systems directly from the Linux operating system on Arm processors. It minimizes proprietary code running on the Broadcom GPU.

Capture a JPEG image with a resolution of \(640{\times}480\) for testing and save it to a file named test_cli_camera.jpg
rpicam-jpeg --output test_cli_camera.jpg --width 640 --height 480
To check that the file was saved, use ls, which lists the contents of the current directory:
 
As before, use scp to view the image:
 
Alternatively, transfer it to your computer using FileZilla.




Power off the Raspi:

sudo shutdown -h now

Connect the USB Webcam (USB Camera Module 30 fps, \(1280{\times}720\)) to your Raspi (this example uses the Raspi-Zero, but the instructions work for all Raspis).

 

Power on again and connect via SSH.
To check if your USB camera is recognized, run:

lsusb
You should see your camera listed in the output.
 

To take a test picture with your USB camera, use:

fswebcam test_image.jpg
This will save an image named “test_image.jpg” in your current directory.
 

Since you are using SSH to connect to the Raspi, transfer the image to your main computer to view it. You can use FileZilla or SCP for this:

Open a terminal on your host computer and run:
scp mjrovai@raspi-zero.local:~/test_image.jpg .

Replace “mjrovai” with your username and “raspi-zero” with Pi’s hostname.

 

If the image quality is not satisfactory, you can adjust various settings; for example, define a resolution that is suitable for YOLO (\(640{\times}640\)):

fswebcam -r 640x640 --no-banner test_image_yolo.jpg
This captures a higher-resolution image without the default banner.
 
An ordinary USB Webcam can also be used:
 
And verified using lsusb
 


To stream video (which is more resource-intensive), install and use mjpg-streamer:
First, install Git:
sudo apt install git
Now install the necessary dependencies for mjpg-streamer, clone the repository, and proceed with the installation:
sudo apt install cmake libjpeg62-turbo-dev
git clone https://github.com/jacksonliam/mjpg-streamer.git
cd mjpg-streamer/mjpg-streamer-experimental
make
sudo make install
Then start the stream with:
mjpg_streamer -i "input_uvc.so" -o "output_http.so -w ./www"
Then open a web browser and navigate to:
http://<your_pi_ip_address>:8080. In my case: http://192.168.4.210:8080
You should see a webpage with options to view the stream. Click on the link that says “Stream” or try accessing:
http://<raspberry_pi_ip_address>:8080/?action=stream
 





So far the Raspberry Pi has been used mainly through terminal commands over SSH, but you can also reach the whole graphical desktop remotely if you installed the complete Raspberry Pi OS (for example, Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit)). This helps with tasks that need a visual interface. It requires a VNC (Virtual Network Computing) server on the Raspberry Pi, set up as follows:

Enable the VNC Server:

Connect to your Raspberry Pi via SSH.
Run the Raspberry Pi configuration tool by entering:
sudo raspi-config
Navigate to Interface Options using the arrow keys.


 

Select VNC and Yes to enable the VNC server.

 

Exit the configuration tool, saving changes when prompted.

 

Install a VNC Viewer on Your Computer:

Download and install a VNC viewer application on your main computer. Popular options include RealVNC Viewer and TightVNC. This tutorial installs VNC Viewer by RealVNC.

Once installed, you should confirm the Raspi IP address. For example, on the terminal, you can use:
hostname -I

 

Connect to Your Raspberry Pi:

Open your VNC viewer application.


 

Enter your Raspberry Pi’s IP address and hostname.
When prompted, enter your Raspberry Pi’s username and password.

 

The Raspberry Pi 5 Desktop should appear on your computer monitor.

 

Adjust Display Settings (if needed):

Once connected, adjust the display resolution to suit your monitor. This can be done through the Raspberry Pi’s desktop settings or by modifying the config.txt file.
Use the desktop settings: open the menu (the Raspberry Icon at the left upper corner) and select the best screen definition for your monitor:


 




Update your system:
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
Install essential software:
sudo apt install python3-pip -y
Install Python packages inside a virtual environment. Raspberry Pi OS marks the system Python as externally managed (PEP 668), so pip install outside a virtual environment is refused by design. Each lab creates its own environment, for example:
python3 -m venv ~/myenv --system-site-packages
source ~/myenv/bin/activate
Do not delete the EXTERNALLY-MANAGED file to bypass this protection: pip could then overwrite packages that the OS depends on.


Avoid using pip for system-level dependencies. Use sudo apt install (outside of a virtual environment, venv) for:

System-level dependencies and libraries
Hardware interface libraries (such as the camera)
Development headers and build tools
Anything that needs to interface directly with hardware


Rule of thumb: Use sudo apt install only for system dependencies and hardware interfaces. Use pip install (without sudo) inside an activated virtual environment for everything else. Inside the venv, pip and pip3 are the same.






Limited processing power, best for lightweight projects
It is better to use a headless setup (SSH) to conserve resources.
Consider increasing swap space for memory-intensive tasks.
It can be used for Image Classification and Object Detection Labs but not for the LLM (SLM).





Suitable for more demanding projects, including AI and machine learning.
It can run the whole desktop environment without difficulty.
Raspi-4 can be used for Image Classification and Object Detection Labs but will not work well with LLMs (SLM) due to high latency.
For Raspi-5, consider using an active cooler for temperature management during intensive tasks, as in the LLMs (SLMs) lab.

Remember to adjust your project requirements based on the specific Raspberry Pi model you’re using. The Raspi-Zero suits low-power, space-constrained projects, while the Raspi-4 or 5 models are better suited for more computationally intensive tasks.




CPU temperature and power consumption on a Raspberry Pi 5 can be measured and monitored with built-in tools and a small shell script.




vcgencmd measure_temp
Example:
temp=47.2'C
This is the SoC (CPU/GPU) temperature in degrees Celsius.



watch -n 2 vcgencmd measure_temp

Updates every 2 seconds.
Press Ctrl+C to stop.




cat /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp
The result is in millidegrees Celsius (for example, 47200 = 47.2 °C). To convert it to a human-readable value:
echo $(($(cat /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp) / 1000))'°C'




The Raspberry Pi 5 exposes its internal PMIC rails through vcgencmd pmic_read_adc:
vcgencmd pmic_read_adc
Example (truncated):
3V3_SYS_A   current(1)=0.06245952A
1V8_SYS_A   current(2)=0.16102850A
...
3V3_SYS_V   volt(13)=3.29687500V
1V8_SYS_V   volt(14)=1.79687500V
...
Power is the sum of \(P_i = V_i \times I_i\) over all rails. This gives the board core power, not the exact wall power, because USB devices and power supply losses are not fully included.



The following script:

Samples once per second for N seconds.
Computes the average CPU temperature.
Sums all PMIC rails to get power.
Applies a linear correction to estimate real board power, based on the RPi5-power calibration.

Create the script:
nano avg_temp_power.sh
Paste:
#!/bin/bash
# avg_temp_power.sh
# Measure average CPU temperature and power on Raspberry Pi 5

SAMPLES=50   # number of samples (1 per second)

TEMP_FILE=$(mktemp)
PMIC_FILE=$(mktemp)

echo "Sampling for ${SAMPLES} seconds..."

for i in $(seq 1 ${SAMPLES}); do
    # --- Temperature (°C) ---
    temp_c=$(vcgencmd measure_temp | cut -d= -f2 | cut -d"'" -f1)
    echo "$temp_c" >> "${TEMP_FILE}"

    # --- PMIC power sum (W) ---
    pmic_line=$(vcgencmd pmic_read_adc)
    volts=($(echo "$pmic_line" \
        | grep -o "volt([^)]*)=[0-9.]*V" | sed 's/.*=//;s/V//'))
    currents=($(echo "$pmic_line" \
        | grep -o "current([^)]*)=[0-9.]*A" | sed 's/.*=//;s/A//'))

    sum_pmic=0
    for idx in "${!volts[@]}"; do
        v=${volts[$idx]}
        i_amp=${currents[$idx]}
        sum_pmic=$(awk -v a="$sum_pmic" -v b="$v" -v c="$i_amp" \
                   'BEGIN{printf "%.8f", a + b*c}')
    done

    echo "$sum_pmic" >> "${PMIC_FILE}"
    sleep 1
done

# --- Compute statistics ---
awk -v corr_a=1.1451 -v corr_b=0.5879 '
function stats(file,   x, n, sum, sum2, mean, std) {
    while ((getline x < file) > 0) {
        n++
        sum  += x
        sum2 += x*x
    }
    close(file)
    if (n > 1) {
        mean = sum / n
        std  = sqrt( (sum2 - (sum*sum)/n) / (n-1) )
    } else {
        mean = sum
        std  = 0
    }
    return mean "|" std
}
BEGIN{
    split(stats("'"${TEMP_FILE}"'"), t, "|")
    t_mean = t[1]
    t_std  = t[2]

    split(stats("'"${PMIC_FILE}"'"), p, "|")
    p_pmic_mean = p[1]
    p_pmic_std  = p[2]

    # Linear correction for real power estimate (RPi5-power calibration)
    p_real_mean = corr_a * p_pmic_mean + corr_b
    p_real_std  = corr_a * p_pmic_std

    printf "Average_temperature = %.2f +/- %.2f °C\n", t_mean, t_std
    printf "Average_pmic_power  = %.3f +/- %.3f W\n", p_pmic_mean, p_pmic_std
    printf "Estimated_real_power = %.3f +/- %.3f W\n", p_real_mean, p_real_std
}
' /dev/null

rm -f "${TEMP_FILE}" "${PMIC_FILE}"
Save, exit, and make it executable:
chmod +x avg_temp_power.sh



Idle baseline:
./avg_temp_power.sh
Example output (50 s window, active fan):
Sampling for 50 seconds...
Average_temperature = 47.25 +/- 0.40 °C
Average_pmic_power  = 2.312 +/- 0.298 W
Estimated_real_power = 3.235 +/- 0.341 W
Then start a heavy workload (for example, Llama 3.2:3B) in another terminal and run the script again during inference. Temperature and power rise, often to around 70–75 °C and 10–11 W with active cooling.
 



Typical Raspberry Pi 5 ranges with active cooling:



State
Temp (°C)
Estimated real power (W)




Idle CLI
40–50
3.0–3.5


Light desktop
50–60
4–5


Moderate CPU load
55–70
5–7

70–80
7–10




Throttling usually starts around 80 °C, with a hard limit at 85 °C.
A board that stays well below that under full load has adequate cooling.

title: Setup
text:
The Raspberry Pi is a versatile single-board computer used by engineers across many disciplines. Developed by the Raspberry Pi Foundation, these compact devices combine low cost, substantial computing capacity, and extensive GPIO (General Purpose Input/Output) capabilities, which suits them to prototyping, embedded systems development, and advanced engineering projects.



Computational Power: Despite their small size, Raspberry Pis offer significant processing capabilities, with the latest models featuring multi-core ARM processors and up to 16 GB of RAM.
GPIO Interface: The 40-pin GPIO header allows direct interaction with sensors, actuators, and other electronic components, which supports hardware-software integration projects.
Extensive Connectivity: Built-in Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Ethernet, and multiple USB ports enable diverse communication and networking projects.
Low-Level Hardware Access: Raspberry Pis provide access to interfaces like I2C, SPI, and UART, allowing detailed control and communication with external devices.
Real-Time Capabilities: With proper configuration, Raspberry Pis can be used for soft real-time applications, making them suitable for control systems and signal processing tasks.
Power Efficiency: Low power consumption enables battery-powered and energy-efficient designs, especially in models like the Pi Zero.





Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W (Raspi-Zero):

Ideal for: Compact embedded systems
Key specs: 1 GHz quad-core CPU (ARM Cortex-A53), 512 MB RAM, minimal power consumption (around 600 mW at idle). The power-off “zombie current” is also very low, around 45 mA (225 mW), well below that of the full-size Raspberry Pi models.

Raspberry Pi 5 (Raspi-5):

Ideal for: More demanding applications such as edge computing, computer vision, and edgeAI applications, including LLMs.
Key specs: 2.4 GHz quad-core CPU (ARM Cortex A-76), up to 16 GB RAM, PCIe interface for expansions, higher power consumption (typically around 3–3.5 W at idle)






Embedded Systems Design: Develop and prototype embedded systems for real-world applications.
IoT and Networked Devices: Create interconnected devices and explore protocols like MQTT, CoAP, and HTTP/HTTPS.
Control Systems: Implement feedback control loops, PID controllers, and interface with actuators.
Computer Vision and AI: Use libraries like OpenCV and TensorFlow Lite for image processing and machine learning at the edge.
Data Acquisition and Analysis: Collect sensor data, perform real-time analysis, and create data logging systems.
Robotics: Build robot controllers, implement motion planning algorithms, and interface with motor drivers.
Signal Processing: Perform real-time signal analysis, filtering, and DSP applications.
Network Security: Set up VPNs, firewalls, and explore network penetration testing.

This tutorial guides you through setting up the most common Raspberry Pi models so that you can start your machine learning project quickly. It covers hardware setup, operating system installation, and initial configuration, with a focus on preparing your Pi for machine learning applications.

title: Setup
text:
Processor: 1 GHz quad-core 64-bit Arm Cortex-A53 CPU
RAM: 512 MB SDRAM
Wireless: 2.4 GHz 802.11 b/g/n wireless LAN, Bluetooth 4.2, BLE
Ports: Mini HDMI, micro USB OTG, CSI-2 camera connector
Power: 5 V/2.5 A via micro USB port (12.5 W Micro USB power supply)




 

Processor:

Pi 5: Quad-core 64-bit Arm Cortex-A76 CPU @ 2.4 GHz
Pi 4: Quad-core Cortex-A72 (ARM v8) 64-bit SoC @ 1.5 GHz

RAM: 2 GB, 4 GB, 8 GB, or 16 GB options (8 GB or more recommended for AI tasks)
Wireless: Dual-band 802.11ac wireless (2.4 GHz and 5 GHz), Bluetooth 5.0
Ports: 2\(\times\) micro HDMI ports, 2\(\times\) USB 3.0 ports, 2\(\times\) USB 2.0 ports, CSI camera port, DSI display port
Power: 5 V/5 A via USB-C connector (27 W USB-C power supply); a 5 V/3 A supply limits USB peripherals to 600 mA


In the labs, we will use different names to address the Raspberry: Raspi, Raspi-5, Raspi-Zero, etc. Usually, Raspi is used when the instructions or comments apply to every model.

title: Setup
text:
An operating system (OS) is the software that manages computer hardware and software resources, providing standard services for computer programs. It is the core software that runs on a computer, acting as an intermediary between hardware and application software. The OS manages the computer’s memory, processes, device drivers, files, and security protocols.

Key functions:

Process management: Allocating CPU time to different programs
Memory management: Allocating and freeing up memory as needed
File system management: Organizing and keeping track of files and directories
Device management: Communicating with connected hardware devices
User interface: Providing a way for users to interact with the computer

Components:

Kernel: The core of the OS that manages hardware resources
Shell: The user interface for interacting with the OS
File system: Organizes and manages data storage
Device drivers: Software that allows the OS to communicate with hardware


The Raspberry Pi runs a specialized version of Linux designed for embedded systems. This operating system, typically a variant of Debian called Raspberry Pi OS (formerly Raspbian), is optimized for the Pi’s ARM-based architecture and limited resources.

The latest version of Raspberry Pi OS (December 2025) is based on Debian Trixie.

Key features:

Lightweight: Tailored to run efficiently on the Pi’s hardware.
Versatile: Supports a wide range of applications and programming languages.
Open-Source: Allows for customization and community-driven improvements.
GPIO support: Enables interaction with sensors and other hardware through the Pi’s pins.
Regular updates: Continuously improved for performance and security.

Embedded Linux on the Raspberry Pi provides a full-featured operating system in a compact package, which suits projects ranging from simple IoT devices to more complex edge machine-learning applications. Its compatibility with standard Linux tools and libraries makes it a capable platform for development and experimentation.



To use the Raspberry Pi, we need an operating system. By default, the Raspberry Pi checks for an operating system on any SD card inserted in the slot, so we should install an operating system using Raspberry Pi Imager.

In November 2025, Raspberry Pi Imager 2.0 was released. It brings a new wizard interface, the option to preconfigure Raspberry Pi Connect, and improved accessibility for screen readers and other assistive technologies.

Raspberry Pi Imager is a tool for downloading and writing images on macOS, Windows, and Linux. It includes many popular operating system images for Raspberry Pi. We will also use the Imager to preconfigure credentials and remote access settings.
Follow the steps to install the OS in your Raspi.

Download and install the Raspberry Pi Imager on your computer.
Insert a microSD card into your computer (a 32GB SD card is recommended) .
Open Raspberry Pi Imager and select your Raspberry Pi model.

 

Choose the appropriate operating system:

For Raspi-Zero: For example, you can select, under Raspberry Pi OS (Other), Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit).


 

Due to its reduced SDRAM (512 MB), the recommended OS for the Raspi-Zero is the 32-bit version. However, to run some machine learning models, such as YOLO from Ultralytics, we should use the 64-bit version. Although Raspi-Zero can run a desktop, we will choose the LITE version (no Desktop) to reduce the RAM needed for regular operation.


For Raspi-5: We can select the full 64-bit version, which includes a desktop: Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit)

 

Select your microSD card as the storage device.
Click Next, then go to the Customization tab. The Imager guides you through setting the hostname, the Raspi username and password, configuring WiFi, and enabling SSH (this step is required).
Write the image to the microSD card.


In the examples here, we will use different hostnames depending on the device used: raspi, raspi-5, raspi-Zero, etc. Replace it with the one you are using.





Insert the microSD card into your Raspberry Pi.
Connect power to boot up the Raspberry Pi. For the Raspi-5, use a 5 V/3 A (or 5 A) external power supply. For the Raspi-Zero, use a 5 V/2.5 A external power supply (for light use, the computer’s USB port can also power the Raspi-Zero).

 

Wait for the initial boot process to complete (it may take a few minutes).


You can find the most common Linux commands to be used with the Raspi here or here.

title: Setup
text:
The easiest way to interact with the Raspi-Zero is via SSH (“Headless”). You can use a Terminal (MAC/Linux), PuTTY (Windows), or any other SSH client.

The Raspberry Pi and the computer should be on the same WiFi network. The Raspberry Pi 5 supports dual-band 802.11ac Wi-Fi (2.4 GHz and 5 GHz), whereas the Raspberry Pi Zero 2W supports only 2.4 GHz.


Find your Raspberry Pi’s IP address (for example, check your router).
On your computer, open a terminal and connect via SSH:
ssh username@[raspberry_pi_ip_address]
Alternatively, if you do not have the IP address, you can try the following: bash ssh username@hostname.local for example, ssh mjrovai@rpi-5.local , ssh mjrovai@raspi.local , etc.



img


When you see the prompt:
mjrovai@rpi-5:~ $
It means that you are interacting remotely with your Raspi. It is a good practice to update/upgrade the system regularly. For that, you should run:
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt upgrade
sudo reboot  # Reboot to ensure all updates take effect
You should confirm the Raspi IP address. On the terminal, you can use:
hostname -I

 
Also check the current Python version:
python3 --version
With the latest Raspberry Pi OS (based on Debian Trixie), it should be 3.13:
 
As of January 2026, some packages, such as ExecuTorch, officially support only Python 3.10 to 3.12. Because Debian Trixie ships with Python 3.13 by default, those packages need a compatible Python version installed alongside the system one. One solution is Pyenv, which manages several Python versions for different projects without affecting the system Python. The labs that need it say so; for now, keep the system Python.

On the legacy Raspberry Pi OS (Debian Bookworm), the Python version is 3.11, and Pyenv is not needed.




When you want to turn off your Raspberry Pi, do not simply pull the power cord. The Raspi may still be writing data to the SD card, and cutting power at that moment can cause data loss or a corrupted SD card.
To shut down safely, use the command line:
sudo shutdown -h now

To avoid possible data loss and SD card corruption, before removing the power, you should wait a few seconds after shutdown for the Raspberry Pi’s LED to stop blinking and go dark. Once the LED goes out, it is safe to power down.




Transferring files between the Raspi and our main computer can be done using a pen drive, directly on the terminal (with scp), or an FTP program over the network.




Create a text file on your computer, for example, test.txt.
 

You can use any text editor. In the same terminal, an option is the nano.

To copy the file named test.txt from your personal computer to a user’s home folder on your Raspberry Pi, run the following command from the directory containing test.txt, replacing the <username> placeholder with the username you use to log in to your Raspberry Pi and the <pi_ip_address> placeholder with your Raspberry Pi’s IP address:
$ scp test.txt <username>@<pi_ip_address>:~/

Note that ~/ means that we will move the file to the ROOT of our Raspi. You can choose any folder in your Raspi. But you should create the folder before you run scp, since scp does not create folders automatically.

For example, transfer the file test.txt to the ROOT of the Raspi-Zero, which has an IP of 192.168.4.210:
scp test.txt mjrovai@192.168.4.210:~/
 
The terminals use different profiles to tell them apart. The above action happens on your computer. Now go to the Raspi (using SSH) and check that the file is there:
 



To copy a file named test.txt from a user’s home directory on a Raspberry Pi to the current directory on another computer, run the following command on your Host Computer:
$ scp <username>@<pi_ip_address>:myfile.txt .
For example:
On the Raspi, create a copy of the file with another name:
cp test.txt test_2.txt
And on the Host Computer (in my case, a Mac)
scp mjrovai@192.168.4.210:test_2.txt .
 




Transferring files using FTP, such as FileZilla FTP Client, is also possible. Follow the instructions, install the program for your Desktop OS, and use the Raspi IP address as the Host. For example:
sftp://192.168.4.210
 and enter your Raspi username and password. Pressing Quickconnect will open two windows, one for your host computer desktop (right) and another for the Raspi (left).

title: Setup
text:
Using htop, a cross-platform interactive process viewer, you can monitor the resources in use on your Raspi, such as the list of processes, the running CPUs, and the memory used in real time. To launch htop, enter this command in the terminal:
htop
 
Regarding memory, among the devices in the Raspberry Pi family, the Raspi-Zero has the smallest amount of RAM (512 MB), compared to a selection of 2 GB to 16 GB on the Raspis 4 or 5. For any Raspi, it is possible to increase the memory available to the system with “Swap.” Swap memory, also known as swap space, is a technique that lets an operating system temporarily store data from RAM (Random Access Memory) on the SD card when the physical RAM is full. This allows the operating system (OS) to keep running when RAM is full, which can prevent crashes and slowdowns.
Swap memory benefits devices with limited RAM, such as the Raspi-Zero. Increasing swap can help run more demanding applications or processes, but frequent disk access slows the system, so the two must be balanced.
Check the swap memory with htop or with the command:
sudo swapon --show
 

On Debian Trixie, 2 GB of swap memory is configured by default on the Raspi-5 and 512 MB on the Raspi-Zero. Swap is managed by rpi-swap, which reads drop-in configuration files from /etc/rpi/swap.conf.d/. The same mechanism works on both boards. The legacy dphys-swapfile tool used in earlier versions of Raspberry Pi OS no longer applies.




Create the drop-in folder (if it does not exist):
sudo mkdir -p /etc/rpi/swap.conf.d
Create a configuration file, for example, fixedzram.conf:
sudo nano /etc/rpi/swap.conf.d/fixedzram.conf
Set the zram swap (in this case, 4 GiB):
[Main]
Mechanism=zram+file

[Zram]
RamMultiplier=2
MaxSizeMiB=4096

RamMultiplier=2: up to 2\(\times\) the physical RAM (limited by MaxSizeMiB).
MaxSizeMiB=4096: caps it at 4 GB, even if the multiplier permits more.

Reboot:
sudo reboot
Check the result:
swapon --show
free -h

The output should show /dev/zram0 with the new size, 4.0Gi.



By default, the Raspi-Zero’s swap is provided by zram, sized to roughly the physical RAM. This is insufficient for demanding machine learning applications such as YOLO, and on this particular board zram is not merely insufficient but counterproductive.

For machine learning work on the Zero 2 W, use a swap file and disable zram. This is the opposite of the usual advice. zram is a compressed swap device that lives inside RAM: it never removes a page from physical memory, it only stores it more densely. On a board with memory to spare, that is a good trade. The Zero 2 W has about 415 MB usable, and a full zram device consumes roughly a third of it to hold compressed cold pages, memory the running program can no longer use. A swap file on the SD card can genuinely evict a cold page and free real RAM.
Measured on a Zero 2 W running YOLO inference from a notebook (see the Object Detection lab), with zram compared to the same work using an SD swap file only:



Test
zram
SD swap file




YOLO11n, 320
7562 ms
1946 ms


YOLO11n, 640
13541 ms
5426 ms


Segmentation
36552 ms
8409 ms



With zram active, the Linux OOM killer repeatedly terminated the Python process before it could complete. The general lesson for edge AI is that an optimization that helps a laptop can be harmful on a board where RAM is the scarce resource. Always measure on the target hardware.

Two configurations follow: a fixed swap file (on SD/SSD), which is the recommended one for this board, and a fixed zram size, included for completeness.



Create the override directory (if it does not exist):
sudo mkdir -p /etc/rpi/swap.conf.d
Create an override file:
sudo nano /etc/rpi/swap.conf.d/fixedswapsize.conf
Add the following (2 GB = 2048 MiB):
[Main]
Mechanism=swapfile

[File]
FixedSizeMiB=2048

Mechanism=swapfile tells rpi-swap to use a classic swap file.
FixedSizeMiB is the exact size, in MiB.

Apply:
sudo systemctl restart rpi-swap
swapon --show

The output should show /var/swap with the configured size.



If the board runs only light tasks and SD card wear is a concern, a fixed zram size can be used instead. Do not use this configuration for the machine learning labs (see the warning above).

Create the drop-in file:
sudo nano /etc/rpi/swap.conf.d/fixedzram.conf
Set the zram swap:
[Main]
Mechanism=zram

[Zram]
FixedSizeMiB=2048
Apply and check:
sudo systemctl restart rpi-swap
swapon --show

The output should show /dev/zram0 with the new size.




By default, Trixie on the Zero 2 W uses rpi-swap with zram sized roughly to RAM$$1, capped by MaxSizeMiB (usually 2048), and no swap file unless one is added.
Multiple drop-in files in /etc/rpi/swap.conf.d/ are merged, so keep one clear override file per board and use case.

Always verify the result. Setting Mechanism=swapfile should leave the swap file as the only device, but some images also ship a separate systemd zram generator that survives the rpi-swap configuration:
swapon --show
free -h
If /dev/zram0 still appears alongside the swap file, disable it explicitly and reboot:
sudo systemctl mask systemd-zram-setup@zram0.service
sudo reboot
swapon --show
A correct result for machine learning work on the Zero 2 W shows a single entry, the swap file, and no zram device.

A note on the hardware watchdog. systemd arms the BCM2835 hardware watchdog with a 60-second timeout. Under heavy swapping to the SD card, systemd itself can be starved long enough to miss that deadline, and the board resets with no log entry. If the board reboots spontaneously during long, memory-heavy operations such as model conversion, lengthen the timeout in /etc/systemd/system.conf:
sudo sed -i \
  's/^#*RuntimeWatchdogSec=.*/RuntimeWatchdogSec=10min/' \
  /etc/systemd/system.conf
sudo systemctl daemon-reexec
Enabling a persistent journal first makes such events diagnosable, since by default the log does not survive a reboot:
sudo mkdir -p /var/log/journal
sudo systemd-tmpfiles --create --prefix /var/log/journal
sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald


To keep htop running, open another terminal window to continue working with your Raspi.

title: Setup
text:
The Raspi suits computer vision applications, which need a camera. You can install a camera module connected to the Raspi CSI (Camera Serial Interface) port, or a standard USB webcam on the micro-USB port using a USB OTG adapter (Raspi-Zero) or directly on a USB port (Raspi-5).

USB webcams generally have lower quality than camera modules that connect to the CSI port. They also cannot be controlled using the raspistill and raspivid commands in the terminal or the picamera recording package in Python. Nevertheless, a USB camera can be a reasonable choice: it is much easier to set up multiple cameras on a single Raspberry Pi, long cables are possible, or you may simply have such a camera on hand.



There are now several Raspberry Pi camera modules. The original 5-megapixel model was released in 2013, followed by an 8-megapixel Camera Module 2 that was later released in 2016. The latest camera model is the 12-megapixel Camera Module 3, released in 2023.
The original 5 MP camera (Arducam OV5647) is no longer available from Raspberry Pi but can be found from several alternative suppliers. Below is an example of such a camera on a Raspi-Zero.
 
Here is another example of a v2 Camera Module, which has a Sony IMX219 8-megapixel sensor:
 
First, list the installed cameras:
rpicam-hello --list-cameras
If the command is not recognized, install it:
sudo apt install libcamera-apps
List the installed cameras again. If the camera is detected, the output looks like this:
 
Any camera module will work on the Raspberry Pis, but the config.txt file may need to be updated:
sudo nano /boot/firmware/config.txt
At the bottom of the file, for example, to use the 5 MP Arducam OV5647 camera, add the line:
dtoverlay=ov5647,cam0
Or for the v2 module, which has the 8MP Sony IMX219 camera:
dtoverlay=imx219,cam0
Save the file (CTRL+O [ENTER] CTRL+X) and reboot the Raspi:
sudo reboot
After the boot, you can see if the camera is listed:
rpicam-hello --list-cameras
 
 

libcamera is an open-source software library that supports camera systems directly from the Linux operating system on Arm processors. It minimizes proprietary code running on the Broadcom GPU.

Capture a JPEG image with a resolution of \(640{\times}480\) for testing and save it to a file named test_cli_camera.jpg
rpicam-jpeg --output test_cli_camera.jpg --width 640 --height 480
To check that the file was saved, use ls, which lists the contents of the current directory:
 
As before, use scp to view the image:
 
Alternatively, transfer it to your computer using FileZilla.




Power off the Raspi:

sudo shutdown -h now

Connect the USB Webcam (USB Camera Module 30 fps, \(1280{\times}720\)) to your Raspi (this example uses the Raspi-Zero, but the instructions work for all Raspis).

 

Power on again and connect via SSH.
To check if your USB camera is recognized, run:

lsusb
You should see your camera listed in the output.
 

To take a test picture with your USB camera, use:

fswebcam test_image.jpg
This will save an image named “test_image.jpg” in your current directory.
 

Since you are using SSH to connect to the Raspi, transfer the image to your main computer to view it. You can use FileZilla or SCP for this:

Open a terminal on your host computer and run:
scp mjrovai@raspi-zero.local:~/test_image.jpg .

Replace “mjrovai” with your username and “raspi-zero” with Pi’s hostname.

 

If the image quality is not satisfactory, you can adjust various settings; for example, define a resolution that is suitable for YOLO (\(640{\times}640\)):

fswebcam -r 640x640 --no-banner test_image_yolo.jpg
This captures a higher-resolution image without the default banner.
 
An ordinary USB Webcam can also be used:
 
And verified using lsusb
 


To stream video (which is more resource-intensive), install and use mjpg-streamer:
First, install Git:
sudo apt install git
Now install the necessary dependencies for mjpg-streamer, clone the repository, and proceed with the installation:
sudo apt install cmake libjpeg62-turbo-dev
git clone https://github.com/jacksonliam/mjpg-streamer.git
cd mjpg-streamer/mjpg-streamer-experimental
make
sudo make install
Then start the stream with:
mjpg_streamer -i "input_uvc.so" -o "output_http.so -w ./www"
Then open a web browser and navigate to:
http://<your_pi_ip_address>:8080. In my case: http://192.168.4.210:8080
You should see a webpage with options to view the stream. Click on the link that says “Stream” or try accessing:
http://<raspberry_pi_ip_address>:8080/?action=stream

title: Setup
text:
So far the Raspberry Pi has been used mainly through terminal commands over SSH, but you can also reach the whole graphical desktop remotely if you installed the complete Raspberry Pi OS (for example, Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit)). This helps with tasks that need a visual interface. It requires a VNC (Virtual Network Computing) server on the Raspberry Pi, set up as follows:

Enable the VNC Server:

Connect to your Raspberry Pi via SSH.
Run the Raspberry Pi configuration tool by entering:
sudo raspi-config
Navigate to Interface Options using the arrow keys.


 

Select VNC and Yes to enable the VNC server.

 

Exit the configuration tool, saving changes when prompted.

 

Install a VNC Viewer on Your Computer:

Download and install a VNC viewer application on your main computer. Popular options include RealVNC Viewer and TightVNC. This tutorial installs VNC Viewer by RealVNC.

Once installed, you should confirm the Raspi IP address. For example, on the terminal, you can use:
hostname -I

 

Connect to Your Raspberry Pi:

Open your VNC viewer application.


 

Enter your Raspberry Pi’s IP address and hostname.
When prompted, enter your Raspberry Pi’s username and password.

 

The Raspberry Pi 5 Desktop should appear on your computer monitor.

 

Adjust Display Settings (if needed):

Once connected, adjust the display resolution to suit your monitor. This can be done through the Raspberry Pi’s desktop settings or by modifying the config.txt file.
Use the desktop settings: open the menu (the Raspberry Icon at the left upper corner) and select the best screen definition for your monitor:

title: Setup
text:
Update your system:
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
Install essential software:
sudo apt install python3-pip -y
Install Python packages inside a virtual environment. Raspberry Pi OS marks the system Python as externally managed (PEP 668), so pip install outside a virtual environment is refused by design. Each lab creates its own environment, for example:
python3 -m venv ~/myenv --system-site-packages
source ~/myenv/bin/activate
Do not delete the EXTERNALLY-MANAGED file to bypass this protection: pip could then overwrite packages that the OS depends on.


Avoid using pip for system-level dependencies. Use sudo apt install (outside of a virtual environment, venv) for:

System-level dependencies and libraries
Hardware interface libraries (such as the camera)
Development headers and build tools
Anything that needs to interface directly with hardware


Rule of thumb: Use sudo apt install only for system dependencies and hardware interfaces. Use pip install (without sudo) inside an activated virtual environment for everything else. Inside the venv, pip and pip3 are the same.

title: Setup
text:
Limited processing power, best for lightweight projects
It is better to use a headless setup (SSH) to conserve resources.
Consider increasing swap space for memory-intensive tasks.
It can be used for Image Classification and Object Detection Labs but not for the LLM (SLM).





Suitable for more demanding projects, including AI and machine learning.
It can run the whole desktop environment without difficulty.
Raspi-4 can be used for Image Classification and Object Detection Labs but will not work well with LLMs (SLM) due to high latency.
For Raspi-5, consider using an active cooler for temperature management during intensive tasks, as in the LLMs (SLMs) lab.

Remember to adjust your project requirements based on the specific Raspberry Pi model you’re using. The Raspi-Zero suits low-power, space-constrained projects, while the Raspi-4 or 5 models are better suited for more computationally intensive tasks.

title: Setup
text:
CPU temperature and power consumption on a Raspberry Pi 5 can be measured and monitored with built-in tools and a small shell script.




vcgencmd measure_temp
Example:
temp=47.2'C
This is the SoC (CPU/GPU) temperature in degrees Celsius.



watch -n 2 vcgencmd measure_temp

Updates every 2 seconds.
Press Ctrl+C to stop.




cat /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp
The result is in millidegrees Celsius (for example, 47200 = 47.2 °C). To convert it to a human-readable value:
echo $(($(cat /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp) / 1000))'°C'




The Raspberry Pi 5 exposes its internal PMIC rails through vcgencmd pmic_read_adc:
vcgencmd pmic_read_adc
Example (truncated):
3V3_SYS_A   current(1)=0.06245952A
1V8_SYS_A   current(2)=0.16102850A
...
3V3_SYS_V   volt(13)=3.29687500V
1V8_SYS_V   volt(14)=1.79687500V
...
Power is the sum of \(P_i = V_i \times I_i\) over all rails. This gives the board core power, not the exact wall power, because USB devices and power supply losses are not fully included.



The following script:

Samples once per second for N seconds.
Computes the average CPU temperature.
Sums all PMIC rails to get power.
Applies a linear correction to estimate real board power, based on the RPi5-power calibration.

Create the script:
nano avg_temp_power.sh
Paste:
#!/bin/bash
# avg_temp_power.sh
# Measure average CPU temperature and power on Raspberry Pi 5

SAMPLES=50   # number of samples (1 per second)

TEMP_FILE=$(mktemp)
PMIC_FILE=$(mktemp)

echo "Sampling for ${SAMPLES} seconds..."

for i in $(seq 1 ${SAMPLES}); do
    # --- Temperature (°C) ---
    temp_c=$(vcgencmd measure_temp | cut -d= -f2 | cut -d"'" -f1)
    echo "$temp_c" >> "${TEMP_FILE}"

    # --- PMIC power sum (W) ---
    pmic_line=$(vcgencmd pmic_read_adc)
    volts=($(echo "$pmic_line" \
        | grep -o "volt([^)]*)=[0-9.]*V" | sed 's/.*=//;s/V//'))
    currents=($(echo "$pmic_line" \
        | grep -o "current([^)]*)=[0-9.]*A" | sed 's/.*=//;s/A//'))

    sum_pmic=0
    for idx in "${!volts[@]}"; do
        v=${volts[$idx]}
        i_amp=${currents[$idx]}
        sum_pmic=$(awk -v a="$sum_pmic" -v b="$v" -v c="$i_amp" \
                   'BEGIN{printf "%.8f", a + b*c}')
    done

    echo "$sum_pmic" >> "${PMIC_FILE}"
    sleep 1
done

# --- Compute statistics ---
awk -v corr_a=1.1451 -v corr_b=0.5879 '
function stats(file,   x, n, sum, sum2, mean, std) {
    while ((getline x < file) > 0) {
        n++
        sum  += x
        sum2 += x*x
    }
    close(file)
    if (n > 1) {
        mean = sum / n
        std  = sqrt( (sum2 - (sum*sum)/n) / (n-1) )
    } else {
        mean = sum
        std  = 0
    }
    return mean "|" std
}
BEGIN{
    split(stats("'"${TEMP_FILE}"'"), t, "|")
    t_mean = t[1]
    t_std  = t[2]

    split(stats("'"${PMIC_FILE}"'"), p, "|")
    p_pmic_mean = p[1]
    p_pmic_std  = p[2]

    # Linear correction for real power estimate (RPi5-power calibration)
    p_real_mean = corr_a * p_pmic_mean + corr_b
    p_real_std  = corr_a * p_pmic_std

    printf "Average_temperature = %.2f +/- %.2f °C\n", t_mean, t_std
    printf "Average_pmic_power  = %.3f +/- %.3f W\n", p_pmic_mean, p_pmic_std
    printf "Estimated_real_power = %.3f +/- %.3f W\n", p_real_mean, p_real_std
}
' /dev/null

rm -f "${TEMP_FILE}" "${PMIC_FILE}"
Save, exit, and make it executable:
chmod +x avg_temp_power.sh



Idle baseline:
./avg_temp_power.sh
Example output (50 s window, active fan):
Sampling for 50 seconds...
Average_temperature = 47.25 +/- 0.40 °C
Average_pmic_power  = 2.312 +/- 0.298 W
Estimated_real_power = 3.235 +/- 0.341 W
Then start a heavy workload (for example, Llama 3.2:3B) in another terminal and run the script again during inference. Temperature and power rise, often to around 70–75 °C and 10–11 W with active cooling.
 



Typical Raspberry Pi 5 ranges with active cooling:



State
Temp (°C)
Estimated real power (W)




Idle CLI
40–50
3.0–3.5


Light desktop
50–60
4–5


Moderate CPU load
55–70
5–7


Heavy CPU/GPU
70–80
7–10




Throttling usually starts around 80 °C, with a hard limit at 85 °C.
A board that stays well below that under full load has adequate cooling.

title: IDE Setup
text:
Every lab depends on a working development environment. Unlike cloud-based ML development, where the infrastructure is hidden, embedded work requires you to understand the whole toolchain, from compiling code to deploying it on the board.
Environment setup typically takes 30-60 minutes, depending on platform choice and internet speed. These procedures are designed for students with no prior embedded systems experience.


Before beginning installation, verify your development computer meets these requirements:
Development Computer:

Operating System: Windows 10/11, macOS 10.15+, or Linux (Ubuntu 18.04+)
Memory: 8GB RAM minimum (16GB recommended for Raspberry Pi development)
Storage: 10GB free space for development tools and libraries
USB Ports: At least one USB 2.0/3.0 port for device connection
Internet Connection: Required for software installation and library downloads

Software Prerequisites:

Arduino IDE 2.0+ for Arduino-based platforms (XIAO, Nicla Vision)
Python 3.8+ for Raspberry Pi development
Git for version control and example code access
Text Editor/IDE such as VS Code or PyCharm

Hardware Accessories:

USB cables: USB-C or Micro-USB (must support data transfer, not power-only)
SD Card: 32GB+ Class 10 for Raspberry Pi
Power adapters: Appropriate for each platform
Camera modules: Included with most kits or available separately




Each platform uses a different development approach, as in real embedded engineering. Arduino-based boards stress resource efficiency and real-time constraints, the Raspberry Pi is a full edge computer, the Arduino UNO Q pairs a Linux processor with a microcontroller, and the Grove Vision AI V2 adds a dedicated accelerator.
Select the installation procedures appropriate for your chosen hardware platform.


Arduino-based boards give direct hardware control with few abstraction layers, which makes resource constraints and optimization easy to see. Each code change shows its effect on the board right away.
Arduino IDE Installation:

Download Arduino IDE 2.0 from arduino.cc/software
Install following the platform-specific setup wizard
Launch Arduino IDE and navigate to File → Preferences
Add board support URLs:

For XIAOML Kit: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json
For Nicla Vision: URL provided in Arduino IDE Board Manager


Board Package Installation:

Open Tools → Board → Boards Manager
Search for your platform:

XIAOML Kit: Search “ESP32” and install “esp32 by Espressif Systems”
Nicla Vision: Search “Arduino Mbed OS Nicla Boards” and install

Select your board from Tools → Board menu
Install required libraries via Library Manager

Essential Libraries:

TensorFlow Lite Micro
Platform-specific camera drivers
Sensor interface libraries (I2C, SPI)




This platform introduces hardware-accelerated AI through a dedicated neural processing unit, which runs inference faster than a general-purpose processor can. The visual interface supports quick prototyping, and the Arduino IDE allows more customization.
SenseCraft AI Setup:

Create an account at sensecraft.seeed.cc
Connect Grove Vision AI V2 via USB
Access the device through the SenseCraft AI web interface
No local software installation required for the visual programming workflow

Arduino IDE Setup (for custom development):
Follow Arduino-based platform instructions above, using the Seeed Studio board package URL in the board manager.



The Raspberry Pi combines embedded constraints with a full computer, so students work with both resource optimization and full ML frameworks. Comparing the two shows how available compute shapes the choice of algorithm and system design.
Operating System Installation:

Download Raspberry Pi Imager
Flash Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit recommended) to a microSD card (32GB minimum)
Configure SSH access and WiFi credentials during the imaging process
Insert the flashed SD card and boot the Raspberry Pi

Software Environment Setup:
The following commands install a Python ML development environment and isolate its packages in a virtual environment:
# Update system packages
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

# Install Python development tools
# python3-pip: Python package installer
# python3-venv: Virtual environment creation
# python3-dev: Python development headers
sudo apt install python3-pip \
                 python3-venv \
                 python3-dev -y

# Install ML framework dependencies
# libatlas-base-dev: Linear algebra library (BLAS/LAPACK)
# libhdf5-dev: HDF5 data format library
# libhdf5-serial-dev: HDF5 serial version
sudo apt install libatlas-base-dev \
                 libhdf5-dev \
                 libhdf5-serial-dev -y

# Install computer vision dependencies
# libcamera-dev: Camera interface library
# python3-libcamera: Python bindings for libcamera
# python3-kms++: Kernel mode setting library
sudo apt install libcamera-dev \
                 python3-libcamera \
                 python3-kms++ -y

# Create virtual environment for projects
python3 -m venv ~/ml_projects
source ~/ml_projects/bin/activate

# Install core ML packages
# tensorflow: Main ML framework
# tensorflow-lite: Optimized for edge/mobile devices
# opencv-python: Computer vision library
# numpy: Numerical computing foundation
pip install tensorflow \
            tensorflow-lite \
            opencv-python \
            numpy



The UNO Q runs Debian Linux on its microprocessor and an Arduino sketch on its microcontroller, so development happens over a terminal rather than through the Arduino IDE. Apps combine Python code on Linux with a sketch on the MCU, and arduino-app-cli builds and runs both.
Host Tools:

Install ADB (android-tools-adb on Debian/Ubuntu, android-platform-tools with Homebrew on macOS, or SDK Platform-Tools on Windows)
Use the SSH and SCP clients built into Linux and macOS, or available on Windows
Optionally, install VS Code with the Remote-SSH extension

Board Setup:

Optionally, flash the latest Debian image with arduino-flasher-cli
Connect over USB-C and open a shell with adb shell
Change the default password and connect the board to Wi-Fi with nmcli
Enable network mode with arduino-app-cli system network-mode enable, then connect with ssh arduino@<UNO_Q_IP_ADDRESS>

The UNO Q Setup lab walks through each step.




These settings let your computer communicate reliably with the board. Every lab uses them to upload code, debug, and monitor performance.


Serial communication is the main way to debug an embedded system and read its data. It shows how the system behaves, including where it hits performance limits.
Windows:

Install appropriate USB-to-serial drivers (CH340, FTDI, or platform-specific)
Configure Device Manager to recognize the development board

macOS/Linux:

Most USB-to-serial adapters work without additional drivers
Verify device detection: ls /dev/tty* (macOS/Linux)
Add user to dialout group: sudo usermod -a -G dialout $USER (Linux)




These settings determine how quickly you can write, test, and upload code. A correct configuration shortens debugging and gives clear feedback on system performance.
Arduino IDE Settings:

Configure the appropriate COM port under Tools → Port
Set the correct board and processor selection
Verify upload speed (typically 115200 baud)
Enable verbose output during compilation for debugging

Raspberry Pi Development:

Configure SSH keys for remote development
Install VS Code with Python and Remote SSH extensions
Set up Jupyter notebook access for interactive development





These tests confirm that your computer can communicate with the board and run basic programs. Run them before starting the more complex labs.

Software Environment Setup:
The following commands install a Python ML development environment and isolate its packages in a virtual environment:
# Update system packages
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

# Install Python development tools
# python3-pip: Python package installer
# python3-venv: Virtual environment creation
# python3-dev: Python development headers
sudo apt install python3-pip \
                 python3-venv \
                 python3-dev -y

# Install ML framework dependencies
# libatlas-base-dev: Linear algebra library (BLAS/LAPACK)
# libhdf5-dev: HDF5 data format library
# libhdf5-serial-dev: HDF5 serial version
sudo apt install libatlas-base-dev \
                 libhdf5-dev \
                 libhdf5-serial-dev -y

# Install computer vision dependencies
# libcamera-dev: Camera interface library
# python3-libcamera: Python bindings for libcamera
# python3-kms++: Kernel mode setting library
sudo apt install libcamera-dev \
                 python3-libcamera \
                 python3-kms++ -y

# Create virtual environment for projects
python3 -m venv ~/ml_projects
source ~/ml_projects/bin/activate

# Install core ML packages
# tensorflow: Main ML framework
# tensorflow-lite: Optimized for edge/mobile devices
# opencv-python: Computer vision library
# numpy: Numerical computing foundation
pip install tensorflow \
            tensorflow-lite \
            opencv-python \
            numpy
