TipBest For: IoT & Wireless ML



The XIAOML Kit excels at wireless connectivity and cost-sensitive deployments. It suits IoT sensor networks, remote monitoring systems, and wireless ML inference, where a device needs reliable connectivity in a compact, low-cost package.


The XIAOML Kit bundles the XIAO ESP32S3 Sense board with an expansion board, providing a complete TinyML development environment. The XIAO ESP32S3 Sense alone provides camera and microphone capabilities (vision and sound), while the kit’s expansion board adds a 6-axis IMU for motion classification. The name “XIAO” (小) translates to “tiny” in Chinese, reflecting the board’s \(21{\times}17.5\) mm form factor.



XIAOML Kit with expansion board


Processor Architecture: ESP32-S3 dual-core Xtensa LX7 running at 240MHz
Memory Hierarchy: 8MB PSRAM and 8MB Flash storage
Connectivity: WiFi 802.11 b/g/n and Bluetooth 5.0
Included Sensors:

XIAO ESP32S3 Sense: OV2640 camera sensor, digital microphone
Expansion Board: 6-axis inertial measurement unit (IMU), 0.42” OLED display

Power Characteristics: 3.3V operation with multiple low-power modes
Development Environment: Arduino IDE and PlatformIO support, with a large library collection. Supports C/C++ programming with Arduino-style abstractions and direct ESP-IDF for advanced users.
Application Focus: IoT sensor networks, remote monitoring systems, wireless ML inference, cost-sensitive deployments









TipBest For: Ultra-Low Power Design



The Arduino Nicla Vision is optimized for battery-powered devices and always-on sensing applications. It suits ultra-low-power design, image classification, and object detection, where battery life is measured in months, not hours.


The Nicla Vision is a professional-grade embedded vision board built around the STM32H7 microcontroller. It runs ML inference within tight memory and power limits.



Arduino Nicla Vision with camera module


Processor Architecture: STM32H747 dual-core ARM Cortex-M7/M4 running at 480MHz
Memory Hierarchy: 1MB integrated SRAM and 2MB Flash storage, plus 16MB external QSPI Flash
Integrated Sensors: GC2145 camera sensor, MP34DT05 digital microphone, 6-axis IMU
Power Characteristics: 3.3V operation optimized for battery-powered deployment
Development Environment: Arduino IDE and OpenMV IDE support with specialized computer vision libraries. MicroPython support for rapid prototyping alongside C/C++ for production deployments.
Application Focus: Battery-powered devices, image classification systems, object detection applications, always-on sensing









TipBest For: Hardware Acceleration



The Grove Vision AI V2 has a dedicated neural processing unit (NPU) that runs inference much faster than software alone. It suits industrial inspection, real-time video analytics, and object detection that needs NPU-accelerated inference.


The Grove Vision AI V2 includes a neural processing unit (NPU) for hardware-accelerated inference. This platform shows how a specialized AI processor runs inference much faster than a software-only implementation.



Grove Vision AI V2 with NPU


Processor Architecture: ARM Cortex-M55 with integrated Ethos-U55 NPU
Memory Hierarchy: 16MB external memory for model and data storage
Neural Processing Unit: Dedicated hardware accelerator for ML inference
Camera Interface: Standard CSI connector supporting various camera modules
Audio Input: Onboard digital microphone
Development Environment: SenseCraft AI visual programming platform for no-code development, with Arduino IDE support for custom applications. Supports both graphical programming and traditional C/C++ development workflows.
Application Focus: Industrial inspection systems, real-time video analytics, advanced object detection, NPU-accelerated inference









TipBest For: Full ML Frameworks



The Raspberry Pi bridges embedded systems and traditional computing, providing a complete Linux environment for advanced ML applications. It suits edge AI gateways, advanced computer vision, language model deployment, and multi-modal applications that need a full computer.


The Raspberry Pi family bridges embedded systems and traditional computing, providing a full Linux environment at a price students can afford. Its extra compute and memory allow more demanding ML applications.



Raspberry Pi 5 and Pi Zero 2W comparison


Processor Architecture: ARM Cortex-A76 (Pi 5) or Cortex-A53 (Zero 2W)
Memory Hierarchy: 1-16GB DDR4 RAM depending on model
Storage: MicroSD card primary storage with USB 3.0 expansion
Connectivity: Gigabit Ethernet, WiFi, Bluetooth, multiple USB ports
Camera Interface: Dedicated CSI connector plus USB camera support
Operating System: Debian-based Raspberry Pi OS (full Linux distribution)
Development Environment: Full Linux development environment with native Python, C/C++, and JavaScript support. Package managers (apt, pip) provide access to extensive ML libraries including TensorFlow, PyTorch, and OpenCV.
Application Focus: Edge AI gateways, advanced computer vision systems, language model deployment, multi-modal AI applications









TipBest For: Linux and Microcontroller Co-design



The Arduino UNO Q pairs a Linux microprocessor with a real-time microcontroller on one board. It suits small language and vision-language models, agents that act on hardware, and vision applications where the model runs on Linux while the microcontroller drives LEDs, sensors, and actuators.


The UNO Q is a hybrid single-board computer in the classic UNO form factor. Its two processors talk through Bridge, an RPC library that lets Python code on Linux call functions in an Arduino sketch, so one board shows the split between AI inference and real-time control found in many edge products.



Arduino UNO Q


Processor Architecture: Qualcomm Dragonwing QRB2210 quad-core Arm Cortex-A53 at 2.0 GHz with Adreno 702 GPU (MPU), plus STMicroelectronics STM32U585 Arm Cortex-M33 at 160 MHz (MCU)
Memory Hierarchy: 2 GB or 4 GB LPDDR4X RAM with 16 GB or 32 GB eMMC storage
Connectivity: Dual-band WiFi 5, Bluetooth 5.1, and a single USB-C port for power, data, and video
Onboard I/O: 8×13 LED matrix, RGB LEDs, Qwiic connector, and UNO-compatible headers (camera through USB or MIPI-CSI)
Operating System: Debian Linux on the MPU; Arduino Core on Zephyr OS on the MCU
Development Environment: SSH and arduino-app-cli (or Arduino App Lab) for dual-brain apps that combine Python and an Arduino sketch. Supports llama.cpp for generative models and Edge Impulse for vision models.
Application Focus: Small language and vision-language models, agentic AI with physical actions, image classification and object detection with real-time I/O

title: Setup
text:
This chapter sets up the Arduino UNO Q with terminal tools (ADB and SSH). It skips the graphical Arduino App Lab wherever possible and follows a command-line workflow instead. The same setup supports every other UNO Q lab.


A terminal-first workflow has several advantages:

Full control over the board’s Debian Linux environment.
Code lives on the host machine under Git, not locked inside the board.
Linux, SSH, and SCP skills transfer directly to real embedded and edge AI deployments.
Build and deployment steps can be scripted and automated.
It works with any editor (VS Code, Vim, or any other), since nothing depends on a specific tool.

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to connect to the UNO Q headlessly, configure its network, run dual-brain applications (Python plus an Arduino sketch) over SSH, and, optionally, edit code on the board from VS Code.



 
The Arduino UNO Q is a hybrid single-board computer that combines two processors on one board with the classic UNO form factor:








Component
Role
Details




MPU (Microprocessor Unit)
High-level computing, AI, and networking
Qualcomm Dragonwing QRB2210: quad-core Arm Cortex-A53 at 2.0 GHz, Adreno 702 GPU, dual ISP. Runs Debian Linux.


MCU (Microcontroller Unit)
Real-time hardware control
STMicroelectronics STM32U585: Arm Cortex-M33 at 160 MHz. Runs the Arduino Core on Zephyr OS.



The two processors communicate through Bridge, Arduino’s RPC (Remote Procedure Call) library. Python code on the MPU can call functions running in an Arduino sketch on the MCU, and vice versa.
 











Variant
RAM
Storage (eMMC)
Best For




2 GB
2 GB LPDDR4X
16 GB
Headless SSH development, lightweight edge AI, and TinyML


4 GB
4 GB LPDDR4X
32 GB
Desktop (SBC) mode with a display, larger AI models, and multitasking



Both variants share the same processors, connectivity (dual-band Wi-Fi 5 and Bluetooth 5.1), USB-C port, UNO-compatible headers, Qwiic connector, 8×13 LED matrix, and four RGB LEDs.




USB-C: A single multi-function port for power, data (ADB), and DisplayPort video output.
Wi-Fi: Dual-band 802.11ac (2.4 GHz and 5 GHz).
Bluetooth: 5.1.


The UNO Q uses its single USB-C port for everything, so use a data-capable USB-C cable, not a charge-only one. Some USB hubs and Apple USB-C adapters are not recognized.

More details are in the Arduino UNO Q User Manual.







Arduino UNO Q (2 GB or 4 GB variant)
USB-C data cable (verify that it is not charge-only)
Host computer (Linux, macOS, or Windows)
Wi-Fi network (the UNO Q and the host must be on the same network for SSH)











Tool
Purpose




ADB (Android Debug Bridge)
Initial headless connection over USB-C


SSH client
Remote access over Wi-Fi (built into Linux and macOS; available on Windows)


SCP
Secure file transfer to the board


VS Code (optional)
Full editor on the board’s filesystem through Remote-SSH







ADB (Android Debug Bridge) opens a shell on the UNO Q over the USB-C cable, with no network or monitor required. It is the entry point for the initial setup.


sudo apt update
sudo apt install android-tools-adb



With Homebrew:
brew install android-platform-tools




Download SDK Platform-Tools from the Android developer site.
Extract the ZIP file to a folder (for example, C:\platform-tools).
Add that folder to the system PATH environment variable, or open a terminal (PowerShell or Command Prompt) in that folder.


For a more Unix-like experience on Windows, with native ssh and scp commands, install WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux). Inside WSL, ADB installs the same way as on Ubuntu.




With the UNO Q disconnected, run:
adb version
The output should look like Android Debug Bridge version X.X.X. If it does not, revisit the installation steps.
 










TipOptional but recommended



This step is optional but strongly recommended, especially for boards fresh out of the box. The first batches of the UNO Q shipped with an older Debian image that can cause random desktop and application restarts (no ZRAM memory compression), ADB defaulting to root (a security concern), and missing HDMI audio. Flashing the latest image fixes all of these and gives every board in a classroom the same starting point.
If the board is already up to date (for example, it was purchased recently and boots correctly), skip to Section 0.6.


Flashing uses Arduino’s arduino-flasher-cli tool, which runs entirely from a terminal on the host computer. It downloads the latest Debian image and writes it to the UNO Q’s eMMC storage.

Warning: Flashing erases everything on the board and restores it to its factory state. Back up any existing projects on the UNO Q first.



Download the version for your operating system from the Arduino Software page or the Flasher CLI releases page.







OS
File to Download




Linux
arduino-flasher-cli_X.X.X_Linux_64bit.tar.gz


macOS
arduino-flasher-cli_X.X.X_macOS_64bit.tar.gz


Windows
arduino-flasher-cli_X.X.X_Windows_64bit.zip



Extract the archive to a convenient location.



With the board powered off (USB cable disconnected):

Locate the JCTL header on the UNO Q (a small 10-pin header).
With a jumper wire or shunt, short the two pins furthest from the USB-C connector.
With the jumper in place, connect the USB-C cable to the computer.

The board boots into EDL (Emergency Download) mode, and the LED matrix shows the Arduino logo continuously.
 



Open a terminal on the host computer, go to the folder where the flasher CLI was extracted, and run:
Linux / macOS:
./arduino-flasher-cli flash latest
Windows (PowerShell):
.\arduino-flasher-cli.exe flash latest

The latest keyword is deprecated and will be removed; newer versions of the flasher use unoq instead.

The tool then:

Asks whether to download the latest Debian image. Type yes and press Enter.
Downloads the image (about 2.3 GB), which can take several minutes.
Extracts the image.
Flashes it to the UNO Q’s eMMC.

Do not disconnect the USB cable or interrupt the process. Wait for the message confirming that the partition is now bootable.
 

On Linux, if the flasher cannot access the device, run it with sudo or add a udev rule for the Qualcomm EDL device.





Disconnect the USB cable.
Remove the jumper from the JCTL header.
Reconnect the USB cable.

The board boots from the fresh image. The LED matrix plays the Arduino logo animation and briefly ends with a heart, which indicates a successful flash; one of the blue LEDs also turns on. The board is now in a factory-fresh state.
 



If the Debian image file is already on the host, flash it directly without downloading it again:
./arduino-flasher-cli flash path/to/downloaded/image

This is useful in a classroom: download the image once and distribute it on a shared drive or USB stick.








Plug the USB-C data cable into the UNO Q and into the computer.
Wait about 30 seconds for the board to boot. The LED matrix shows an animated Arduino logo that briefly ends with a heart, and the blue QRB LED 2 turns on.




adb devices
Expected output:
List of devices attached
XXXXXXXX    device
 
If the list is empty:

Confirm that the USB-C cable carries data.
Try a different USB port, preferably a USB-C or USB 3.0 port directly on the computer rather than through a hub.
On Linux, configure udev rules for the device.




adb shell
This opens a shell in the UNO Q’s Debian Linux environment. The default credentials are:







Field
Value




Username
arduino


Password
arduino






The default password arduino must be changed; the system keeps reminding you until it is.
sudo passwd arduino
Enter and confirm the new password. SSH uses the same password, so keep it at hand.



From the ADB shell, inspect the system:
# Check OS version
cat /etc/os-release

# Check available storage
df -h

# Check RAM
free -h

# Check CPU info
lscpu

Type exit to leave the ADB shell and return to the host terminal.





SSH needs Wi-Fi, and the whole configuration can be done from the ADB shell.


adb shell



nmcli dev wifi list
The command lists every visible Wi-Fi network with its SSID, signal strength, and security type.



sudo nmcli dev wifi connect "YOUR_WIFI_SSID" password "YOUR_WIFI_PASSWORD"
Replace YOUR_WIFI_SSID and YOUR_WIFI_PASSWORD with the network credentials. Keep the quotes if the SSID contains spaces.



nmcli device status
 
The wlan0 interface should show connected. Then get the board’s IP address:
hostname -I
 
For more detail, use:
ip addr show wlan0
The inet line shows an address such as 192.168.1.XXX/YY. Note this IP address; SSH needs it.

If the router supports it, assign a static IP to the UNO Q using its MAC address (shown under link/ether in the output of ip addr show wlan0). The IP then stays the same across reboots, which helps in classrooms with many boards.




To change Wi-Fi networks later, over SSH or ADB:
# Disconnect from current network
nmcli device disconnect wlan0

# Connect to a different network
sudo nmcli dev wifi connect "NEW_SSID" password "NEW_PASSWORD"






When Wi-Fi credentials are entered during the first setup, the board enables SSH automatically, but network mode still has to be activated manually. Run this command in the board’s shell:
arduino-app-cli system network-mode enable
 



Exit the ADB shell:
exit
Then, from the host computer’s terminal, connect via SSH:
ssh arduino@<UNO_Q_IP_ADDRESS>
Replace <UNO_Q_IP_ADDRESS> with the IP noted earlier (for example, 192.168.1.42).

On the first connection, SSH asks you to accept the host fingerprint. Type yes.
Enter the password set earlier.

The host now has a remote Debian shell on the UNO Q over Wi-Fi.


On networks that support mDNS, the hostname also works:
ssh arduino@uno-q.local
If the board was given a custom name during setup, use that name instead:
ssh arduino@<boardname>.local
 



Reset the password through ADB:
adb shell
sudo passwd arduino
Set a new password, exit, and try SSH again.




In the SSH terminal, run:
htop
The 2 GB UNO Q shows something like this:
 
And the 4 GB version:
 

Both the RAM and the swap are twice as large on the 4 GB variant.




sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade
sudo reboot





A graphical SFTP client such as the FileZilla FTP Client is the easiest way to move files. Install it on the host and use the UNO Q’s IP address as the Host, for example:
sftp://192.168.5.85
Enter the UNO Q username and password and press Quickconnect. Two panes open: one for the host computer and one for the UNO Q.
 



On the host, go to the directory with the files to transfer. For example, to copy all of its files to the board:
cd <folder>
scp -r * arduino@<UNO_Q_IP_ADDRESS>:~/ArduinoApps/<folder>/
Enter the password when prompted, and the transfer starts.





Visual Studio Code with the Remote-SSH extension gives a full IDE (file browser, integrated terminal, IntelliSense, and extensions) that works directly on the UNO Q’s filesystem. It is optional, since every lab also works with nano and scp or rsync, but it makes projects that span Python and an Arduino sketch much easier to manage.


Download and install VS Code for your operating system.




Open VS Code.
Open the Extensions view (Ctrl+Shift+X or Cmd+Shift+X).
Search for Remote - SSH (by Microsoft).
Click Install.





Click the Remote Connection icon (><) in the bottom-left corner or in the left menu.
Select + or Connect to Host…
Enter arduino@<UNO_Q_IP_ADDRESS>.

 

Press Enter when prompted. The UNO Q’s IP address appears under SSH.
Click the terminal + icon.

 

Enter the password (or let VS Code authenticate automatically if SSH keys are set up).

VS Code installs a lightweight server component on the UNO Q, which can take a minute on the first connection.



Once connected:

Go to File → Open Folder…
Navigate to /home/arduino/ArduinoApps/.

 

Click OK.

VS Code now browses, edits, and runs terminals directly on the UNO Q.
 



If no terminal is open, press Ctrl+` (backtick). This terminal runs on the UNO Q, so arduino-app-cli commands, package installs, and project management all work from inside VS Code. Any terminal command in the UNO Q labs can run here instead of in a separate SSH session.



The UNO Q has limited RAM, especially the 2 GB variant. To avoid memory problems while a language model is also running:

Disable GitHub Copilot and other AI assistants on the remote connection.
Disable any extension not strictly needed for Python or C++ editing.
Keep the remote extensions to a minimum: Python, C/C++, and Pylance are usually enough.

Extensions can be disabled for the SSH connection alone, without affecting the local setup: right-click the extension and choose Disable (SSH: arduino@…).






The UNO Q ships with a set of pre-installed example applications, from basic LED control to AI-powered computer vision. All of them can be discovered, run, studied, and customized from an SSH terminal, with no App Lab GUI required.

To make sure the board has the latest pre-loaded models, update the system with arduino-app-cli system update. The update can take a long time.

From an SSH terminal, run:
arduino-app-cli app list --examples
The command lists every installed app, including user-created ones:
 
The examples: apps are not stored in ~/ArduinoApps/. Only user-created apps (such as Blink) live there; the examples are managed internally by the CLI elsewhere on the board’s filesystem. The UNO Q therefore has two classes of apps:

examples:*: read-only, managed by the CLI.
user:*: your apps in ~/ArduinoApps/, the only ones visible with ls.




Any example can run directly from an SSH terminal:
arduino-app-cli app start examples:inspirational/blink

Check the app names listed on your board and adapt the commands if needed.

 

The first run can take several minutes while the system downloads and installs the Arduino libraries and sets up the Python container.

At the end, the output shows:
Progress[]: 100%
✓ App "Blink LED from Python" started successfully
On the board, the built-in LED blinks on and off every second.
 
To inspect the logs:
arduino-app-cli app logs examples:inspirational/blink
 
And to stop the app:
arduino-app-cli app stop examples:inspirational/blink
 




The arduino-app-cli tool comes pre-installed on the UNO Q and manages the whole lifecycle of dual-brain applications: Apps, Bricks, AI models, and system settings. The tables below list the commands used most often in the UNO Q labs, based on Arduino App CLI 0.14. Check the version on the board with:
arduino-app-cli version
The full list of commands and options is in the Arduino App CLI Command Reference.

App paths and App IDs. Every command that takes an <app_path> also accepts an App ID, such as user:my-app for your own Apps or examples:inspirational/blink for the built-in examples.










Command
Description




arduino-app-cli app new <name>
Create a new App (--from-app copies an existing App or example; -b adds Bricks)


arduino-app-cli app list
List your Apps; add --examples for the examples or --all for everything


arduino-app-cli app ps
Show the live status of Apps that are starting, running, stopping, or failed (--all includes stopped ones)


arduino-app-cli app details <app_path>
Show an App’s details


arduino-app-cli app start <app_path>
Start an App (-v for verbose output)


arduino-app-cli app stop <app_path>
Stop a running App


arduino-app-cli app restart <app_path>
Restart an App, or start it if it is stopped


arduino-app-cli app logs <app_path>
Show the Python-side logs (--follow to stream, --tail N for the last N lines)


arduino-app-cli app ports <app_path>
Show the network ports an App and its Bricks expose


arduino-app-cli app export <app_path>
Export an App to a zip file (an optional second argument names the file)


arduino-app-cli app import <file.zip>
Import an App from a zip file


arduino-app-cli app destroy <app_path>
Delete an App



Note that app list shows the catalog, not what is running. To see which Apps are active on the board, use app ps.










Command
Description




arduino-app-cli brick list
List all available Bricks


arduino-app-cli brick details <brick_id>
Show the details of a Brick


arduino-app-cli app brick config
Set a Brick variable in an App: add <app_path>, <brick_id>, and name=value (--model selects the AI model the Brick runs)


arduino-app-cli model list
List the installed models (--exclude-builtin hides Arduino’s own)


arduino-app-cli model install <model>
Install a model from the catalog, from Hugging Face, or from a URL


arduino-app-cli model delete <model_id>
Delete a custom model



The model install command accepts a llama.cpp Hugging Face ID in the form llamacpp:owner/repo:quant, for example:
arduino-app-cli model install \
  llamacpp:unsloth/Qwen3.5-0.8B-GGUF:Q4_K_M
In version 0.14 the quantization is required: llamacpp:owner/repo alone fails. For vision models, --mmproj-url points to the companion projector file.










Command
Description




arduino-app-cli system check
Verify that the board provides what the Apps need


arduino-app-cli system update
Update the upgradable system packages (--only-arduino limits it to Arduino packages; --yes skips prompts)


arduino-app-cli system cleanup
Remove unused and obsolete App images to free disk space


arduino-app-cli system set-name <name>
Set a custom name for the board


arduino-app-cli system keyboard [layout]
Show or change the keyboard layout


arduino-app-cli system network-mode <mode>
Manage the board’s network mode (enable, disable, or status)


arduino-app-cli properties set default <app>
Set the App that starts at boot (none unsets it)


arduino-app-cli properties get default
Show the default App


arduino-app-cli monitor
Attach to the microcontroller’s serial monitor



All commands accept --format json for machine-readable output and --log-level debug for troubleshooting.




The UNO Q runs Debian Linux, so these commands come up often:


# OS version
cat /etc/os-release

# CPU information
lscpu

# Memory usage
free -h

# Disk usage
df -h

# Running processes (install with: sudo apt install htop)
htop



# Show network interfaces and IPs
ip addr show

# Show Wi-Fi connection status
nmcli device status

# Show current Wi-Fi connection details
nmcli connection show

# List available Wi-Fi networks
nmcli dev wifi list

# Connect to a Wi-Fi network
sudo nmcli dev wifi connect "SSID" password "PASSWORD"

# Get board IP address (short form)
hostname -I



# Update package lists
sudo apt update

# Upgrade installed packages
sudo apt upgrade -y

# Install a package
sudo apt install <package-name> -y

# Remove a package
sudo apt remove <package-name>

# Clean up unused packages and cache
sudo apt autoremove -y
sudo apt clean



# List files (detailed)
ls -la

# Navigate directories
cd ~/ArduinoApps

# Create a directory
mkdir -p my_project/python my_project/sketch

# Copy files
cp source.txt destination.txt

# Move/rename files
mv old_name.py new_name.py

# Remove a file
rm filename.txt

# Remove a directory and its contents
rm -rf directory_name

# View file contents
cat filename.txt

# Edit a file (nano is pre-installed)
nano filename.txt



# Check SSH service status
sudo systemctl status sshd

# Restart SSH
sudo systemctl restart sshd

# Reboot the board
sudo reboot

# Shut down the board
sudo shutdown -h now







Use a data-capable USB-C cable, not a charge-only one.
Use a USB-C or USB 3.0 port directly on the computer, and avoid USB hubs when possible.
Some Apple USB-C hubs are not compatible.
The board takes about 30 seconds to boot, so wait before running adb devices.
On Linux, udev rules may be needed. The Android developer documentation explains how to set them up.




Check that the SSH server is running:
adb shell
sudo systemctl status sshd
If it is not running:
sudo apt install openssh-server -y
sudo systemctl enable ssh
sudo ssh-keygen -A
sudo systemctl start sshd




Check that the SSID and password are correct (both are case-sensitive).
Try the 2.4 GHz band if 5 GHz fails; some access points have issues.
Check that the router is not blocking new devices (MAC filtering).




If an app fails to start with errors such as Stopped decode loop: EOF, make sure its Python code includes:
App.run(user_loop=loop)
This line is mandatory: the runtime needs it to start the application.




Avoid large AI models and prefer models optimized for the edge.
Monitor memory usage with free -h or htop.
Close unused applications and services.
With VS Code Remote-SSH (Section 0.9), disable unnecessary extensions on the remote host, since its server process adds its own RAM footprint.




Over time, Docker images, logs, and cached packages can fill the eMMC:
# Check available space
df -h

# Clean apt cache
sudo apt clean
sudo apt autoremove -y

# Remove unused App images
arduino-app-cli system cleanup

# If using Docker directly
docker system prune -a



Git can sync code with the board instead of SCP:
sudo apt install git -y
Repositories can then be cloned directly on the board or kept in sync with the host, which helps in team projects and keeps code backed up.



For iterative development, rsync is faster than scp because it transfers only the files that changed:
# On the host, from inside the project directory:
rsync -avz --progress ./ \
  arduino@<UNO_Q_IP_ADDRESS>:~/ArduinoApps/uno_q_blink/
Install rsync on the UNO Q if it is not present:
sudo apt install rsync -y




With a working command-line environment in place, several paths are open.



Pre-loaded AI models: The UNO Q comes with models for object detection, image classification, sound recognition, and keyword spotting. List them with arduino-app-cli model list, and the example Apps that use them with arduino-app-cli app list --examples.
Edge Impulse integration: Train custom models in Edge Impulse Studio and deploy them to the UNO Q. See the Edge Impulse Arduino UNO Q documentation.
TinyML with Python: Run LiteRT (TensorFlow Lite) or ONNX Runtime inference on the Linux side.
Generative AI at the edge: Run small language and vision-language models with llama.cpp.





Camera modules: Connect a USB camera through a USB hub, or a MIPI-CSI camera, for computer vision projects.
Modulino nodes: Use the Qwiic connector for plug-and-play sensors and actuators.
Arduino shields: Traditional UNO shields fit the header layout.





This chapter covered a complete terminal-first workflow for the Arduino UNO Q: headless setup via ADB, Wi-Fi and SSH configuration, an optional VS Code Remote-SSH editor, and running dual-brain apps such as Blink with arduino-app-cli.



One board, two worlds: The dual-brain architecture shows the boundary between high-level AI inference (Python on Linux) and real-time physical control (C++ on an RTOS). That boundary is central to real edge AI systems but hard to convey with a single-processor board.
Professional development workflow: Working over SSH, transferring files with SCP or rsync, and using CLI tools mirrors how edge AI systems are developed and maintained in industry, which is very different from the “click upload” experience of a traditional Arduino.
Gradual complexity: Simple LED examples introduce the Bridge architecture, and the same hardware then runs language models, vision-language models, image classification, and object detection.
Ecosystem continuity: Skills learned on the UNO Q (Linux administration, Python ML frameworks, and Arduino sketches) transfer to both simpler MCU boards and more powerful SBCs.

Technical strengths include:

The Adreno 702 GPU can accelerate some vision workloads through LiteRT delegates, although the gains depend heavily on the model and runtime. It is not a usable target for llama.cpp, so the language models in these labs run entirely on the CPU.
Pre-loaded Edge Impulse models give immediate hands-on experience with production ML pipelines.
arduino-app-cli orchestrates the build, deploy, and run cycle for both processors from a single command.
Standard Debian Linux gives full access to pip, apt, Docker, Git, and any Python ML library that fits in memory.




The UNO Q’s constraints matter when choosing it over the other platforms in these labs:

Compute power: The Cortex-A53 cores perform at roughly the level of a Raspberry Pi 3. Language models beyond about 2B parameters are impractical. For heavy inference, a Raspberry Pi 5 or an accelerator (such as a MemryX MX3 or Google Coral) is the better choice.
RAM: The 2 GB variant can feel tight when it runs a remote editor server, a Python container, and an AI model at the same time. The 4 GB variant is recommended for demanding workloads, particularly generative AI.
Single USB-C port: Power, data, and video all go through one port, so desktop (SBC) mode needs a hub. Cable compatibility problems are a recurring frustration.
Maturing software ecosystem: Arduino App Lab and arduino-app-cli are still evolving (pre-1.0), and the documentation is catching up. Rough edges are both a limitation and a learning opportunity, since early-stage tooling is a reality of edge AI development.
No dedicated NPU: Unlike the Arduino VENTUNO Q (40 TOPS through its Dragonwing IQ8 NPU), the UNO Q relies on the CPU and GPU for inference, which is a bottleneck for compute-intensive models.
External camera: Unlike the Nicla Vision or the XIAO ESP32S3 Sense, which have built-in cameras, the UNO Q needs a USB webcam or a MIPI-CSI camera with a carrier board.

title: Setup
text:
A terminal-first workflow has several advantages:

Full control over the board’s Debian Linux environment.
Code lives on the host machine under Git, not locked inside the board.
Linux, SSH, and SCP skills transfer directly to real embedded and edge AI deployments.
Build and deployment steps can be scripted and automated.
It works with any editor (VS Code, Vim, or any other), since nothing depends on a specific tool.

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to connect to the UNO Q headlessly, configure its network, run dual-brain applications (Python plus an Arduino sketch) over SSH, and, optionally, edit code on the board from VS Code.

title: Setup
text:
The Arduino UNO Q is a hybrid single-board computer that combines two processors on one board with the classic UNO form factor:








Component
Role
Details




MPU (Microprocessor Unit)
High-level computing, AI, and networking
Qualcomm Dragonwing QRB2210: quad-core Arm Cortex-A53 at 2.0 GHz, Adreno 702 GPU, dual ISP. Runs Debian Linux.


MCU (Microcontroller Unit)
Real-time hardware control
STMicroelectronics STM32U585: Arm Cortex-M33 at 160 MHz. Runs the Arduino Core on Zephyr OS.



The two processors communicate through Bridge, Arduino’s RPC (Remote Procedure Call) library. Python code on the MPU can call functions running in an Arduino sketch on the MCU, and vice versa.
 











Variant
RAM
Storage (eMMC)
Best For




2 GB
2 GB LPDDR4X
16 GB
Headless SSH development, lightweight edge AI, and TinyML


4 GB
4 GB LPDDR4X
32 GB
Desktop (SBC) mode with a display, larger AI models, and multitasking



Both variants share the same processors, connectivity (dual-band Wi-Fi 5 and Bluetooth 5.1), USB-C port, UNO-compatible headers, Qwiic connector, 8×13 LED matrix, and four RGB LEDs.




USB-C: A single multi-function port for power, data (ADB), and DisplayPort video output.
Wi-Fi: Dual-band 802.11ac (2.4 GHz and 5 GHz).
Bluetooth: 5.1.


The UNO Q uses its single USB-C port for everything, so use a data-capable USB-C cable, not a charge-only one. Some USB hubs and Apple USB-C adapters are not recognized.

More details are in the Arduino UNO Q User Manual.

title: Setup
text:
Arduino UNO Q (2 GB or 4 GB variant)
USB-C data cable (verify that it is not charge-only)
Host computer (Linux, macOS, or Windows)
Wi-Fi network (the UNO Q and the host must be on the same network for SSH)











Tool
Purpose




ADB (Android Debug Bridge)
Initial headless connection over USB-C


SSH client
Remote access over Wi-Fi (built into Linux and macOS; available on Windows)


SCP
Secure file transfer to the board


VS Code (optional)
Full editor on the board’s filesystem through Remote-SSH

title: Setup
text:
ADB (Android Debug Bridge) opens a shell on the UNO Q over the USB-C cable, with no network or monitor required. It is the entry point for the initial setup.


sudo apt update
sudo apt install android-tools-adb



With Homebrew:
brew install android-platform-tools




Download SDK Platform-Tools from the Android developer site.
Extract the ZIP file to a folder (for example, C:\platform-tools).
Add that folder to the system PATH environment variable, or open a terminal (PowerShell or Command Prompt) in that folder.


For a more Unix-like experience on Windows, with native ssh and scp commands, install WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux). Inside WSL, ADB installs the same way as on Ubuntu.




With the UNO Q disconnected, run:
adb version
The output should look like Android Debug Bridge version X.X.X. If it does not, revisit the installation steps.

title: Setup
text:
TipOptional but recommended



This step is optional but strongly recommended, especially for boards fresh out of the box. The first batches of the UNO Q shipped with an older Debian image that can cause random desktop and application restarts (no ZRAM memory compression), ADB defaulting to root (a security concern), and missing HDMI audio. Flashing the latest image fixes all of these and gives every board in a classroom the same starting point.
If the board is already up to date (for example, it was purchased recently and boots correctly), skip to Section 0.6.


Flashing uses Arduino’s arduino-flasher-cli tool, which runs entirely from a terminal on the host computer. It downloads the latest Debian image and writes it to the UNO Q’s eMMC storage.

Warning: Flashing erases everything on the board and restores it to its factory state. Back up any existing projects on the UNO Q first.



Download the version for your operating system from the Arduino Software page or the Flasher CLI releases page.







OS
File to Download




Linux
arduino-flasher-cli_X.X.X_Linux_64bit.tar.gz


macOS
arduino-flasher-cli_X.X.X_macOS_64bit.tar.gz


Windows
arduino-flasher-cli_X.X.X_Windows_64bit.zip



Extract the archive to a convenient location.



With the board powered off (USB cable disconnected):

Locate the JCTL header on the UNO Q (a small 10-pin header).
With a jumper wire or shunt, short the two pins furthest from the USB-C connector.
With the jumper in place, connect the USB-C cable to the computer.

The board boots into EDL (Emergency Download) mode, and the LED matrix shows the Arduino logo continuously.
 



Open a terminal on the host computer, go to the folder where the flasher CLI was extracted, and run:
Linux / macOS:
./arduino-flasher-cli flash latest
Windows (PowerShell):
.\arduino-flasher-cli.exe flash latest

The latest keyword is deprecated and will be removed; newer versions of the flasher use unoq instead.

The tool then:

Asks whether to download the latest Debian image. Type yes and press Enter.
Downloads the image (about 2.3 GB), which can take several minutes.
Extracts the image.
Flashes it to the UNO Q’s eMMC.

Do not disconnect the USB cable or interrupt the process. Wait for the message confirming that the partition is now bootable.
 

On Linux, if the flasher cannot access the device, run it with sudo or add a udev rule for the Qualcomm EDL device.





Disconnect the USB cable.
Remove the jumper from the JCTL header.
Reconnect the USB cable.

The board boots from the fresh image. The LED matrix plays the Arduino logo animation and briefly ends with a heart, which indicates a successful flash; one of the blue LEDs also turns on. The board is now in a factory-fresh state.
 



If the Debian image file is already on the host, flash it directly without downloading it again:
./arduino-flasher-cli flash path/to/downloaded/image

This is useful in a classroom: download the image once and distribute it on a shared drive or USB stick.

title: Setup
text:
Plug the USB-C data cable into the UNO Q and into the computer.
Wait about 30 seconds for the board to boot. The LED matrix shows an animated Arduino logo that briefly ends with a heart, and the blue QRB LED 2 turns on.




adb devices
Expected output:
List of devices attached
XXXXXXXX    device
 
If the list is empty:

Confirm that the USB-C cable carries data.
Try a different USB port, preferably a USB-C or USB 3.0 port directly on the computer rather than through a hub.
On Linux, configure udev rules for the device.




adb shell
This opens a shell in the UNO Q’s Debian Linux environment. The default credentials are:







Field
Value




Username
arduino


Password
arduino






The default password arduino must be changed; the system keeps reminding you until it is.
sudo passwd arduino
Enter and confirm the new password. SSH uses the same password, so keep it at hand.



From the ADB shell, inspect the system:
# Check OS version
cat /etc/os-release

# Check available storage
df -h

# Check RAM
free -h

# Check CPU info
lscpu

Type exit to leave the ADB shell and return to the host terminal.

title: Setup
text:
SSH needs Wi-Fi, and the whole configuration can be done from the ADB shell.


adb shell



nmcli dev wifi list
The command lists every visible Wi-Fi network with its SSID, signal strength, and security type.



sudo nmcli dev wifi connect "YOUR_WIFI_SSID" password "YOUR_WIFI_PASSWORD"
Replace YOUR_WIFI_SSID and YOUR_WIFI_PASSWORD with the network credentials. Keep the quotes if the SSID contains spaces.



nmcli device status
 
The wlan0 interface should show connected. Then get the board’s IP address:
hostname -I
 
For more detail, use:
ip addr show wlan0
The inet line shows an address such as 192.168.1.XXX/YY. Note this IP address; SSH needs it.

If the router supports it, assign a static IP to the UNO Q using its MAC address (shown under link/ether in the output of ip addr show wlan0). The IP then stays the same across reboots, which helps in classrooms with many boards.




To change Wi-Fi networks later, over SSH or ADB:
# Disconnect from current network
nmcli device disconnect wlan0

# Connect to a different network
sudo nmcli dev wifi connect "NEW_SSID" password "NEW_PASSWORD"

title: Setup
text:
When Wi-Fi credentials are entered during the first setup, the board enables SSH automatically, but network mode still has to be activated manually. Run this command in the board’s shell:
arduino-app-cli system network-mode enable
 



Exit the ADB shell:
exit
Then, from the host computer’s terminal, connect via SSH:
ssh arduino@<UNO_Q_IP_ADDRESS>
Replace <UNO_Q_IP_ADDRESS> with the IP noted earlier (for example, 192.168.1.42).

On the first connection, SSH asks you to accept the host fingerprint. Type yes.
Enter the password set earlier.

The host now has a remote Debian shell on the UNO Q over Wi-Fi.


On networks that support mDNS, the hostname also works:
ssh arduino@uno-q.local
If the board was given a custom name during setup, use that name instead:
ssh arduino@<boardname>.local
 



Reset the password through ADB:
adb shell
sudo passwd arduino
Set a new password, exit, and try SSH again.




In the SSH terminal, run:
htop
The 2 GB UNO Q shows something like this:
 
And the 4 GB version:
 

Both the RAM and the swap are twice as large on the 4 GB variant.




sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade
sudo reboot





A graphical SFTP client such as the FileZilla FTP Client is the easiest way to move files. Install it on the host and use the UNO Q’s IP address as the Host, for example:
sftp://192.168.5.85
Enter the UNO Q username and password and press Quickconnect. Two panes open: one for the host computer and one for the UNO Q.
 



On the host, go to the directory with the files to transfer. For example, to copy all of its files to the board:
cd <folder>
scp -r * arduino@<UNO_Q_IP_ADDRESS>:~/ArduinoApps/<folder>/
Enter the password when prompted, and the transfer starts.

title: Setup
text:
Visual Studio Code with the Remote-SSH extension gives a full IDE (file browser, integrated terminal, IntelliSense, and extensions) that works directly on the UNO Q’s filesystem. It is optional, since every lab also works with nano and scp or rsync, but it makes projects that span Python and an Arduino sketch much easier to manage.


Download and install VS Code for your operating system.




Open VS Code.
Open the Extensions view (Ctrl+Shift+X or Cmd+Shift+X).
Search for Remote - SSH (by Microsoft).
Click Install.





Click the Remote Connection icon (><) in the bottom-left corner or in the left menu.
Select + or Connect to Host…
Enter arduino@<UNO_Q_IP_ADDRESS>.

 

Press Enter when prompted. The UNO Q’s IP address appears under SSH.
Click the terminal + icon.

 

Enter the password (or let VS Code authenticate automatically if SSH keys are set up).

VS Code installs a lightweight server component on the UNO Q, which can take a minute on the first connection.



Once connected:

Go to File → Open Folder…
Navigate to /home/arduino/ArduinoApps/.

 

Click OK.

VS Code now browses, edits, and runs terminals directly on the UNO Q.
 



If no terminal is open, press Ctrl+` (backtick). This terminal runs on the UNO Q, so arduino-app-cli commands, package installs, and project management all work from inside VS Code. Any terminal command in the UNO Q labs can run here instead of in a separate SSH session.



The UNO Q has limited RAM, especially the 2 GB variant. To avoid memory problems while a language model is also running:

Disable GitHub Copilot and other AI assistants on the remote connection.
Disable any extension not strictly needed for Python or C++ editing.
Keep the remote extensions to a minimum: Python, C/C++, and Pylance are usually enough.

Extensions can be disabled for the SSH connection alone, without affecting the local setup: right-click the extension and choose Disable (SSH: arduino@…).

title: Setup
text:
The UNO Q ships with a set of pre-installed example applications, from basic LED control to AI-powered computer vision. All of them can be discovered, run, studied, and customized from an SSH terminal, with no App Lab GUI required.

To make sure the board has the latest pre-loaded models, update the system with arduino-app-cli system update. The update can take a long time.

From an SSH terminal, run:
arduino-app-cli app list --examples
The command lists every installed app, including user-created ones:
 
The examples: apps are not stored in ~/ArduinoApps/. Only user-created apps (such as Blink) live there; the examples are managed internally by the CLI elsewhere on the board’s filesystem. The UNO Q therefore has two classes of apps:

examples:*: read-only, managed by the CLI.
user:*: your apps in ~/ArduinoApps/, the only ones visible with ls.




Any example can run directly from an SSH terminal:
arduino-app-cli app start examples:inspirational/blink

Check the app names listed on your board and adapt the commands if needed.

 

The first run can take several minutes while the system downloads and installs the Arduino libraries and sets up the Python container.

At the end, the output shows:
Progress[]: 100%
✓ App "Blink LED from Python" started successfully
On the board, the built-in LED blinks on and off every second.
 
To inspect the logs:
arduino-app-cli app logs examples:inspirational/blink
 
And to stop the app:
arduino-app-cli app stop examples:inspirational/blink

title: Setup
text:
The arduino-app-cli tool comes pre-installed on the UNO Q and manages the whole lifecycle of dual-brain applications: Apps, Bricks, AI models, and system settings. The tables below list the commands used most often in the UNO Q labs, based on Arduino App CLI 0.14. Check the version on the board with:
arduino-app-cli version
The full list of commands and options is in the Arduino App CLI Command Reference.

App paths and App IDs. Every command that takes an <app_path> also accepts an App ID, such as user:my-app for your own Apps or examples:inspirational/blink for the built-in examples.










Command
Description




arduino-app-cli app new <name>
Create a new App (--from-app copies an existing App or example; -b adds Bricks)


arduino-app-cli app list
List your Apps; add --examples for the examples or --all for everything


arduino-app-cli app ps
Show the live status of Apps that are starting, running, stopping, or failed (--all includes stopped ones)


arduino-app-cli app details <app_path>
Show an App’s details


arduino-app-cli app start <app_path>
Start an App (-v for verbose output)


arduino-app-cli app stop <app_path>
Stop a running App


arduino-app-cli app restart <app_path>
Restart an App, or start it if it is stopped


arduino-app-cli app logs <app_path>
Show the Python-side logs (--follow to stream, --tail N for the last N lines)


arduino-app-cli app ports <app_path>
Show the network ports an App and its Bricks expose


arduino-app-cli app export <app_path>
Export an App to a zip file (an optional second argument names the file)


arduino-app-cli app import <file.zip>
Import an App from a zip file


arduino-app-cli app destroy <app_path>
Delete an App



Note that app list shows the catalog, not what is running. To see which Apps are active on the board, use app ps.










Command
Description




arduino-app-cli brick list
List all available Bricks


arduino-app-cli brick details <brick_id>
Show the details of a Brick


arduino-app-cli app brick config
Set a Brick variable in an App: add <app_path>, <brick_id>, and name=value (--model selects the AI model the Brick runs)


arduino-app-cli model list
List the installed models (--exclude-builtin hides Arduino’s own)


arduino-app-cli model install <model>
Install a model from the catalog, from Hugging Face, or from a URL


arduino-app-cli model delete <model_id>
Delete a custom model



The model install command accepts a llama.cpp Hugging Face ID in the form llamacpp:owner/repo:quant, for example:
arduino-app-cli model install \
  llamacpp:unsloth/Qwen3.5-0.8B-GGUF:Q4_K_M
In version 0.14 the quantization is required: llamacpp:owner/repo alone fails. For vision models, --mmproj-url points to the companion projector file.










Command
Description




arduino-app-cli system check
Verify that the board provides what the Apps need


arduino-app-cli system update
Update the upgradable system packages (--only-arduino limits it to Arduino packages; --yes skips prompts)


arduino-app-cli system cleanup
Remove unused and obsolete App images to free disk space


arduino-app-cli system set-name <name>
Set a custom name for the board


arduino-app-cli system keyboard [layout]
Show or change the keyboard layout


arduino-app-cli system network-mode <mode>
Manage the board’s network mode (enable, disable, or status)


arduino-app-cli properties set default <app>
Set the App that starts at boot (none unsets it)


arduino-app-cli properties get default
Show the default App


arduino-app-cli monitor
Attach to the microcontroller’s serial monitor



All commands accept --format json for machine-readable output and --log-level debug for troubleshooting.

title: Setup
text:
The UNO Q runs Debian Linux, so these commands come up often:


# OS version
cat /etc/os-release

# CPU information
lscpu

# Memory usage
free -h

# Disk usage
df -h

# Running processes (install with: sudo apt install htop)
htop



# Show network interfaces and IPs
ip addr show

# Show Wi-Fi connection status
nmcli device status

# Show current Wi-Fi connection details
nmcli connection show

# List available Wi-Fi networks
nmcli dev wifi list

# Connect to a Wi-Fi network
sudo nmcli dev wifi connect "SSID" password "PASSWORD"

# Get board IP address (short form)
hostname -I



# Update package lists
sudo apt update

# Upgrade installed packages
sudo apt upgrade -y

# Install a package
sudo apt install <package-name> -y

# Remove a package
sudo apt remove <package-name>

# Clean up unused packages and cache
sudo apt autoremove -y
sudo apt clean



# List files (detailed)
ls -la

# Navigate directories
cd ~/ArduinoApps

# Create a directory
mkdir -p my_project/python my_project/sketch

# Copy files
cp source.txt destination.txt

# Move/rename files
mv old_name.py new_name.py

# Remove a file
rm filename.txt

# Remove a directory and its contents
rm -rf directory_name

# View file contents
cat filename.txt

# Edit a file (nano is pre-installed)
nano filename.txt



# Check SSH service status

title: Setup
text:
Use a data-capable USB-C cable, not a charge-only one.
Use a USB-C or USB 3.0 port directly on the computer, and avoid USB hubs when possible.
Some Apple USB-C hubs are not compatible.
The board takes about 30 seconds to boot, so wait before running adb devices.
On Linux, udev rules may be needed. The Android developer documentation explains how to set them up.




Check that the SSH server is running:
adb shell
sudo systemctl status sshd
If it is not running:
sudo apt install openssh-server -y
sudo systemctl enable ssh
sudo ssh-keygen -A
sudo systemctl start sshd




Check that the SSID and password are correct (both are case-sensitive).
Try the 2.4 GHz band if 5 GHz fails; some access points have issues.
Check that the router is not blocking new devices (MAC filtering).




If an app fails to start with errors such as Stopped decode loop: EOF, make sure its Python code includes:
App.run(user_loop=loop)
This line is mandatory: the runtime needs it to start the application.




Avoid large AI models and prefer models optimized for the edge.
Monitor memory usage with free -h or htop.
Close unused applications and services.
With VS Code Remote-SSH (Section 0.9), disable unnecessary extensions on the remote host, since its server process adds its own RAM footprint.




Over time, Docker images, logs, and cached packages can fill the eMMC:
# Check available space
df -h

# Clean apt cache
sudo apt clean
sudo apt autoremove -y

# Remove unused App images
arduino-app-cli system cleanup

# If using Docker directly
docker system prune -a



Git can sync code with the board instead of SCP:
sudo apt install git -y
Repositories can then be cloned directly on the board or kept in sync with the host, which helps in team projects and keeps code backed up.



For iterative development, rsync is faster than scp because it transfers only the files that changed:
# On the host, from inside the project directory:
rsync -avz --progress ./ \
  arduino@<UNO_Q_IP_ADDRESS>:~/ArduinoApps/uno_q_blink/
Install rsync on the UNO Q if it is not present:
sudo apt install rsync -y

title: Setup
text:
With a working command-line environment in place, several paths are open.



Pre-loaded AI models: The UNO Q comes with models for object detection, image classification, sound recognition, and keyword spotting. List them with arduino-app-cli model list, and the example Apps that use them with arduino-app-cli app list --examples.
Edge Impulse integration: Train custom models in Edge Impulse Studio and deploy them to the UNO Q. See the Edge Impulse Arduino UNO Q documentation.
TinyML with Python: Run LiteRT (TensorFlow Lite) or ONNX Runtime inference on the Linux side.
Generative AI at the edge: Run small language and vision-language models with llama.cpp.





Camera modules: Connect a USB camera through a USB hub, or a MIPI-CSI camera, for computer vision projects.
Modulino nodes: Use the Qwiic connector for plug-and-play sensors and actuators.
Arduino shields: Traditional UNO shields fit the header layout.

title: Setup
text:
This chapter covered a complete terminal-first workflow for the Arduino UNO Q: headless setup via ADB, Wi-Fi and SSH configuration, an optional VS Code Remote-SSH editor, and running dual-brain apps such as Blink with arduino-app-cli.



One board, two worlds: The dual-brain architecture shows the boundary between high-level AI inference (Python on Linux) and real-time physical control (C++ on an RTOS). That boundary is central to real edge AI systems but hard to convey with a single-processor board.
Professional development workflow: Working over SSH, transferring files with SCP or rsync, and using CLI tools mirrors how edge AI systems are developed and maintained in industry, which is very different from the “click upload” experience of a traditional Arduino.
Gradual complexity: Simple LED examples introduce the Bridge architecture, and the same hardware then runs language models, vision-language models, image classification, and object detection.
Ecosystem continuity: Skills learned on the UNO Q (Linux administration, Python ML frameworks, and Arduino sketches) transfer to both simpler MCU boards and more powerful SBCs.

Technical strengths include:

The Adreno 702 GPU can accelerate some vision workloads through LiteRT delegates, although the gains depend heavily on the model and runtime. It is not a usable target for llama.cpp, so the language models in these labs run entirely on the CPU.
Pre-loaded Edge Impulse models give immediate hands-on experience with production ML pipelines.
arduino-app-cli orchestrates the build, deploy, and run cycle for both processors from a single command.
Standard Debian Linux gives full access to pip, apt, Docker, Git, and any Python ML library that fits in memory.




The UNO Q’s constraints matter when choosing it over the other platforms in these labs:

Compute power: The Cortex-A53 cores perform at roughly the level of a Raspberry Pi 3. Language models beyond about 2B parameters are impractical. For heavy inference, a Raspberry Pi 5 or an accelerator (such as a MemryX MX3 or Google Coral) is the better choice.
RAM: The 2 GB variant can feel tight when it runs a remote editor server, a Python container, and an AI model at the same time. The 4 GB variant is recommended for demanding workloads, particularly generative AI.
Single USB-C port: Power, data, and video all go through one port, so desktop (SBC) mode needs a hub. Cable compatibility problems are a recurring frustration.
Maturing software ecosystem: Arduino App Lab and arduino-app-cli are still evolving (pre-1.0), and the documentation is catching up. Rough edges are both a limitation and a learning opportunity, since early-stage tooling is a reality of edge AI development.
No dedicated NPU: Unlike the Arduino VENTUNO Q (40 TOPS through its Dragonwing IQ8 NPU), the UNO Q relies on the CPU and GPU for inference, which is a bottleneck for compute-intensive models.
External camera: Unlike the Nicla Vision or the XIAO ESP32S3 Sense, which have built-in cameras, the UNO Q needs a USB webcam or a MIPI-CSI camera with a carrier board.

title: Agentic AI
text:
In the earlier UNO Q labs, the language model always had a fixed job: answer this prompt, describe this image. The model reasoned, but it never decided what to do. This lab changes that. Qwen3.5 gets a small set of tools (functions it can choose to call) and decides on its own which ones to use, and in what order, to satisfy a plain-language request.
Here is the shape of the goal, taken from a real session in Section 0.9.9:
> Check the free disk space. If there's more than 1GB free, show a
  checkmark on the matrix, otherwise show an X.
[turn 0] tool call: get_system_info({})
[turn 1] tool call: set_led_matrix({"pattern":"check"})
The free disk space is 1.4GB, which is more than 1GB, so the matrix
shows a checkmark.
 
No if statement in the code chose that checkmark. The model received a threshold in English, fetched a number it could not have known, compared the two, and acted on the result.
The tools are deliberately ordinary: ask the board what OS it is running, do some arithmetic, list a few files, switch the built-in LED, draw a pattern on the onboard 8×13 LED matrix. None of it requires a single wire. That is on purpose: this lab runs in any room, on any UNO Q, with nothing attached, which makes it a good choice for a workshop where not everyone has a breadboard.
 
The mechanism is llama-server’s native, OpenAI-compatible tool-calling API (tools=[...] in the request, tool_calls in the response), the same interface hosted LLM APIs use, not a custom prompt-and-parse scheme. The “Building Agents with SLMs” chapter of EdgeML Made Easy routed a query through hand-written JSON classification, a technique that book itself flags as fragile: models struggle to format the classification JSON reliably, especially at 1B parameters and below. The native tools API does not remove that fragility at small model sizes, but it moves the parsing burden onto llama.cpp’s grammar-constrained decoding instead of hopeful prompt engineering, and it is the same shape of code as for a hosted model.
The lab also shows the agent failing. Section 0.9 pushes a 0.8B model past what it can reliably do, then swaps in a 2B model and reruns the same questions with no other change. That comparison matters as much as the working demo: knowing where a model’s capability ends, and what crossing that line costs in latency, is most of the engineering in edge AI.
By the end, the board runs a small, hardware-free agent that any device on the network can talk to, with every tool decision visible, acting on the board’s own files, its own vitals, and its own LEDs.



Explain what makes a model “agentic”, and separate the model from the harness around it.
Use llama-server’s built-in tools from its WebUI, and understand where the permission boundary lives.
Design tools whose risk matches what the model controls, with a workspace boundary and a safe calculator.
Build a tool-calling agent loop in Python, with two tools that reach the MCU over Bridge RPC.
Measure what an agent answer costs on the UNO Q, and where a 0.8B model stops being reliable.





The Setup lab: headless SSH access to the board.
The Small Language Models lab: llama.cpp built from source, the Qwen3.5-0.8B GGUF downloaded, and comfort running llama-server and calling it from Python with the openai client library. This lab reuses its llama-server setup and openai patterns without repeating them.

The Vision-Language Models lab and the vision labs are deliberately not required: nothing here depends on vision or on external sensors. Section 0.12 shows how other tools plug into this same agent loop later.




The word gets used loosely. Pinned down, an agent is a model that does three things a plain chat model does not.
It decides whether to act at all. Ask “What is the capital of Brazil?” and the right move is to answer “Brasília” from what the model already knows, with no tool needed.
Ask “How much free disk space is there?” and the model cannot know: that answer lives on the board. The model has to call a tool and read the result back.
Arithmetic is another example. Ask a plain model “How much is 123456 multiplied by 123456?” and it will almost certainly get it wrong. With access to a tool (a Python calculator, for example), the computation is always right.
 
It picks the tool and fills in the arguments. The model receives a list of available tools and their schemas, and it chooses. The code never contains if "disk" in prompt: get_system_info(). That branch is now the model’s job.
It looks at the result and decides what comes next: another tool call, or a final answer. And the decisions chain, as the trace in the Overview shows: call get_system_info, pull the number out of the returned JSON, compare it against 1 GB, and only then choose which pattern to draw. Two model turns with a comparison in between that nobody hard-coded.
A classifier that always reads the same three sensor values, always calls the model exactly once, always with the same prompt shape, does none of this. That is a pipeline: deterministic, fast, and exactly right for its job (a risk classifier should not wander off to check the disk). What follows is different in kind. It is a loop:
 
Two things the diagram does not show often trip people up on the first read:

The model never runs anything. It emits a request (a function name and a JSON blob of arguments), then stops and waits. The Python code does the actual work and hands the output back. Nothing executes unless the harness executes it, which is also where every safety check belongs.
Nothing guarantees the loop terminates. A confused model can call get_system_info five times in a row. Section 0.8 caps the iterations (MAX_TURNS) and breaks out with a message rather than trusting the model to stop on its own.



Three words get used interchangeably, and separating them is worth a paragraph.
The model is Qwen3.5, sitting behind llama-server. It reads text and writes text. That is all it does: it cannot open a file, read a sensor, or light an LED, and between requests it remembers nothing.
The harness is everything else: the loop in the diagram above, the dispatch table that maps a name to a Python function, the code that formats messages and appends results, and the turn limit that stops runaways. It is ordinary software, about 40 lines here.
The agent is the two together. Neither half is an agent on its own.
That split tells where a problem lives. A tool returning wrong data, a loop that never terminates, an LED that lights when it should go dark: those are harness bugs, and a debugger finds them. A model that picks the wrong tool, or keeps calling tools after it already has the answer: those are not harness bugs, and no amount of Python fixes them. Section 0.9 puts both kinds side by side.
“Harness” is also the vocabulary worth carrying: it is what people mean by “agent framework” or “scaffolding”. LangChain agents, OpenAI’s Assistants API, and the rest are harnesses with more in them (retries, memory, orchestration, tracing), wrapped around exactly the cycle above.

Building a small harness by hand is the fastest way to understand what the large ones are actually doing.




llama-server exposes an OpenAI-compatible tools parameter on /v1/chat/completions. Each tool is described as a JSON Schema (name, description, parameter types), and the server constrains decoding so the model’s function-call arguments come back as valid, parseable JSON rather than prose. Compared to the classify-then-route pattern, where the model had to freehand a JSON object like {"type": "multiplication", "numbers": [7, 8]} and the code hoped it got the shape right, the native API moves that structural guarantee into the inference engine itself. It does not fix everything (Section 0.10 has the honest version of what still goes wrong at 0.8B), but it removes one whole category of failure.
Qwen3.5 supports this function-calling format natively. It needs the chat template active (the --jinja flag), because tool-call formatting is part of the model’s chat template, not a separate code path.







Arduino UNO Q, 2 GB or 4 GB. The 0.8B model fits either; the 2B model used later is more comfortable on 4 GB (see the candidate models in the SLM lab).
USB-C data cable.
Host computer with SSH.

Nothing else. No breadboard, no sensors, no external LEDs: every tool in this lab uses either the Linux filesystem and CLI or the UNO Q’s own onboard LED and LED matrix.






Table 1: Software this lab reuses.





Tool
Purpose




llama.cpp built from source, Qwen3.5-0.8B GGUF
From the SLM lab


llama-server
From the SLM lab; this lab starts it in the foreground with its own flags


openai Python client
From the SLM lab


arduino-app-cli
Builds and runs dual-brain apps






Nothing new is installed on the Python side: openai is all this needs. On the MCU side, the Arduino_LED_Matrix library is bundled with the UNO Q’s Zephyr core and needs no separate install.



This lab uses Qwen3.5-0.8B at first and switches to Qwen3.5-2B partway through Section 0.9. That is not indecision: the swap is the experiment. The small model demonstrates the mechanism and then hits a visible wall, and crossing that wall costs exactly one changed file path and about twice the latency. Section 0.10 has the measurements.
Both models are downloaded in the SLM lab. Check that they are there:
ls ~/models/Qwen_Qwen3.5-0.8B-Q8_0.gguf
ls ~/models/Qwen3.5-2B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf
Only one runs at a time, since they share port 8081.

About the measurements. The numbers in this lab were taken with Unsloth’s Qwen3.5-0.8B-Q8_0.gguf and with the UD-Q4_K_XL file from Unsloth’s Qwen3.5-2B-MTP-GGUF repository. The SLM lab’s files (Bartowski’s 0.8B Q8_0 and the non-MTP 2B UD-Q4_K_XL) are the same quantizations of the same models, so expect similar, but not identical, timings.




Start llama-server as in the SLM lab, with the flags this lab depends on:
~/llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server \
  --model ~/models/Qwen_Qwen3.5-0.8B-Q8_0.gguf \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8081 \
  --jinja \
  --reasoning off --reasoning-budget 0 \
  --ctx-size 8192 --parallel 1 --threads 4 \
  --batch-size 512 --ubatch-size 64 \
  --predict 1024 \
  --alias qwen3.5-0.8b

--jinja activates the chat template. Tool-call formatting lives inside that template, so without this flag tool_calls comes back empty every time, and the model describes its intended tool call in prose instead of making one.
--reasoning off --reasoning-budget 0 disables Qwen3.5’s thinking traces. Thinking and tool calling interact badly at this size: the model spends its token budget reasoning about which tool to call, then emits the reasoning as the answer instead of the call.
--ubatch-size 64 is the single biggest performance flag in this lab. It makes answers more than three times faster, for reasons Section 0.10.2 measures. Do not skip it, and do not judge how slow the agent feels while it is at the default.
--ctx-size 8192 gives the loop room. An agent conversation grows with every tool result, and a read_file result can add a thousand tokens or more on its own. Tool definitions take their share too: the WebUI in Section 0.4 sends about 1,200 tokens of them with every request. At 4096, one large tool result can leave no room for the answer, and the server stops with Context size has been exceeded.
--parallel 1 opens a single slot. By default the server opens several slots that share one KV cache (kv_unified = 'true' in the startup log), so a second request, from another browser tab or a classmate on the same board, takes space and CPU from the first, and both can fail. With one slot, the second request waits its turn.
--predict 1024 caps generation on the server side. main.py sets max_tokens, but Section 0.4 drives the model from the WebUI with no client-side limit, so this is the backstop that keeps a confused model from generating for minutes.
--alias is the model name the server reports to clients, and it must match MODEL in main.py. It is qwen3.5-0.8b throughout this lab, including after the 2B swap, where keeping the same alias means no Python has to change.

This exact command is used three times in the lab: here, in the WebUI section with --tools appended, and in the 2B swap with only the --model path changed. If flags change between sections, something has gone wrong.
This is the server configuration the Python agent needs, and the one to come back to after the WebUI section borrows the port for a different purpose. Two details matter for the agent specifically:

--host 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1. The agent runs inside a container and reaches llama-server across the container gateway, so a server bound to loopback is invisible to it.
No --tools. That flag controls llama.cpp’s own built-in tools, which only the WebUI section uses. The agent supplies its own tool schemas in every request, so the server never needs to know about them in advance.

Only one process can hold port 8081, so stop whichever server is running before starting another:
# Ctrl-C in the terminal running it, or from anywhere:
pkill -f llama-server

If an earlier tutorial left llama-server running as a systemd service that starts at boot, it holds port 8081. This lab runs the server in the foreground instead, to show its output and change its flags between sections. Stop the service first, for example with sudo systemctl disable --now llama-server, and re-enable it later if needed.

Verify tool calling before writing any code:
curl -s http://localhost:8081/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "model": "qwen3.5-0.8b",
  "messages": [{"role":"user","content":"What is 47 times 12?"}],
  "tools": [{"type":"function","function":{
    "name":"calculate",
    "description":"Evaluate an arithmetic expression.",
    "parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{
      "expression":{"type":"string"}},"required":["expression"]}}}]
}' | python3 -m json.tool | grep -A5 tool_calls
 
A tool_calls block with a calculate function and an expression argument means the server is configured correctly. Plain text instead means something is wrong; fix it before continuing, because everything downstream depends on it.




Before writing a line of Python, it is worth seeing an agent loop run with zero code. Recent llama.cpp builds ship a set of built-in tools the model can call from the server’s own WebUI, the same interface used for chat in the SLM lab. This is the fastest way for a room full of students to see tool calling happen, watch each decision, and approve or reject it in real time, before anyone opens an editor.

Keep the built-in agent tools switched off in ordinary chat sessions. This section turns them on deliberately and briefly, with the reasoning made explicit. Read the safety note at the end before the next session.



The built-in tool set is marked experimental upstream, and the list has changed several times. Do not trust the one printed below; ask the binary that was built:
~/llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server --help | grep -A6 -- '--tools'
On a build from around the time of writing:
--tools TOOL1,TOOL2,...  experimental: whether to enable built-in tools
                         for AI agents - do not enable in untrusted
                         environments (default: no tools) specify "all"
                         to enable all tools
                         available tools: read_file, file_glob_search,
                         grep_search, exec_shell_command, write_file,
                         edit_file, get_info
Read the default again: no tools. Nothing is exposed unless it is named on the command line. Naming a tool the build does not have stops the server at startup with unknown tool "...", followed by the list it does have. Older builds listed apply_diff and get_datetime here; both have since left the server. Most builds also offer a -ag, --agent shortcut that switches on every tool plus the MCP CORS proxy in one go. Convenient, and exactly the wrong choice for a classroom: it hands the model a shell before anyone has seen it call a single tool.



This section needs a different server from the rest of the lab: the same command with one flag added, --tools, and bound to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0, so only the board itself can reach it. Stop the running server first, since only one process can hold port 8081:
~/llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server \
  --model ~/models/Qwen_Qwen3.5-0.8B-Q8_0.gguf \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8081 \
  --jinja \
  --reasoning off --reasoning-budget 0 \
  --ctx-size 8192 --parallel 1 --threads 4 \
  --batch-size 512 --ubatch-size 64 \
  --predict 1024 \
  --tools read_file,file_glob_search,grep_search,get_info \
  --alias qwen3.5-0.8b
Then, on the laptop, open an SSH tunnel and browse through it:
ssh -L 8081:127.0.0.1:8081 arduino@<UNO_Q_IP>
# then open http://localhost:8081/ on the laptop

The server now exposes only those four, all of them read-only. The others are not merely switched off: as far as the browser is concerned, they do not exist.

What about the date and time? Older builds had a get_datetime server tool. It now lives in the WebUI itself, as the Current time tool shown in Section 0.4.3: the browser offers it to the model in every chat, with no --tools flag, and answers with the date, time, and time zone of the computer running the browser, not the board’s. Passing --tools get_datetime to a current build stops the server at startup with unknown tool "get_datetime".


Warning: --tools all exposes all seven tools, including exec_shell_command. Each one can be switched off in the WebUI, but that is a browser setting, not a boundary. This lab names the active tools explicitly on the command line instead.


The tunnel also keeps the WebUI working with --tools. Several builds clamp --cors-origins to localhost when tools are enabled, on the reasoning that a server handing out file access should not accept requests from arbitrary origins. Through the tunnel the browser is at http://localhost:8081, so the origins match. Browsing the board’s LAN address instead fails on those builds.




Open the WebUI, click the gear icon (Settings), then Tools in the left-hand list. The tools come in two groups, each tool with its own Enabled and Always allow checkboxes:

Server lists the four tools named with --tools: Read file, Search files, Search in files, and Runtime info (get_info). These run on the board.
Browser lists Current time, a tool the WebUI adds by itself. It runs in the browser, on the computer used for browsing, and never touches the board.

 
Why name get_info at all, when it only reports the OS and working directory? Because the WebUI fills the gap otherwise. Without a server get_info, it adds a browser tool with the same name, Runtime info, in the Browser group. That one reports the OS of the computer running the browser, not the board’s, and tells the model it has no file access and that the user should restart the server with --agent. With file tools on the server, that is false, and its description invites the model to call it exactly when asked about files, which is what Section 0.4.5 does. A small model may believe it and refuse to search. Naming get_info on the command line replaces the browser version with the board’s real answer, and keeps the rule intact: the command line decides what exists. Its answer appears in Section 0.4.5.
If instead only the Browser group appears:
 
…the server was started without --tools. That is the most common stumble in this section, and a productive one, because it shows where the control actually lives:

The command line is the boundary. --tools decides what exists.
The panel is a view onto that list, plus per-browser convenience toggles. Look at the line under the tool list: settings are saved in the browser’s localStorage. Clearing the browser data resets the checkboxes; the server’s allow-list does not move.

A student who only ever sees the checkboxes may come away believing the browser grants permissions. It does not. Section 0.5 builds the same idea from the other direction.



Click Agentic in the same Settings list:
 

Agentic turns: the same idea as the MAX_TURNS cap built by hand later: a hard stop on how many tool-call cycles run before the server gives up. The default (often 10) is fine to start.
MCP request timeout: how long a single tool call may take before it is abandoned.
Mention search depth: how many directory levels the file-search tools descend.




Warm up with one tool call. Right after starting the server, open a new chat and ask:

“Give me the info”

The model calls Runtime info, and the answer comes from the board, not from the computer running the browser: an aarch64 Linux kernel and /home/arduino as the working directory.
 
Before reading the answer, read the two lines of numbers around it. They show where the time goes:

Above the answer: reading the prompt. 1,311 tokens in 2 minutes 3 seconds, at about 10.6 tokens per second. The question is only a handful of those tokens. Almost all the rest are the definitions of the five enabled tools, which the WebUI sends with every request so the model knows what it can call.
Below the answer: writing the reply. 96 tokens in 19 seconds, at about 5 tokens per second.

So with tools on, the wait comes from reading, not writing. Three consequences matter for the rest of this section:

Only the first request after the server starts pays for the tool definitions. The server keeps what it has already read (its prompt cache), and every request starts with the same definitions, so later turns, and even new chats, skip them and start in seconds. Restart the server and the cache is empty again.
Big tool results cost minutes. When a tool returns a file, the model has to read that file before it can answer. A file of 2,000 tokens adds about three minutes.
Fewer tools means a shorter wait. Every tool unticked in the panel is one less definition to read.

Now give it a real task. Try a prompt that cannot be answered from the model’s own knowledge:

“What files are in my home directory, and is there anything in them about edge AI?”

Watch the chat. A confirmation card appears, asking to run a specific tool with specific arguments, before it executes.
 
Approve it, watch the result stream back into the conversation, and see whether the model needs a second call (it likely will: one to list files and one to search inside them) before it gives a final answer.
 
That is the loop diagram happening live, one approved step at a time: send, decide, call, feed the result back, decide again.
