title: Image Classification
text:
With the UNO Q set up for headless development in the Setup lab, this lab builds the first classic vision application: image classification.
Image classification is the “Hello World” of computer vision and machine learning: given an image, the model assigns it to one of several predefined categories. It is one of the most widely deployed ML tasks at the edge, with applications from quality inspection in factories to wildlife monitoring in the field.
This lab has two parts:

Part 1 runs the UNO Q’s pre-installed image classification example, a static image classifier that receives a photo uploaded through a web browser and returns the classification result.
Part 2 builds a custom image classifier from scratch with Edge Impulse Studio, trained to tell a toy robot from a small Brazilian parakeet toy (periquito), and deploys it to the UNO Q with App Lab Bricks, first for static images and then for live webcam inference.

Along the way, the lab uses the UNO Q’s dual-brain architecture: Python on the MPU for AI inference and an Arduino sketch on the MCU for physical feedback on the LED matrix, connected through Bridge RPC.
 



Understand how the pre-installed image classification Brick works (static image to web UI).
Collect image data and train a custom classifier with Edge Impulse Studio.
Deploy a custom model through App Lab Bricks.
Move from static classification to live webcam inference.
Send inference results to the MCU over Bridge for real-time physical feedback.






The Setup lab, with the UNO Q reachable over SSH.
An Edge Impulse account (free).
A USB webcam (most models work, for example a Logitech C270).
A USB hub with power delivery, to connect both the webcam and power to the UNO Q.

 





Table 1: Hardware for this lab.









Item
Purpose




Arduino UNO Q (2 GB or 4 GB)
Edge AI inference and MCU actuation


USB webcam
Image capture for live inference (Part 2)


USB hub with PD
Connects the webcam and power to the single USB-C port


Toy robot and periquito, optional
Classification targets for the custom model












Table 2: Software for this lab.





Tool
Where




Edge Impulse Studio
Browser: studio.edgeimpulse.com


Arduino App Lab
Host computer, to deploy the Edge Impulse model to the board


arduino-app-cli
Pre-installed on the UNO Q







No editor is required: every step works from an SSH terminal. For a full IDE, see the VS Code Remote-SSH section of the Setup lab.





Computer vision lets machines interpret and make decisions from visual data, imitating what the human visual system does. Machine learning greatly extends a system’s ability to understand, interpret, and react to visual input.
 
On embedded devices, the most common computer vision applications are image classification and object detection:

Image classification assigns a single label to the whole image (“This is a robot” or “This is a periquito”).
Object detection locates objects in the image, drawing a bounding box around each one and assigning it a label.

This lab covers image classification; object detection is the topic of the next UNO Q lab.


The Nicla Vision Image Classification lab builds the same kind of classifier on a microcontroller. The UNO Q approach differs in several ways:



Table 3: Image classification on the Nicla Vision and the UNO Q.










Aspect
Nicla Vision
Arduino UNO Q




Camera
Built-in GC2145 (320×240)
External USB webcam (up to 1080p)


Data collection
OpenMV IDE and built-in camera
Edge Impulse Studio (smartphone, webcam, or upload)


Model size
MobileNetV2 0.05/0.1 (96×96, INT8)
MobileNetV2 0.35 or larger (96×96 to 320×320)


Inference engine
TFLite for Microcontrollers (C++)
App Lab Bricks (Python)


RAM for the model
~256 KB SRAM
2–4 GB LPDDR4X


Actuation
Direct GPIO from the MCU
MCU via Bridge RPC


Development
OpenMV IDE / Arduino IDE
SSH terminal, arduino-app-cli, and App Lab (VS Code optional)






The UNO Q can run larger, more accurate models on higher-resolution input, because inference runs on the Linux MPU with gigabytes of RAM. The Nicla Vision wins on power consumption (milliwatts instead of watts) and on latency for very small models.




The UNO Q ships with an image classification example. It combines an ImageClassification Brick and a WebUI Brick into a browser-based interface that uploads an image and shows the classification result.

This step does not need a webcam.



The pre-installed examples:inspirational/image-classification app works as follows:
Browser (your PC)                   UNO Q (MPU / Python)
+-------------------+               +-------------------------+
|                   |  Upload image |                         |
|  Web UI (port     | ------------> |  ImageClassification    |
|  7000)            |  (base64 via  |  Brick                  |
|                   |   WebSocket)  |                         |
|  Shows results    | <------------ |  Returns labels +       |
|  (labels +        |  Classifi-    |  confidence scores      |
|  confidence)      |  cation       |                         |
+-------------------+               +-------------------------+
Key points:

Classification runs on static images uploaded through the browser; there is no live camera feed.
Results appear in the browser, not in the terminal logs.
The example does not communicate with the MCU over Bridge.
The ImageClassification Brick handles model loading, image preprocessing, and inference internally.




SSH into the UNO Q (or use the VS Code integrated terminal) and run:
arduino-app-cli app start examples:inspirational/image-classification
Wait for the app to build and start.
 



On the host computer, open a web browser and go to:
http://<UNO_Q_IP_ADDRESS>:7000
The web interface has an upload button for selecting an image file on the computer.
 




Click the upload button and select a photo (for example, an animal, a car, or a household object).
The image is sent to the UNO Q, where the ImageClassification Brick processes it.
After a moment, the browser shows the detected labels and their confidence scores.

 
Try different images and observe how the model classifies them.

The terminal logs (arduino-app-cli app logs examples:inspirational/image-classification) show the app’s startup messages but not the classification results, which go directly to the browser over WebSocket.

 



Read the example’s source to understand how it works. From an SSH terminal:
cat /var/lib/arduino-app-cli/examples/inspirational/common/\
image-classification/python/main.py
With VS Code Remote-SSH, open the folder and browse python/main.py directly:

File > Open Folder…
Navigate to /var/lib/arduino-app-cli/examples/inspirational/common/image-classification/.
Open python/main.py.

The key components, in a simplified excerpt:
# The Bricks handle all the heavy lifting
from arduino.app_bricks.web_ui import WebUI
from arduino.app_bricks.image_classification import (
    ImageClassification,
)

# Initialize the classification Brick (loads the model internally)
image_classification = ImageClassification()

# Callback: when the browser sends an image, classify it and
# return the result
def on_classify_image(client_id, data):
    image_data = data.get('image')     # Base64 image from browser
    image_bytes = base64.b64decode(image_data)
    pil_image = Image.open(io.BytesIO(image_bytes))
    results = image_classification.classify(pil_image)  # Inference
    response = {'success': True, 'results': results}
    ui.send_message('classification_result', response)  # To browser

# Set up the WebUI and register the callback
ui = WebUI()
ui.on_message('classify_image', on_classify_image)
App.run()
Note that:

ImageClassification() is a Brick, a prebuilt module that encapsulates the model and the inference logic.
WebUI() provides the web server and the WebSocket communication.
App.run() starts the app without a user_loop: it is event-driven, triggered by browser uploads.
There is no Bridge.call(), so the MCU is not involved.




arduino-app-cli app stop examples:inspirational/image-classification



Arduino’s documentation covers App Lab in detail, so here are just the main steps:

Open Arduino App Lab on the host computer and connect to the UNO Q over Wi-Fi.
Enter the board’s password.
Under Examples, open Classify Images.

 

Run it. The web UI opens automatically, as before.




The pre-installed example demonstrates the Brick-based approach: high-level components that hide model loading, image processing, and web communication. That is convenient for quick demos, but it has limitations:

Static images only (no live camera feed).
Results stay in the browser (no MCU actuation).
A generic, pre-trained model.

Part 2 removes all three limitations.




Part 2 builds a custom classifier from scratch. Following the same project as the Nicla Vision Image Classification lab, the model learns three categories:

Robot: a small toy robot.
Periquito: a small toy of a Brazilian parakeet.
Background: no object present.

 


The goal is a system that continuously captures frames from a USB webcam, classifies what it sees, and gives physical feedback through the MCU:
USB webcam -> Python (MPU) -> EI model -> robot / periquito / background
                                                    |
                                  Bridge.call("show_result", label)
                                                    |
                                          MCU (Arduino sketch)
                                          -> LED matrix (icon per class)
This differs fundamentally from Part 1: live inference instead of static uploads, MCU actuation instead of a browser display, and a custom model instead of a generic pre-trained one.
The custom model is deployed in two steps:

Path A (Section 0.8) uses the same ImageClassification Brick as the pre-installed example, with the custom Edge Impulse model. It is quick to set up but limited to static uploads.
Path B (Section 0.9) uses the VideoImageClassification Brick for live webcam inference, and Section 0.10 adds Bridge communication with the MCU. This is the path for real projects.





Collecting a high-quality dataset is the most important step in any ML project.



Go to Edge Impulse Studio and create a new project (for example, “UNO-Q Image Classification”).
Go to Devices and click Connect a new device.
Select Use your mobile phone; a QR code appears.
Scan the QR code with the smartphone.
Once connected, go to Data acquisition.
Set the Label (for example, “periquito”), select Camera, and click Start sampling.
Capture about 50 to 60 images from different angles, distances, and lighting conditions.
Repeat for “robot” and “background”.

 



Images can also be captured directly from the USB webcam on the UNO Q, with a script such as capture_images.py:
import cv2
import os
import time

label = "robot"  # Change for each class
output_dir = f"/home/arduino/dataset/{label}"
os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True)

cap = cv2.VideoCapture(0)
cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_WIDTH, 320)
cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_HEIGHT, 240)

count = 0
print(f"Capturing images for class '{label}'. Press Ctrl+C to stop.")
try:
    while count < 60:
        ret, frame = cap.read()
        if ret:
            filename = f"{output_dir}/{label}_{count:03d}.jpg"
            cv2.imwrite(filename, frame)
            print(f"Saved: {filename}")
            count += 1
            time.sleep(0.5)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass
cap.release()
print(f"Captured {count} images for '{label}'.")
Install OpenCV in a virtual environment and run the script:
# Debian needs the python3-venv package to create environments
sudo apt install python3.13-venv

# 1) Create the environment
python3.13 -m venv ~/envs/cv2-env

# 2) Activate it
source ~/envs/cv2-env/bin/activate

# 3) Install OpenCV (the headless version is enough)
pip install --upgrade pip
pip install opencv-python-headless

# 4) Run the script
python3 capture_images.py

The images are stored on the UNO Q under ~/dataset/<label>/. Copy them to the host with scp (scp -r arduino@<UNO_Q_IP>:~/dataset ./dataset) or by dragging them in VS Code’s file explorer, then upload them to Edge Impulse Studio under Data acquisition > Upload data.




Images collected for the Nicla Vision lab can be uploaded to Edge Impulse Studio under Data acquisition > Upload data, with the correct label for each batch.




About 50 to 60 images per class, at minimum.
Varied angles, lighting, and backgrounds.
A “background” class with images that contain no target object.


More diverse training data produces more robust models.







In Edge Impulse Studio, go to Data acquisition and check that the data is correctly labeled and balanced.
 

The project is public and can be cloned: UNO-Q Image Classification.





Go to Create impulse.
Set the input size to 160×160 for higher accuracy on the UNO Q.
Add Image as the processing block.
Add Transfer Learning (Images) as the learning block.
Check the output features: robot, periquito, and background.
Click Save Impulse.

 




Go to the Image tab.
Set the color depth to RGB.
Click Save parameters, then Generate features.





Go to the Transfer Learning tab.
Select MobileNetV2 160x160 1.0 (recommended for the UNO Q).
Set the training cycles to 20.
Enable Data augmentation.
Click Start training.

Review the accuracy, the confusion matrix, and the estimated on-device performance.
 
The model reached high accuracy in training, with an estimated latency of 100 ms. Models with a smaller width multiplier (alpha), such as 0.35, run faster with similar accuracy, so it is worth testing which parameters suit each project.



Go to Model testing. In the settings, enable Int8, then click Classify all to validate the model on the test set.
 




This path uses the Brick architecture with the custom model. It is quick to set up but limited to static image uploads through the browser.


Copy the example from the command line:
cp -r /var/lib/arduino-app-cli/examples/inspirational/common/\
image-classification/ ~/ArduinoApps/my-classifier-bricks
Or copy it in Arduino App Lab, giving it a new name; the copy appears in the My Apps area.
 




In the copied example in My Apps, go to Bricks/Image Classification, select AI models, and click Train new AI model.

 

A window asks for the Arduino/Edge Impulse account login, then opens the list of Edge Impulse Studio projects. Open the project (here, “UNO-Q Image Classification”).
In the project, go to Deployment.
Select Arduino UNO Q as the target (or Linux AARCH64).
Click Build.

 
When the build finishes, the .eim file downloads to the computer, and a pop-up window with a Go to Arduino button appears. Clicking it sends the model to App Lab.
 

The model can also be tested on a phone or computer with the QR code on the deployment page.




The model now appears in the project’s AI Models area. Download it to the UNO Q and select it.
 
In the project folder (~/ArduinoApps/my-classifier-bricks), the Brick configuration in app.yaml is updated automatically to point to the custom model:
name: My Classifier (Custom Images)
description: Custom Image classification in the browser using a
  web-based interface.
ports: []
bricks:
- arduino:image_classification:
    model: ei-model-947334-1
- arduino:web_ui: {}
icon: 📊
The model (model.eim) is saved in /home/arduino/.arduino-bricks/models/custom-ei/ei-model-947334-1.



cd ~/ArduinoApps/my-classifier-bricks
arduino-app-cli app start .
Open http://<UNO_Q_IP>:7000 in a browser and upload images of the robot, the periquito, or the background. The classifier now uses the custom model.
 

Limitation: this approach still relies on static image uploads through the browser. Path B adds live webcam inference.

Before moving on, modify python/main.py to print information about the new model and each inference result. First, stop the app:
arduino-app-cli app stop .
Then replace python/main.py with:
from arduino.app_utils import App
from arduino.app_bricks.web_ui import WebUI
from arduino.app_bricks.image_classification import (
    ImageClassification,
)
from PIL import Image
import io
import base64
import time

image_classification = ImageClassification()


def print_model_info(image_classification):
    info = image_classification.get_model_info()
    if info is not None:
        print("Model info:")
        for attr in dir(info):
            value = getattr(info, attr)
            if not attr.startswith("_") and not callable(value):
                print(f"  {attr}: {value}")
    else:
        print("Failed to retrieve model info.")


def on_classify_image(client_id, data):
    """Callback function to handle image classification requests."""
    try:
        image_data = data.get('image')
        image_type_raw = data.get('image_type')
        if image_type_raw:
            image_type = image_type_raw.split('/')[-1]
        else:
            image_type = 'jpeg'
        confidence = data.get('confidence', 0.25)
        if not image_data:
            ui.send_message('classification_error',
                            {'error': 'No image data'})
            return

        image_bytes = base64.b64decode(image_data)
        pil_image = Image.open(io.BytesIO(image_bytes))

        start_time = time.time() * 1000
        results = image_classification.classify(
            pil_image, image_type=image_type, confidence=confidence
        )
        print(f"\nInference: {results}")
        diff = time.time() * 1000 - start_time
        print(f"Latency: {diff:.2f} ms")
        if results is None:
            ui.send_message('classification_error',
                            {'error': 'No results returned'})
            return

        response = {
            'success': True,
            'results': results,
            'processing_time': f"{diff:.2f} ms"
        }
        ui.send_message('classification_result', response)

    except Exception as e:
        ui.send_message('classification_error', {'error': str(e)})


print_model_info(image_classification)
ui = WebUI()
ui.on_message('classify_image', on_classify_image)

App.run()

arduino-app-cli app start .
In a second terminal, go to the project folder and follow the logs:
cd ~/ArduinoApps/my-classifier-bricks
arduino-app-cli app logs . --follow
 
The logs show that the custom model takes 160×160 images and that its labels are:
labels: ['background', 'periquito', 'robot']
The latency of this model is around 444 ms, a little over 2 FPS.

For a faster model, train with smaller images (such as 96×96) or a smaller network, for example with an alpha of 0.35.





This path runs live webcam capture and continuous classification, and the next section adds Bridge communication with the MCU.


In Arduino App Lab’s My Apps, click the Create new app button in the upper right.
 
Name it, for example, Image Classification on Camera.



Go to Bricks and click Add Brick.
 
In the list of available Bricks, scroll down to Video Image Classification and click Add brick.
 
As in Path A, once the Brick is installed, go to the AI Models tab and select the UNO-Q Image Classification model deployed earlier.
 
Selecting the model creates app.yaml automatically, pointing to the custom model:

The new app’s python/main.py is a generic template that must be written for this model. The key piece is the VideoImageClassification class:
class VideoImageClassification(camera: BaseCamera | None,
                               confidence: float,
                               debounce_sec: float)
This module classifies images on a live video stream with the selected model, and it calls registered actions in real time when classes are detected. Its parameters are:

camera (BaseCamera): the camera that captures the video. If None, a default camera is initialized.
confidence (float): the minimum confidence for a classification to count. The default is 0.3.
debounce_sec (float): the minimum time, in seconds, between consecutive detections of the same class, to avoid repeated triggers. The default is 0.

The complete code:
from arduino.app_utils import App
from arduino.app_bricks.video_imageclassification import (
    VideoImageClassification,
)

# Create a classification stream with a confidence threshold of 0.5
classification_stream = VideoImageClassification(confidence=0.5)

# Callback when "periquito" is detected
def periquito_detected():
    print("Detected periquito!")

# Callback when "robot" is detected
def robot_detected():
    print("Detected robot!")

# Subscribe to specific labels
classification_stream.on_detect("periquito", periquito_detected)
classification_stream.on_detect("robot", robot_detected)

# Optional: callback for all classifications (useful for debugging)
def all_detected(results):
    # results maps each label to its confidence,
    # for example {"periquito": 0.85}
    print("Classification results:", results)

classification_stream.on_detect_all(all_detected)

# Run the app
App.run()

cd ~/ArduinoApps/image-classification-on-camera
arduino-app-cli app start .
In a second terminal, go to the project folder and follow the logs:
cd ~/ArduinoApps/image-classification-on-camera
arduino-app-cli app logs . --follow
 




Live classification now runs through the VideoImageClassification Brick, with callbacks printing results to the log. This section adds the MCU side, using Bridge RPC to drive the LED matrix according to what the camera sees.


USB webcam -> VideoImageClassification Brick -> on_detect_all(callback)
                                                       |

                                                       |
                                              MCU (Arduino sketch)
                                              -> LED matrix: face = robot
                                              -> LED matrix: bird = periquito
                                              -> LED matrix: empty = background



The image-classification-on-camera project has no sketch/ folder yet, since the MCU is not involved. Create one (in VS Code or in a terminal), unless it already exists:

The sketch includes the Arduino_LED_Matrix.h library and calls matrix.renderBitmap(frame, 8, 13) to draw on the 8×13 matrix. The patterns are simple pixel art that can be refined later with the Arduino LED Matrix Editor (adjusted to 13 columns instead of 12).

void setup() {
    matrix.begin();
    matrix.renderBitmap(empty_frame, 8, 13);

    Bridge.begin();
    Bridge.provide("show_result", show_result);
}

void loop() {
}

void show_result(String label) {
    if (label == "robot") {
        matrix.renderBitmap(robot_frame, 8, 13);

Create (or modify) sketch/sketch.yaml:
profiles:
  default:
    platforms:
      - platform: arduino:zephyr
    libraries:
      - Arduino_RouterBridge (0.3.0)
      - dependency: Arduino_RPClite (0.2.1)
      - dependency: ArxContainer (0.7.0)
      - dependency: ArxTypeTraits (0.3.2)
      - dependency: DebugLog (0.8.4)
      - dependency: MsgPack (0.4.2)
default_profile: default



Modify python/main.py to send the classification results to the MCU over Bridge. Instead of separate on_detect callbacks per class, this version uses only on_detect_all and picks the top class from its results. The current_label check sends a Bridge call only when the result actually changes.
The confidence threshold is also lowered to 0.3, so that “background” detections, which sometimes have lower confidence, still come through. Tune it after testing.
from arduino.app_utils import App, Bridge
from arduino.app_bricks.video_imageclassification import (
    VideoImageClassification,
)

classification_stream = VideoImageClassification(confidence=0.3)

current_label = ""

# Priority order: robot and periquito take precedence over background
PRIORITY = {"robot": 2, "periquito": 1, "background": 0}

def all_detected(results):
    global current_label
    print(f"Raw results: {results}")

    if results:
        # Pick the highest-priority label from the results
        label = max(results, key=lambda r: PRIORITY.get(r, -1))
    else:
        label = "background"

    if label != current_label:
        current_label = label
        Bridge.call("show_result", label)
        print(f"==> {label}")

classification_stream.on_detect_all(all_detected)
App.run()

The current_label variable avoids redundant Bridge calls on every frame: the LED matrix changes only when the detected class changes.

The Arduino sketch can be extended with other kinds of feedback.
External LEDs:
#include "Arduino_RouterBridge.h"

// Digital pins for external LEDs
#define MY_LED_BLUE   2
#define MY_LED_GREEN  3

The two latencies come from very different models and input sizes (MobileNetV2 0.1 at 96×96 is far smaller than MobileNetV2 1.0 at 160×160), so they show the range of each platform, not a head-to-head result. Accuracy is left out on purpose: the two labs used different datasets and splits, so their accuracy figures are not comparable. Exercise 5 below sets up a fair comparison.
The UNO Q power figure is a practical estimate of the total for live classification with the USB camera and hub:

UNO Q board: about 2 to 3.5 W while the CPU is busy.
USB camera: about 0.5 to 1.25 W.
Powered hub: about 0.5 to 1 W.
Total: about 3 to 6 W from the wall (5 V, about 0.6 to 1.2 A) for a typical setup with one camera and one hub.


The UNO Q runs larger, more accurate models but uses much more power. The Nicla Vision suits battery-powered, always-on applications; the UNO Q excels when accuracy matters and the AI result must drive real-time hardware actions.






Add a fourth class. Collect images of a new object, retrain the model in Edge Impulse, redeploy it to the UNO Q, and update the Python code and the Arduino sketch. How does adding more classes affect accuracy?
Experiment with model size. Train the same dataset with MobileNetV2 0.1 (96×96) and MobileNetV2 1.0 (160×160). Deploy both to the UNO Q and compare inference time, accuracy, and LED responsiveness in a table.
Log to CSV. Modify main.py to log each detection event (timestamp and label) to a CSV file on the UNO Q. After 5 minutes, download the CSV and plot the detection frequency per class.
Design new LED matrix icons. Draw your own 8×13 patterns for each class with the Arduino LED Matrix Editor and display them on the UNO Q’s matrix.
Cross-platform comparison. With a Nicla Vision, deploy a 96×96 MobileNetV2 0.1 model to both platforms. Compare inference time, accuracy, power consumption, and development workflow.
Debounce tuning. Experiment with the debounce_sec parameter in VideoImageClassification(confidence=0.5, debounce_sec=1.0). How does a longer debounce time affect the responsiveness and stability of the LED feedback?




This lab went through three levels of image classification on the Arduino UNO Q:

Part 1: the pre-installed static image classifier (ImageClassification Brick and WebUI), with images uploaded through a browser and results shown in the web interface.
Path A: the custom model deployed through the same Brick, still with static uploads, but classifying the lab’s own robot, periquito, and background classes.
Path B: live camera classification with the VideoImageClassification Brick, with detection callbacks driving the LED matrix on the MCU over Bridge RPC.

Key takeaways:

The Edge Impulse → App Lab → UNO Q pipeline works. Collect data, train in Edge Impulse Studio, deploy to App Lab, and run, all guided through the UI.
Two Bricks, two modes. The ImageClassification Brick handles static images (good for testing), and the VideoImageClassification Brick handles live camera streams (essential for real applications).
The dual-brain architecture adds value. Python handles the camera and ML inference on the MPU, while the Arduino sketch on the MCU provides real-time control of the LED matrix, LEDs, servos, or buzzers. Bridge RPC connects the two.
Model selection matters. The UNO Q runs larger, more accurate models than any MCU, but there is always a trade-off between accuracy and inference speed. Test several configurations to find the best balance for each project.

The next UNO Q lab extends these skills to object detection, which finds not just what is in the image but also where it is, opening the door to tracking, counting, and spatial awareness.

title: Image Classification
text:
With the UNO Q set up for headless development in the Setup lab, this lab builds the first classic vision application: image classification.
Image classification is the “Hello World” of computer vision and machine learning: given an image, the model assigns it to one of several predefined categories. It is one of the most widely deployed ML tasks at the edge, with applications from quality inspection in factories to wildlife monitoring in the field.
This lab has two parts:

Part 1 runs the UNO Q’s pre-installed image classification example, a static image classifier that receives a photo uploaded through a web browser and returns the classification result.
Part 2 builds a custom image classifier from scratch with Edge Impulse Studio, trained to tell a toy robot from a small Brazilian parakeet toy (periquito), and deploys it to the UNO Q with App Lab Bricks, first for static images and then for live webcam inference.

Along the way, the lab uses the UNO Q’s dual-brain architecture: Python on the MPU for AI inference and an Arduino sketch on the MCU for physical feedback on the LED matrix, connected through Bridge RPC.
 



Understand how the pre-installed image classification Brick works (static image to web UI).
Collect image data and train a custom classifier with Edge Impulse Studio.
Deploy a custom model through App Lab Bricks.
Move from static classification to live webcam inference.
Send inference results to the MCU over Bridge for real-time physical feedback.

title: Image Classification
text:
Computer vision lets machines interpret and make decisions from visual data, imitating what the human visual system does. Machine learning greatly extends a system’s ability to understand, interpret, and react to visual input.
 
On embedded devices, the most common computer vision applications are image classification and object detection:

Image classification assigns a single label to the whole image (“This is a robot” or “This is a periquito”).
Object detection locates objects in the image, drawing a bounding box around each one and assigning it a label.

This lab covers image classification; object detection is the topic of the next UNO Q lab.


The Nicla Vision Image Classification lab builds the same kind of classifier on a microcontroller. The UNO Q approach differs in several ways:



Table 3: Image classification on the Nicla Vision and the UNO Q.










Aspect
Nicla Vision
Arduino UNO Q

External USB webcam (up to 1080p)

Inference engine

MCU via Bridge RPC


Development

The UNO Q can run larger, more accurate models on higher-resolution input, because inference runs on the Linux MPU with gigabytes of RAM. The Nicla Vision wins on power consumption (milliwatts instead of watts) and on latency for very small models.

title: Image Classification
text:
The UNO Q ships with an image classification example. It combines an ImageClassification Brick and a WebUI Brick into a browser-based interface that uploads an image and shows the classification result.

This step does not need a webcam.



The pre-installed examples:inspirational/image-classification app works as follows:
Browser (your PC)                   UNO Q (MPU / Python)
+-------------------+               +-------------------------+
|                   |  Upload image |                         |
|  Web UI (port     | ------------> |  ImageClassification    |
|  7000)            |  (base64 via  |  Brick                  |
|                   |   WebSocket)  |                         |
|  Shows results    | <------------ |  Returns labels +       |
|  (labels +        |  Classifi-    |  confidence scores      |
|  confidence)      |  cation       |                         |
+-------------------+               +-------------------------+
Key points:

Classification runs on static images uploaded through the browser; there is no live camera feed.
Results appear in the browser, not in the terminal logs.
The example does not communicate with the MCU over Bridge.
The ImageClassification Brick handles model loading, image preprocessing, and inference internally.




SSH into the UNO Q (or use the VS Code integrated terminal) and run:
arduino-app-cli app start examples:inspirational/image-classification
Wait for the app to build and start.
 



On the host computer, open a web browser and go to:
http://<UNO_Q_IP_ADDRESS>:7000
The web interface has an upload button for selecting an image file on the computer.
 




Click the upload button and select a photo (for example, an animal, a car, or a household object).
The image is sent to the UNO Q, where the ImageClassification Brick processes it.
After a moment, the browser shows the detected labels and their confidence scores.

 
Try different images and observe how the model classifies them.

The terminal logs (arduino-app-cli app logs examples:inspirational/image-classification) show the app’s startup messages but not the classification results, which go directly to the browser over WebSocket.

 



Read the example’s source to understand how it works. From an SSH terminal:
cat /var/lib/arduino-app-cli/examples/inspirational/common/\
image-classification/python/main.py
With VS Code Remote-SSH, open the folder and browse python/main.py directly:

File > Open Folder…
Navigate to /var/lib/arduino-app-cli/examples/inspirational/common/image-classification/.
Open python/main.py.

The key components, in a simplified excerpt:
# The Bricks handle all the heavy lifting
from arduino.app_bricks.web_ui import WebUI
from arduino.app_bricks.image_classification import (
    ImageClassification,
)

# Initialize the classification Brick (loads the model internally)
image_classification = ImageClassification()

# Callback: when the browser sends an image, classify it and
# return the result
def on_classify_image(client_id, data):
    image_data = data.get('image')     # Base64 image from browser
    image_bytes = base64.b64decode(image_data)
    pil_image = Image.open(io.BytesIO(image_bytes))
    results = image_classification.classify(pil_image)  # Inference
    response = {'success': True, 'results': results}
    ui.send_message('classification_result', response)  # To browser

# Set up the WebUI and register the callback
ui = WebUI()
ui.on_message('classify_image', on_classify_image)
App.run()
Note that:

ImageClassification() is a Brick, a prebuilt module that encapsulates the model and the inference logic.
WebUI() provides the web server and the WebSocket communication.
App.run() starts the app without a user_loop: it is event-driven, triggered by browser uploads.
There is no Bridge.call(), so the MCU is not involved.




arduino-app-cli app stop examples:inspirational/image-classification



Arduino’s documentation covers App Lab in detail, so here are just the main steps:

Open Arduino App Lab on the host computer and connect to the UNO Q over Wi-Fi.
Enter the board’s password.
Under Examples, open Classify Images.

 

Run it. The web UI opens automatically, as before.




The pre-installed example demonstrates the Brick-based approach: high-level components that hide model loading, image processing, and web communication. That is convenient for quick demos, but it has limitations:

Static images only (no live camera feed).
Results stay in the browser (no MCU actuation).
A generic, pre-trained model.

Part 2 removes all three limitations.

title: Image Classification
text:
Part 2 builds a custom classifier from scratch. Following the same project as the Nicla Vision Image Classification lab, the model learns three categories:

Robot: a small toy robot.
Periquito: a small toy of a Brazilian parakeet.
Background: no object present.

 


The goal is a system that continuously captures frames from a USB webcam, classifies what it sees, and gives physical feedback through the MCU:
USB webcam -> Python (MPU) -> EI model -> robot / periquito / background
                                                    |
                                  Bridge.call("show_result", label)
                                                    |
                                          MCU (Arduino sketch)
                                          -> LED matrix (icon per class)
This differs fundamentally from Part 1: live inference instead of static uploads, MCU actuation instead of a browser display, and a custom model instead of a generic pre-trained one.
The custom model is deployed in two steps:

Path A (Section 0.8) uses the same ImageClassification Brick as the pre-installed example, with the custom Edge Impulse model. It is quick to set up but limited to static uploads.
Path B (Section 0.9) uses the VideoImageClassification Brick for live webcam inference, and Section 0.10 adds Bridge communication with the MCU. This is the path for real projects.

title: Image Classification
text:
Collecting a high-quality dataset is the most important step in any ML project.



Go to Edge Impulse Studio and create a new project (for example, “UNO-Q Image Classification”).
Go to Devices and click Connect a new device.
Select Use your mobile phone; a QR code appears.
Scan the QR code with the smartphone.
Once connected, go to Data acquisition.
Set the Label (for example, “periquito”), select Camera, and click Start sampling.
Capture about 50 to 60 images from different angles, distances, and lighting conditions.
Repeat for “robot” and “background”.

 



Images can also be captured directly from the USB webcam on the UNO Q, with a script such as capture_images.py:
import cv2
import os
import time

label = "robot"  # Change for each class
output_dir = f"/home/arduino/dataset/{label}"
os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True)

cap = cv2.VideoCapture(0)
cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_WIDTH, 320)
cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_HEIGHT, 240)

count = 0
print(f"Capturing images for class '{label}'. Press Ctrl+C to stop.")
try:
    while count < 60:
        ret, frame = cap.read()
        if ret:
            filename = f"{output_dir}/{label}_{count:03d}.jpg"
            cv2.imwrite(filename, frame)
            print(f"Saved: {filename}")
            count += 1
            time.sleep(0.5)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass
cap.release()
print(f"Captured {count} images for '{label}'.")
Install OpenCV in a virtual environment and run the script:
# Debian needs the python3-venv package to create environments
sudo apt install python3.13-venv

# 1) Create the environment
python3.13 -m venv ~/envs/cv2-env

# 2) Activate it
source ~/envs/cv2-env/bin/activate

# 3) Install OpenCV (the headless version is enough)
pip install --upgrade pip
pip install opencv-python-headless

# 4) Run the script
python3 capture_images.py

The images are stored on the UNO Q under ~/dataset/<label>/. Copy them to the host with scp (scp -r arduino@<UNO_Q_IP>:~/dataset ./dataset) or by dragging them in VS Code’s file explorer, then upload them to Edge Impulse Studio under Data acquisition > Upload data.




Images collected for the Nicla Vision lab can be uploaded to Edge Impulse Studio under Data acquisition > Upload data, with the correct label for each batch.




About 50 to 60 images per class, at minimum.
Varied angles, lighting, and backgrounds.
A “background” class with images that contain no target object.


More diverse training data produces more robust models.

title: Image Classification
text:
In Edge Impulse Studio, go to Data acquisition and check that the data is correctly labeled and balanced.
 

The project is public and can be cloned: UNO-Q Image Classification.





Go to Create impulse.
Set the input size to 160×160 for higher accuracy on the UNO Q.
Add Image as the processing block.
Add Transfer Learning (Images) as the learning block.
Check the output features: robot, periquito, and background.
Click Save Impulse.

 




Go to the Image tab.
Set the color depth to RGB.
Click Save parameters, then Generate features.





Go to the Transfer Learning tab.
Select MobileNetV2 160x160 1.0 (recommended for the UNO Q).
Set the training cycles to 20.
Enable Data augmentation.
Click Start training.

Review the accuracy, the confusion matrix, and the estimated on-device performance.
 
The model reached high accuracy in training, with an estimated latency of 100 ms. Models with a smaller width multiplier (alpha), such as 0.35, run faster with similar accuracy, so it is worth testing which parameters suit each project.



Go to Model testing. In the settings, enable Int8, then click Classify all to validate the model on the test set.

title: Image Classification
text:
This path uses the Brick architecture with the custom model. It is quick to set up but limited to static image uploads through the browser.


Copy the example from the command line:
cp -r /var/lib/arduino-app-cli/examples/inspirational/common/\
image-classification/ ~/ArduinoApps/my-classifier-bricks
Or copy it in Arduino App Lab, giving it a new name; the copy appears in the My Apps area.
 




In the copied example in My Apps, go to Bricks/Image Classification, select AI models, and click Train new AI model.

 

A window asks for the Arduino/Edge Impulse account login, then opens the list of Edge Impulse Studio projects. Open the project (here, “UNO-Q Image Classification”).
In the project, go to Deployment.
Select Arduino UNO Q as the target (or Linux AARCH64).
Click Build.

 
When the build finishes, the .eim file downloads to the computer, and a pop-up window with a Go to Arduino button appears. Clicking it sends the model to App Lab.
 

The model can also be tested on a phone or computer with the QR code on the deployment page.




The model now appears in the project’s AI Models area. Download it to the UNO Q and select it.
 
In the project folder (~/ArduinoApps/my-classifier-bricks), the Brick configuration in app.yaml is updated automatically to point to the custom model:
name: My Classifier (Custom Images)
description: Custom Image classification in the browser using a
  web-based interface.
ports: []
bricks:
- arduino:image_classification:
    model: ei-model-947334-1
- arduino:web_ui: {}
icon: 📊
The model (model.eim) is saved in /home/arduino/.arduino-bricks/models/custom-ei/ei-model-947334-1.



cd ~/ArduinoApps/my-classifier-bricks
arduino-app-cli app start .
Open http://<UNO_Q_IP>:7000 in a browser and upload images of the robot, the periquito, or the background. The classifier now uses the custom model.
 

Limitation: this approach still relies on static image uploads through the browser. Path B adds live webcam inference.

Before moving on, modify python/main.py to print information about the new model and each inference result. First, stop the app:
arduino-app-cli app stop .
Then replace python/main.py with:
from arduino.app_utils import App
from arduino.app_bricks.web_ui import WebUI
from arduino.app_bricks.image_classification import (
    ImageClassification,
)
from PIL import Image
import io
import base64
import time

image_classification = ImageClassification()


def print_model_info(image_classification):
    info = image_classification.get_model_info()
    if info is not None:
        print("Model info:")
        for attr in dir(info):
            value = getattr(info, attr)
            if not attr.startswith("_") and not callable(value):
                print(f"  {attr}: {value}")
    else:
        print("Failed to retrieve model info.")


def on_classify_image(client_id, data):
    """Callback function to handle image classification requests."""
    try:
        image_data = data.get('image')
        image_type_raw = data.get('image_type')
        if image_type_raw:
            image_type = image_type_raw.split('/')[-1]
        else:
            image_type = 'jpeg'
        confidence = data.get('confidence', 0.25)
        if not image_data:
            ui.send_message('classification_error',
                            {'error': 'No image data'})
            return

        image_bytes = base64.b64decode(image_data)
        pil_image = Image.open(io.BytesIO(image_bytes))

        start_time = time.time() * 1000
        results = image_classification.classify(
            pil_image, image_type=image_type, confidence=confidence
        )
        print(f"\nInference: {results}")
        diff = time.time() * 1000 - start_time
        print(f"Latency: {diff:.2f} ms")
        if results is None:
            ui.send_message('classification_error',
                            {'error': 'No results returned'})
            return

        response = {
            'success': True,
            'results': results,
            'processing_time': f"{diff:.2f} ms"
        }
        ui.send_message('classification_result', response)

    except Exception as e:
        ui.send_message('classification_error', {'error': str(e)})


print_model_info(image_classification)
ui = WebUI()
ui.on_message('classify_image', on_classify_image)

App.run()
Run the app:
arduino-app-cli app start .
In a second terminal, go to the project folder and follow the logs:
cd ~/ArduinoApps/my-classifier-bricks
arduino-app-cli app logs . --follow
 
The logs show that the custom model takes 160×160 images and that its labels are:
labels: ['background', 'periquito', 'robot']
The latency of this model is around 444 ms, a little over 2 FPS.

For a faster model, train with smaller images (such as 96×96) or a smaller network, for example with an alpha of 0.35.

title: Image Classification
text:
This path runs live webcam capture and continuous classification, and the next section adds Bridge communication with the MCU.


In Arduino App Lab’s My Apps, click the Create new app button in the upper right.
 
Name it, for example, Image Classification on Camera.



Go to Bricks and click Add Brick.
 
In the list of available Bricks, scroll down to Video Image Classification and click Add brick.
 
As in Path A, once the Brick is installed, go to the AI Models tab and select the UNO-Q Image Classification model deployed earlier.
 
Selecting the model creates app.yaml automatically, pointing to the custom model:
name: Image Classification on Camera
description: ""
ports: []
bricks:
- arduino:video_image_classification:
    model: ei-model-947334-1
icon: 😀



The new app’s python/main.py is a generic template that must be written for this model. The key piece is the VideoImageClassification class:
class VideoImageClassification(camera: BaseCamera | None,
                               confidence: float,
                               debounce_sec: float)
This module classifies images on a live video stream with the selected model, and it calls registered actions in real time when classes are detected. Its parameters are:

camera (BaseCamera): the camera that captures the video. If None, a default camera is initialized.
confidence (float): the minimum confidence for a classification to count. The default is 0.3.
debounce_sec (float): the minimum time, in seconds, between consecutive detections of the same class, to avoid repeated triggers. The default is 0.

The complete code:
from arduino.app_utils import App
from arduino.app_bricks.video_imageclassification import (
    VideoImageClassification,
)

# Create a classification stream with a confidence threshold of 0.5
classification_stream = VideoImageClassification(confidence=0.5)

# Callback when "periquito" is detected
def periquito_detected():
    print("Detected periquito!")

# Callback when "robot" is detected
def robot_detected():
    print("Detected robot!")

# Subscribe to specific labels
classification_stream.on_detect("periquito", periquito_detected)
classification_stream.on_detect("robot", robot_detected)

# Optional: callback for all classifications (useful for debugging)
def all_detected(results):
    # results maps each label to its confidence,
    # for example {"periquito": 0.85}
    print("Classification results:", results)

classification_stream.on_detect_all(all_detected)

# Run the app
App.run()
Run the app:
cd ~/ArduinoApps/image-classification-on-camera
arduino-app-cli app start .
In a second terminal, go to the project folder and follow the logs:
cd ~/ArduinoApps/image-classification-on-camera
arduino-app-cli app logs . --follow

The logs from the previous sections show the inference performance:

Path A (ImageClassification Brick, 160×160, MobileNetV2 1.0): about 444 ms per image (about 2 FPS).
Path B (VideoImageClassification Brick, live camera): depends on the model, typically faster thanks to the continuous pipeline.

The ~444 ms for MobileNetV2 1.0 at 160×160 is the Path A measurement above. The other latencies and the relative accuracy labels are starting points for the trade-off, not results from this board: measure each candidate with the Path A script before choosing one.

For faster inference (for example, for more responsive LED feedback), retrain with a smaller model such as MobileNetV2 0.35 at 96×96, and test several configurations to find the best balance for the project.







Table 5: The two deployment paths compared.

The two latencies come from very different models and input sizes (MobileNetV2 0.1 at 96×96 is far smaller than MobileNetV2 1.0 at 160×160), so they show the range of each platform, not a head-to-head result. Accuracy is left out on purpose: the two labs used different datasets and splits, so their accuracy figures are not comparable. Exercise 5 below sets up a fair comparison.
The UNO Q power figure is a practical estimate of the total for live classification with the USB camera and hub:

UNO Q board: about 2 to 3.5 W while the CPU is busy.
USB camera: about 0.5 to 1.25 W.
Powered hub: about 0.5 to 1 W.
Total: about 3 to 6 W from the wall (5 V, about 0.6 to 1.2 A) for a typical setup with one camera and one hub.


The UNO Q runs larger, more accurate models but uses much more power. The Nicla Vision suits battery-powered, always-on applications; the UNO Q excels when accuracy matters and the AI result must drive real-time hardware actions.

title: Image Classification
text:
Add a fourth class. Collect images of a new object, retrain the model in Edge Impulse, redeploy it to the UNO Q, and update the Python code and the Arduino sketch. How does adding more classes affect accuracy?
Experiment with model size. Train the same dataset with MobileNetV2 0.1 (96×96) and MobileNetV2 1.0 (160×160). Deploy both to the UNO Q and compare inference time, accuracy, and LED responsiveness in a table.
Log to CSV. Modify main.py to log each detection event (timestamp and label) to a CSV file on the UNO Q. After 5 minutes, download the CSV and plot the detection frequency per class.
Design new LED matrix icons. Draw your own 8×13 patterns for each class with the Arduino LED Matrix Editor and display them on the UNO Q’s matrix.
Cross-platform comparison. With a Nicla Vision, deploy a 96×96 MobileNetV2 0.1 model to both platforms. Compare inference time, accuracy, power consumption, and development workflow.
Debounce tuning. Experiment with the debounce_sec parameter in VideoImageClassification(confidence=0.5, debounce_sec=1.0). How does a longer debounce time affect the responsiveness and stability of the LED feedback?

title: Image Classification
text:
This lab went through three levels of image classification on the Arduino UNO Q:

Part 1: the pre-installed static image classifier (ImageClassification Brick and WebUI), with images uploaded through a browser and results shown in the web interface.
Path A: the custom model deployed through the same Brick, still with static uploads, but classifying the lab’s own robot, periquito, and background classes.
Path B: live camera classification with the VideoImageClassification Brick, with detection callbacks driving the LED matrix on the MCU over Bridge RPC.

Key takeaways:

The Edge Impulse → App Lab → UNO Q pipeline works. Collect data, train in Edge Impulse Studio, deploy to App Lab, and run, all guided through the UI.
Two Bricks, two modes. The ImageClassification Brick handles static images (good for testing), and the VideoImageClassification Brick handles live camera streams (essential for real applications).
The dual-brain architecture adds value. Python handles the camera and ML inference on the MPU, while the Arduino sketch on the MCU provides real-time control of the LED matrix, LEDs, servos, or buzzers. Bridge RPC connects the two.
Model selection matters. The UNO Q runs larger, more accurate models than any MCU, but there is always a trade-off between accuracy and inference speed. Test several configurations to find the best balance for each project.

The next UNO Q lab extends these skills to object detection, which finds not just what is in the image but also where it is, opening the door to tracking, counting, and spatial awareness.

title: Setup
text:
DALL·E 3 Prompt: Illustration reminiscent of a 1950s cartoon where the Arduino NICLA VISION board, equipped with various sensors including a camera, is the focal point on an old-fashioned desk. In the background, a computer screen with rounded edges displays the Arduino IDE. The code is related to LED configurations and machine learning voice command detection. Outputs on the Serial Monitor explicitly display the words ‘yes’ and ‘no’.




The Arduino Nicla Vision (sometimes called NiclaV) is a development board that includes two processors that can run tasks in parallel. It is part of a family of development boards with the same form factor but designed for specific tasks, such as the Nicla Sense ME and the Nicla Voice. The Niclas can efficiently run processes created with TensorFlow Lite. For example, one of the cores of the NiclaV runs a computer vision algorithm on the fly (inference). At the same time, the other executes low-level operations like controlling a motor and communicating or acting as a user interface. The onboard wireless module allows the simultaneous management of WiFi and Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) connectivity.
 





The central processor is the dual-core STM32H747, including a Cortex M7 at 480 MHz and a Cortex M4 at 240 MHz. The two cores communicate via a Remote Procedure Call mechanism that allows calling functions on the other processor. Both processors share all the on-chip peripherals and can run:

Arduino sketches on top of the Arm Mbed OS
Native Mbed applications
MicroPython / JavaScript via an interpreter
TensorFlow Lite

 



Memory is a central constraint for embedded machine learning projects. The NiclaV board can host up to 16 MB of QSPI Flash for storage. However, machine learning inference uses the MCU SRAM, which is only 1 MB on the STM32H747 and is shared by both processors. This MCU also has incorporated 2 MB of FLASH, mainly for code storage.




Camera: A GC2145 2 MP Color CMOS Camera.
Microphone: The MP34DT05 is an ultra-compact, low-power, omnidirectional, digital MEMS microphone built with a capacitive sensing element and the IC interface.
6-Axis IMU: 3D gyroscope and 3D accelerometer data from the LSM6DSOX 6-axis IMU.
Time of Flight Sensor: The VL53L1CBV0FY Time-of-Flight sensor adds accurate and low-power-ranging capabilities to Nicla Vision. The invisible near-infrared VCSEL laser (including the analog driver) is encapsulated with receiving optics in an all-in-one small module below the camera.





Start connecting the board (micro USB) to your computer:
 
Install the Mbed OS core for Nicla boards in the Arduino IDE. Having the IDE open, navigate to Tools > Board > Board Manager, look for Arduino Nicla Vision on the search window, and install the board.
 
Next, go to Tools > Board > Arduino Mbed OS Nicla Boards and select Arduino Nicla Vision. Having your board connected to the USB, you should see the Nicla on Port and select it.

Open the Blink sketch on Examples/Basic and run it using the IDE Upload button. You should see the Built-in LED (green RGB) blinking, which means the Nicla board is correctly installed and functional.



On Arduino IDE, go to Examples > PDM > PDMSerialPlotter, open it, and run the sketch. Open the Plotter and see the audio representation from the microphone:
 

Vary the frequency of the sound you generate and confirm that the mic is working correctly.




Before testing the IMU, it will be necessary to install the LSM6DSOX library. To do so, go to Library Manager and look for LSM6DSOX. Install the library provided by Arduino:
 
Next, go to Examples > Arduino_LSM6DSOX > SimpleAccelerometer and run the accelerometer test (you can also run Gyro and board temperature):
 



As we did with IMU, installing the VL53L1X ToF library is necessary. To do that, go to Library Manager and look for VL53L1X. Install the library provided by Pololu:
 
Next, run the sketch proximity_detection.ino:
 
On the Serial Monitor, you will see the distance from the camera to an object in front of it (max of 4 m).
 



We can also test the camera using, for example, the code provided on Examples > Camera > CameraCaptureRawBytes. We cannot see the image directly, but we can get the raw image data generated by the camera.
We can use the Web Serial Camera (API) to see the image generated by the camera. This web application streams the camera image over Web Serial from camera-equipped Arduino boards.
The Web Serial Camera example shows you how to send image data over the wire from your Arduino board and how to unpack the data in JavaScript for rendering. In addition, in the source code of the web application, we can find some example image filters that show us how to manipulate pixel data to achieve visual effects.
The Arduino sketch (CameraCaptureWebSerial) for sending the camera image data can be found here and is also directly available from the “Examples→Camera” menu in the Arduino IDE when selecting the Nicla board.
The web application for displaying the camera image can be accessed here. We may also look at [this tutorial, which explains the setup in more detail.
 




OpenMV IDE is the integrated development environment for OpenMV cameras, which are similar to the Nicla Vision. It includes a text editor, debug terminal, and frame buffer viewer with a histogram display. We will use MicroPython to program the camera.
Go to the OpenMV IDE page, download the correct version for your Operating System, and follow the instructions for its installation on your computer.
 
The IDE should open, defaulting to the helloworld_1.py code on its Code Area. If not, you can open it from Files > Examples > HelloWord > helloword.py
 
Any messages sent through a serial connection (using print() or error messages) will be displayed on the Serial Terminal during run time. The image captured by a camera will be displayed in the Camera Viewer Area (or Frame Buffer) and in the Histogram area, immediately below the Camera Viewer.


Before connecting the Nicla to the OpenMV IDE, ensure you have the latest bootloader version. Go to your Arduino IDE, select the Nicla board, and open the sketch on Examples > STM_32H747_System STM32H747_manageBootloader. Upload the code to your board. The Serial Monitor will guide you.



After updating the bootloader, put the Nicla Vision in bootloader mode by double-pressing the reset button on the board. The built-in green LED will start fading in and out. Now return to the OpenMV IDE and click on the connect icon (Left ToolBar):
 
A pop-up will tell you that a board in DFU mode was detected and ask how you would like to proceed. First, select Install the latest release firmware (vX.Y.Z). This action will install the latest OpenMV firmware on the Nicla Vision.
 
You can leave the option Erase internal file system unselected and click [OK].
Nicla’s green LED will start flashing while the OpenMV firmware is uploaded to the board, and a terminal window will then open, showing the flashing progress.
 
Wait until the green LED stops flashing and fading. When the process ends, you will see a message saying, “DFU firmware update complete!”. Press [OK].
 
A green play button appears when the Nicla Vison connects to the Tool Bar.
 
A drive named “NO NAME” will appear on your computer.
 
Every time you press the [RESET] button on the board, the main.py script stored on it automatically executes. You can load the main.py code on the IDE (File > Open File...).
 

This code is the “Blink” code, confirming that the HW is OK.




To test the camera, run helloword_1.py. For that, select the script on File > Examples > HelloWorld > helloword.py,
When clicking the green play button, the MicroPython script (helloworld.py) on the Code Area will be uploaded and run on the Nicla Vision. On-Camera Viewer, you will start to see the video streaming. The Serial Monitor will show us the FPS (Frames per second), which should be around 27fps.
 
Here is the helloworld.py script:
import sensor, time

sensor.reset()                      # Reset and initialize
                                    # the sensor.
sensor.set_pixformat(sensor.RGB565) # Set pixel format to RGB565
                                    # (or GRAYSCALE)
sensor.set_framesize(sensor.QVGA)   # Set frame size to
                                    # QVGA (320x240)
sensor.skip_frames(time = 2000)     # Wait for settings take
                                    # effect.
clock = time.clock()                # Create a clock object
                                    # to track the FPS.

while(True):
    clock.tick()                    # Update the FPS clock.
    img = sensor.snapshot()         # Take a picture and return
                                    # the image.
    print(clock.fps())
In GitHub, you can find the Python scripts used here.
The code can be split into two parts:

Setup: Where the libraries are imported, initialized and the variables are defined and initiated.
Loop: (while loop) part of the code that runs continually. The image (img variable) is captured (one frame). Each of those frames can be used for inference in Machine Learning Applications.

To interrupt the program execution, press the red [X] button.

Note: OpenMV Cam runs about half as fast when connected to the IDE. The FPS should increase once disconnected.

In the GitHub, You can find other Python scripts. Try to test the onboard sensors.




We will need the Edge Impulse Studio later in other labs. Edge Impulse is a development platform for machine learning on edge devices.
Edge Impulse officially supports the Nicla Vision. To start, create a new project on the Studio and connect the Nicla to it. For that, follow the steps:

Download the Arduino CLI for your specific computer architecture (OS)
Download the most updated EI Firmware.
Unzip both files and place all the files in the same folder.
Put the Nicla-Vision on Boot Mode, pressing the reset button twice.
Run the uploader (EI FW) corresponding to your OS:

 

Executing the specific batch code for your OS will upload the binary arduino-nicla-vision.bin to your board.


Using Chrome, WebUSB can be used to connect the Nicla to the EI Studio. The EI CLI is not needed.

Go to your project on the Studio, and on the Data Acquisition tab, select WebUSB (1). A window will pop up; choose the option that shows that the Nicla is paired (2) and press [Connect] (3).
 
You can choose which sensor data to pick in the Collect Data section on the Data Acquisition tab.
 
For example. IMU data (inertial):
 
Or Image (Camera):
 
You can also test an external sensor connected to the ADC (Nicla pin 0) and the other onboard sensors, such as the built-in microphone, the ToF (Proximity) or a combination of sensors (fusion).



During prototyping, it is often necessary to experiment with external sensors and devices. A useful expansion for the Nicla is the Arduino MKR Connector Carrier (Grove compatible).
The shield has 14 Grove connectors: five single analog inputs (A0-A5), one double analog input (A5/A6), five single digital I/Os (D0-D4), one double digital I/O (D5/D6), one I2C (TWI), and one UART (Serial). All connectors are 5V compatible.

Note that all 17 Nicla Vision pins will be connected to the Shield Groves, but some Grove connections remain disconnected.

 
This shield is MKR compatible and can be used with the Nicla Vision and Portenta.
 
For example, suppose that on a TinyML project, you want to send inference results using a LoRaWAN device and add information about local luminosity. Often, with offline operations, a local low-power display such as an OLED is advised. This setup can be seen here:

title: Setup
text: The Arduino Nicla Vision (sometimes called NiclaV) is a development board that includes two processors that can run tasks in parallel. It is part of a family of development boards with the same form factor but designed for specific tasks, such as the Nicla Sense ME and the Nicla Voice. The Niclas can efficiently run processes created with TensorFlow Lite. For example, one of the cores of the NiclaV runs a computer vision algorithm on the fly (inference). At the same time, the other executes low-level operations like controlling a motor and communicating or acting as a user interface. The onboard wireless module allows the simultaneous management of WiFi and Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) connectivity.

title: Setup
text:
The central processor is the dual-core STM32H747, including a Cortex M7 at 480 MHz and a Cortex M4 at 240 MHz. The two cores communicate via a Remote Procedure Call mechanism that allows calling functions on the other processor. Both processors share all the on-chip peripherals and can run:

Arduino sketches on top of the Arm Mbed OS
Native Mbed applications
MicroPython / JavaScript via an interpreter
TensorFlow Lite

 



Memory is a central constraint for embedded machine learning projects. The NiclaV board can host up to 16 MB of QSPI Flash for storage. However, machine learning inference uses the MCU SRAM, which is only 1 MB on the STM32H747 and is shared by both processors. This MCU also has incorporated 2 MB of FLASH, mainly for code storage.




Camera: A GC2145 2 MP Color CMOS Camera.
Microphone: The MP34DT05 is an ultra-compact, low-power, omnidirectional, digital MEMS microphone built with a capacitive sensing element and the IC interface.
6-Axis IMU: 3D gyroscope and 3D accelerometer data from the LSM6DSOX 6-axis IMU.
Time of Flight Sensor: The VL53L1CBV0FY Time-of-Flight sensor adds accurate and low-power-ranging capabilities to Nicla Vision. The invisible near-infrared VCSEL laser (including the analog driver) is encapsulated with receiving optics in an all-in-one small module below the camera.

title: Setup
text:
Start connecting the board (micro USB) to your computer:
 
Install the Mbed OS core for Nicla boards in the Arduino IDE. Having the IDE open, navigate to Tools > Board > Board Manager, look for Arduino Nicla Vision on the search window, and install the board.
 
Next, go to Tools > Board > Arduino Mbed OS Nicla Boards and select Arduino Nicla Vision. Having your board connected to the USB, you should see the Nicla on Port and select it.

Open the Blink sketch on Examples/Basic and run it using the IDE Upload button. You should see the Built-in LED (green RGB) blinking, which means the Nicla board is correctly installed and functional.



On Arduino IDE, go to Examples > PDM > PDMSerialPlotter, open it, and run the sketch. Open the Plotter and see the audio representation from the microphone:
 

Vary the frequency of the sound you generate and confirm that the mic is working correctly.




Before testing the IMU, it will be necessary to install the LSM6DSOX library. To do so, go to Library Manager and look for LSM6DSOX. Install the library provided by Arduino:
 
Next, go to Examples > Arduino_LSM6DSOX > SimpleAccelerometer and run the accelerometer test (you can also run Gyro and board temperature):
 



As we did with IMU, installing the VL53L1X ToF library is necessary. To do that, go to Library Manager and look for VL53L1X. Install the library provided by Pololu:
 
Next, run the sketch proximity_detection.ino:
 
On the Serial Monitor, you will see the distance from the camera to an object in front of it (max of 4 m).
 



We can also test the camera using, for example, the code provided on Examples > Camera > CameraCaptureRawBytes. We cannot see the image directly, but we can get the raw image data generated by the camera.
We can use the Web Serial Camera (API) to see the image generated by the camera. This web application streams the camera image over Web Serial from camera-equipped Arduino boards.
The Web Serial Camera example shows you how to send image data over the wire from your Arduino board and how to unpack the data in JavaScript for rendering. In addition, in the source code of the web application, we can find some example image filters that show us how to manipulate pixel data to achieve visual effects.
The Arduino sketch (CameraCaptureWebSerial) for sending the camera image data can be found here and is also directly available from the “Examples→Camera” menu in the Arduino IDE when selecting the Nicla board.
The web application for displaying the camera image can be accessed here. We may also look at [this tutorial, which explains the setup in more detail.

title: Setup
text:
OpenMV IDE is the integrated development environment for OpenMV cameras, which are similar to the Nicla Vision. It includes a text editor, debug terminal, and frame buffer viewer with a histogram display. We will use MicroPython to program the camera.
Go to the OpenMV IDE page, download the correct version for your Operating System, and follow the instructions for its installation on your computer.
 
The IDE should open, defaulting to the helloworld_1.py code on its Code Area. If not, you can open it from Files > Examples > HelloWord > helloword.py
 
Any messages sent through a serial connection (using print() or error messages) will be displayed on the Serial Terminal during run time. The image captured by a camera will be displayed in the Camera Viewer Area (or Frame Buffer) and in the Histogram area, immediately below the Camera Viewer.


Before connecting the Nicla to the OpenMV IDE, ensure you have the latest bootloader version. Go to your Arduino IDE, select the Nicla board, and open the sketch on Examples > STM_32H747_System STM32H747_manageBootloader. Upload the code to your board. The Serial Monitor will guide you.



After updating the bootloader, put the Nicla Vision in bootloader mode by double-pressing the reset button on the board. The built-in green LED will start fading in and out. Now return to the OpenMV IDE and click on the connect icon (Left ToolBar):
 
A pop-up will tell you that a board in DFU mode was detected and ask how you would like to proceed. First, select Install the latest release firmware (vX.Y.Z). This action will install the latest OpenMV firmware on the Nicla Vision.
 
You can leave the option Erase internal file system unselected and click [OK].
Nicla’s green LED will start flashing while the OpenMV firmware is uploaded to the board, and a terminal window will then open, showing the flashing progress.
 
Wait until the green LED stops flashing and fading. When the process ends, you will see a message saying, “DFU firmware update complete!”. Press [OK].
 
A green play button appears when the Nicla Vison connects to the Tool Bar.
 
A drive named “NO NAME” will appear on your computer.
 
Every time you press the [RESET] button on the board, the main.py script stored on it automatically executes. You can load the main.py code on the IDE (File > Open File...).
 

This code is the “Blink” code, confirming that the HW is OK.




To test the camera, run helloword_1.py. For that, select the script on File > Examples > HelloWorld > helloword.py,
When clicking the green play button, the MicroPython script (helloworld.py) on the Code Area will be uploaded and run on the Nicla Vision. On-Camera Viewer, you will start to see the video streaming. The Serial Monitor will show us the FPS (Frames per second), which should be around 27fps.
 
Here is the helloworld.py script:
import sensor, time

sensor.reset()                      # Reset and initialize
                                    # the sensor.
sensor.set_pixformat(sensor.RGB565) # Set pixel format to RGB565
                                    # (or GRAYSCALE)
sensor.set_framesize(sensor.QVGA)   # Set frame size to
                                    # QVGA (320x240)
sensor.skip_frames(time = 2000)     # Wait for settings take
                                    # effect.
clock = time.clock()                # Create a clock object
                                    # to track the FPS.

while(True):
    clock.tick()                    # Update the FPS clock.
    img = sensor.snapshot()         # Take a picture and return
                                    # the image.
    print(clock.fps())
In GitHub, you can find the Python scripts used here.
The code can be split into two parts:

Setup: Where the libraries are imported, initialized and the variables are defined and initiated.
Loop: (while loop) part of the code that runs continually. The image (img variable) is captured (one frame). Each of those frames can be used for inference in Machine Learning Applications.

To interrupt the program execution, press the red [X] button.

Note: OpenMV Cam runs about half as fast when connected to the IDE. The FPS should increase once disconnected.

In the GitHub, You can find other Python scripts. Try to test the onboard sensors.
